Analyzing the relationships between variables in EMA data

A visual, step-by-step guide for psychology researchers who collect intensive longitudinal data.

Work in progress

This document is a work in progress. Some parts are still under construction, in particular the R version of the walkthrough and the tab on investigating heterogeneity with DSEM, and the content of every tab may still change.

In the meantime, for feedback and questions, please contact Yashvin Seetahul at Yashvin.Seetahul@uibk.ac.at.

The current text was written with the help of Claude, an AI model by Anthropic, and the interactive features were programmed with the help of Claude.

Concepts and models

How multilevel regression, multilevel SEM, RI-CLPM, and DSEM represent intensive longitudinal data, what each one estimates, and where they overlap. Using one emotion regulation study throughout, the tab covers within- and between-person effects, person-specific dynamics, measurement error, missing prompts, unequal time intervals, day-level variation, Bayesian estimation in Mplus, and the choice of a model for a given research question.

This guide is about analysis. It assumes that you already know the basics of experience sampling research, such as how to design a study, write the questionnaire items, and prepare the data. We strongly encourage all readers to read The Open Handbook of Experience Sampling Methodology first. Many citations in this guide refer to its chapters.

Myin-Germeys, I., & Kuppens, P. (Eds.). (2026). The open handbook of experience sampling methodology: A step-by-step guide to designing, conducting and analysing ESM studies (3rd ed.). Leuven University Press. https://doi.org/10.11116/9789461666932

The third edition (2026) is the most recent one, and it is open access: the link above leads to a free PDF and EPUB.

Emotion regulation (ER)Positive affect (PA)Negative affect (NA)

Three simulated days for one participant, six prompts per day, generated from the lag matrix in Section 10.3. These three colors identify the three variables in every figure of the guide.

What this document is about

For your researchThis guide follows one example from the first section to the last, so that you can see what each section adds when it is applied to the same data. The example topic is emotion regulation (ER), chosen because it is one of the most widely studied topics in psychology of the past decade and is familiar to most readers. PubMed alone lists more than 18,000 articles with "emotion regulation" in their title or abstract, and the yearly count rose from fewer than 20 in 2000 to about 2,500 in 2025 (PubMed search, October 2026). ER is studied in developmental, social, personality, and clinical psychology and in cognitive and affective neuroscience (Rahaman et al., 2024), and in organizational psychology, for example in research on emotional labor (Grandey, 2000). Our example is simple: 150 adults answer a short smartphone questionnaire six times a day for 30 days, reporting how much they used one regulation strategy, reappraisal, and how much positive affect (PA) and negative affect (NA) they feel (Section 1).

The minimum you need to know about ER. Emotion regulation refers to the processes by which people influence which emotions they have, when they have them, and how they experience and express them (Gross, 1998). People do this with cognitive strategies, such as reappraisal (rethinking what a situation means, for example "this criticism is useful feedback"), and with behavioral strategies, such as seeking support or leaving a situation, most often to reduce negative affect or increase positive affect. Whether a strategy helps depends on the person and the situation. In daily life, regulation and emotion also influence each other: distress tends to trigger regulation, and regulation may then reduce distress. Because this two-way relationship unfolds over time, ER is a useful example for the models in this guide.

Imagine that you repeatedly measure emotion regulation (ER), positive affect (PA), and negative affect (NA) in everyday life. You want to know whether using an emotion regulation strategy is associated with people's emotions, whether it predicts their emotions later, whether people differ in these relationships, and whether emotions and regulation influence one another over time.

Several methods could be relevant:

  • Multilevel modeling (MLM), including mixed-effects regression using R's lmer().
  • Multilevel structural equation modeling (MSEM).
  • Random-intercept cross-lagged panel modeling (RI-CLPM).
  • Dynamic structural equation modeling (DSEM).

The capabilities of these four methods overlap more than their names suggest. An appropriately specified mixed model can include lagged effects, an MSEM can be dynamic, and a simple RI-CLPM can express almost the same within-person process as a constrained DSEM. For this reason, the guide compares the methods by what each statistical model estimates.

Five distinctions organize the guide:

  1. Contemporaneous associations versus temporal dependencies: Are two variables associated at the same occasion, or does an earlier observation help predict a later one?
  2. Within-person versus between-person differences: Are we comparing a person with themselves over time, or comparing different people?
  3. Common versus person-specific temporal relationships: Must an ER-NA relationship have the same coefficient for everyone, or can that coefficient vary between individuals?
  4. Separate equations versus a dynamic system: Do we model NA alone, or the jointly evolving relationships among ER, PA, and NA?
  5. Measurement error and temporal covariance: How do inaccurate measures, correlated shocks, and serial dependence influence what the coefficients mean and how uncertain we are about them?

Time is a sixth, practical concern throughout the guide. EMA prompts are not equally spaced (there is a long gap every night), and moments are nested within days. Section 14 treats unequal spacing, and Section 15 introduces three-level DSEM, which became available in Mplus 9 (2025) and was extended in Mplus 9.1 (2026). Section 13 collects practical advice for estimating DSEM in the current version of Mplus. Section 10.8 explains, through the Kalman filter, how DSEM handles missed and unevenly spaced prompts. A second tab at the top of this page, the walkthrough tab, presents the supplementary materials of the DSEM chapter by Hamaker et al. (2023) in simplified form, translated into our emotion regulation example. Many explanations also draw on chapters of The Open Handbook of Experience Sampling Methodology (Myin-Germeys & Kuppens, 2026). ESM (experience sampling method) is another name for EMA, and the two terms are used largely interchangeably.

The discussion gradually introduces formal notation. All numerical observations and coefficient estimates are invented for teaching purposes and are not empirical findings. Where the guide reports a calculation or a simulation, the numbers were computed, and the assumptions behind them are stated next to them.

1Our hypothetical emotion regulation study

For your researchEvery example in the guide uses this study: 150 people answering six short questionnaires a day for 30 days about reappraisal, PA, and NA.

We recruit 150 participants and assess them six times a day for 30 days using ecological momentary assessment (EMA). Assuming complete participation, that yields:

6×30=180 assessments per person.

In plain EnglishSix questionnaires a day for 30 days gives each person up to 180 answers.

Across the sample, that is 27,000 person-occasion records. Real studies will usually have some missing prompts. In two meta-analyses, participants answered about 79% of prompts on average (Cloos et al., 2026, p. 63), so a realistic expectation for our design is roughly 140 answered prompts per person.

Strictly speaking, these data have three levels: prompts are nested within days, and days are nested within persons. Most of this guide follows common practice and treats the data as two-level (occasions within persons). Section 15 explains what is lost when the day level is ignored and how three-level DSEM handles it.

EMA data compared with other research designs

For your researchAn EMA design can show what a one-time survey cannot. Because you measure the same people many times, you can follow each person's NA as it rises and falls around their own usual level, and check whether reappraisal tends to come before those changes.

All psychological data can be represented as a box with three sides, persons, variables, and occasions, known as Cattell's data box (Hamaker et al., 2017). Each research design takes a different slice of it:

  • A cross-sectional study measures many persons once. It is a thin slice: many persons, one occasion.
  • A panel study measures many persons a few times, for example four waves over a year.
  • A time-series (N = 1) study measures one person very many times.
  • An intensive longitudinal study, such as our EMA study, measures many persons many times. It fills most of the box.

Time-series analysis can be described as "looking at the movie" (Hamaker et al., 2017). A cross-sectional study gives one snapshot of many people. Many occasions per person show how each person's states change from one moment to the next. Only designs with many occasions per person can show within-person dynamics directly: to study a process within individuals, "we need to observe the process as it is taking place" (Hamaker, 2012, p. 4 of the preprint).

At every occasion, participants report:

  • ER: How much they engaged in cognitive reappraisal, a strategy involving changing how they interpret a situation.
  • PA: How much positive affect they are experiencing.
  • NA: How much negative affect they are experiencing.

To simplify the example, all scores range from 0 to 100. Here are illustrative observations:

Person Measurement occasion ER PA NA
Jayce Day 1, 10 a.m. 20 30 80
Jayce Day 1, noon 70 35 75
Jayce Day 1, 2 p.m. 80 65 40
Jayce Day 1, 4 p.m. 40 75 25
Jayce Day 1, 6 p.m. 10 70 30
Vi Day 1, 10 a.m. 60 70 20
Vi Day 1, noon 30 65 30
Vi Day 1, 2 p.m. 70 75 25
Vi Day 1, 4 p.m. 50 80 15

The questions we might investigate include:

  1. At moments when people use more reappraisal, do they also have less NA or more PA?
  2. Does greater-than-usual reappraisal predict lower NA two hours later?
  3. Is NA persistent over time? Does PA predict later ER use, or does NA trigger more ER use?
  4. Do the temporal relationships differ across people?
  5. Can we describe ER, PA, and NA as an interacting system rather than isolated outcomes?

Before choosing software or a model family, we need to specify what each question is estimating.

A brief notation guide

For your researchThis list defines the symbols used in the equations, and you can return to it whenever a symbol is unclear. Most equations are built from two quantities: a person's usual level (their long-run average) and a moment's distance from that usual level.

Throughout:

  • i identifies a person: Jayce, Vi, and so forth.
  • t identifies a measurement occasion for that person.
  • ERit​ is person i's ER score at occasion t.
  • NAi,t−1​ is that person's NA score at the preceding occasion.
  • μER,i​ is person i's true long-run mean of ER. It is a latent (unobserved) quantity: the value that person's average would approach if we could observe them indefinitely under the same conditions.
  • A bar, as in ERi​, denotes the observed average across that person's occasions. It is an estimate of μER,i​, not the same thing.
  • A superscript W, as in ERitW​=ERit​−μER,i​, denotes the within-person deviation from the true mean. This is the conceptual quantity used in most equations in this guide.
  • A superscript c, as in ERitc​=ERit​−ERi​, denotes the observed person-mean-centered score: the deviation from the observed average. It is what we compute ourselves before running lmer(), and it serves as an estimate of ERitW​.
  • ε generally denotes variation that remains unexplained after accounting for variables in an equation. Its exact meaning depends on the model.

When W and c differ. With many occasions per person, the two are nearly identical. With few occasions, or in models that contain lagged outcomes, the difference produces bias (Sections 3.5 and 5.4). MSEM and DSEM can work with W directly by treating the person mean as a latent variable, a technique called latent centering (or latent mean centering).

The expression "ER → subsequent NA" will mean a lagged predictive coefficient. It does not, by itself, mean that ER causes NA to change.

2First distinction: Contemporaneous associations versus temporal dependencies

For your researchThis section helps you decide which kind of question you are asking: whether reappraisal and NA go together at the same prompt, or whether reappraisal at one prompt predicts NA at the next one. The two questions can have different answers without either analysis being wrong.

The two kinds of question target two different estimands.

2.1What is an estimand?

For your researchBefore you run any model, write down in one sentence the exact number you want to learn, for example "how much lower is NA two hours after a person reappraises more than usual?" That sentence is your estimand, and it tells you which model fits.

An estimand is the exact quantity that a statistical analysis is trying to learn about. It is the target of inference, not the particular numerical estimate produced by our sample.

For example, we might want to estimate:

  • The association between ER and NA at the same measurement occasion, within people.
  • The association between ER at one occasion and NA at the next occasion, controlling for previous NA.

Both involve ER and NA, but they are not the same estimand. Consequently, the models could legitimately produce different answers.

2.2Contemporaneous association: "What happens at the same time?"

For your researchUse this kind of analysis when your question is "at prompts where people reappraise more than usual, is their NA lower at that same prompt?" It describes what goes together. It cannot tell you whether reappraisal lowered NA or whether high NA led people to reappraise.

Contemporaneous means at the same occasion. It does not imply that the underlying experiences occurred at the same instant, because the items of one EMA prompt may ask about different recall windows.

Same prompt does not always mean same moment. When one item asks about "right now" (as NA usually does) and another asks about the time "since the last prompt" (as ER items often do), their association at the same prompt is mostly prospective: it links reappraisal during the preceding interval to NA at the moment of the prompt (Eisele et al., 2026, pp. 79-80). For example, an event recalled from a roughly 90-minute interval happened, on average, about 45 minutes before the affect rating if it was equally likely to occur at any point in the interval (Viechtbauer, 2026b, pp. 180-181). The same arithmetic applies to reappraisal. Section 14.4 returns to this design issue.

Suppose Jayce reports the following at 2 p.m.:

  • ER = 80.
  • NA = 40.

An analysis of contemporaneous association addresses this question:

On occasions when Jayce reports more ER than is usual for him, does he also tend to report more or less NA than is usual for him?

A simplified regression would be:

NAitW​=βW​ERitW​+εit​.

In plain EnglishHow far a person's NA is from their usual level at this prompt is predicted from how far their reappraisal is from their usual level at the same prompt. The number βW​ says how much NA differs, on average, per extra point of reappraisal at that prompt. The term ε is the part of NA at that prompt that reappraisal does not account for.

If βW​=−0.20, a 10-point higher-than-usual ER score is associated with an expected 2-point lower NA score at that same occasion (assuming these are unstandardized coefficients on the original scales).

What we have not established: whether ER preceded NA, NA preceded ER, the two evolved together, or a third event influenced both. Perhaps Jayce used reappraisal because he was distressed. Perhaps he used it after his distress had started declining. The contemporaneous coefficient cannot resolve that ordering.

Contemporaneous associations can also be conditional. For instance, a same-occasion ER-NA coefficient adjusted for PA is different from the unadjusted same-occasion correlation. Always state what the association is conditional on, that is, which other variables are held constant.

2.3Temporal dependency: "Does what happened earlier predict what happens later?"

For your researchUse this when your question is "does reappraising more than usual predict lower NA at the next prompt, beyond what the person's earlier NA already predicts?" In an observational EMA study, this is the most direct evidence available about which comes first.

Temporal means involving time. A dependency means that the distribution or expected value of a later observation depends statistically on earlier information.

Suppose we ask:

When Jayce uses more ER than usual at 2 p.m., is his NA at 4 p.m. lower than we would predict from his affective state at 2 p.m.?

A simple model is:

NAitW​=ϕNAi,t−1W​+βERi,t−1W​+εit​.

In plain EnglishA person's NA (relative to their usual level) at this prompt is predicted by two things from the previous prompt: their NA then, weighted by ϕ (the carry-over), and their reappraisal then, weighted by β. The term ε is the new part that these two earlier scores do not predict.

It contains two kinds of temporal coefficients:

  • ϕ: an autoregressive coefficient. Does previous NA predict subsequent NA?
  • β: a cross-lagged coefficient. Does previous ER predict subsequent NA?

For illustration, let ϕ=0.70 and β=−0.30. Holding previous NA constant, 10 additional points of ER at the earlier occasion predict 3 points lower NA at the later occasion.

The lagged coefficient is a different estimand from the contemporaneous coefficient. It has a specified direction in time and a specified time horizon.

The lagged model as a model of change. Subtracting NAi,t−1W​ from both sides of the equation gives an equivalent model for the change in NA:

NAitW​−NAi,t−1W​=(ϕ−1)NAi,t−1W​+βERi,t−1W​+εit​.

In plain EnglishThe same model, rewritten to predict how much NA went up or down since the last prompt. The reappraisal weight β stays the same. Only the weight on earlier NA changes, decreasing by exactly 1.

The left side is now a change score, and the coefficient β is numerically identical in both versions. Only the coefficient on prior NA changes, from ϕ to ϕ−1. So the statement "earlier ER predicts change in NA, conditional on earlier NA" describes the lagged model exactly.

An unconditional change-score model is different. It regresses NAit​−NAi,t−1​ on earlier ER without adjusting for prior NA. Algebraically, that model fixes the coefficient on prior NA at exactly 1 instead of estimating it. It targets a different estimand, and the two models can legitimately disagree, which is the logic behind Lord's paradox (Lord, 1967). When a paper says that a variable "predicts change," check which of the two models was fitted.

2.4Why contemporaneous and lagged results can disagree

For your researchPeople may report more reappraisal at the same prompts where their NA is high (for example, because distress prompts regulation), and reappraisal may still predict lower NA at the next prompt. Both findings can hold in the same data, because they answer different questions.

Suppose Jayce tends to use reappraisal during emotionally difficult moments:

  • At the same occasion: More ER accompanies higher NA, because distress prompts strategy use.
  • At the next occasion: More ER predicts lower NA, because the episode may subsequently subside, or because the regulation strategy may help, or for another reason.

It is therefore possible to estimate:

βcontemporaneous​>0,βlagged​<0.

In plain EnglishAt the same prompt, more reappraisal can go with higher NA, while reappraisal at one prompt can predict lower NA at the next prompt.

The two parameters do not contradict each other, because they answer different questions.

Checking the idea against Jayce's first day. The five day-1 prompts in Section 1 were constructed to show this pattern. At noon, Jayce reports ER = 70 together with NA = 75 (regulation deployed under distress), and his NA then falls to 40 and 25. Computing simple correlations on these five prompts:

  • Same-prompt ER-NA correlation: r≈+0.11 (5 pairs).
  • ER at one prompt with NA at the next prompt: r≈−0.77 (4 pairs).

With 5 and 4 pairs, these correlations cannot support any inference, and they are not adjusted for prior NA. They only illustrate the pattern in raw numbers.

A simulated illustration. Consider a person whose within-person deviations follow two rules: (a) ER is deployed in response to current NA (a same-occasion effect of +0.60), and (b) ER at one prompt lowers NA at the next prompt (a lagged effect of −0.35), while NA also persists (ϕ=0.60). In a long simulated series generated from exactly these rules, the same-occasion ER-NA correlation was about +0.63, the unadjusted correlation between earlier ER and later NA was about +0.04, and the lagged ER coefficient adjusted for prior NA was about −0.35, recovering the generating value.

Without adjustment, the lagged association between earlier ER and later NA is close to zero (+0.04), because people use more ER when NA is high, and high NA persists. The negative lagged relationship appears only after conditioning on prior NA. For this reason, the lagged model in Section 2.3 includes NAi,t−1​.

The same lesson in real data. In an example dataset of 328 adults (10 prompts a day for 6 days), the pleasantness of the most important event reported at the previous prompt predicted current positive affect with an average coefficient of 0.08. After the model also included the previous prompt's positive affect and the time of day, the coefficient for the healthy control group was close to zero (−0.004, p=.74) (Viechtbauer, 2026b, pp. 180 and 185-186). In those data, conditioning on the outcome's own past made a lagged association disappear. In our simulation, the same conditioning made a lagged association appear. A lagged coefficient therefore cannot be interpreted without knowing which earlier variables it was adjusted for.

Statisticians call this kind of lagged predictive relationship Granger-type predictability: earlier ER "Granger-predicts" NA if it improves the prediction of NA beyond what earlier NA already provides. In econometrics the same idea is called "Granger causality," but it describes predictability only, not an effect of intervening on ER (Section 17).

2.5A lag is part of the estimand

For your researchWhen you report a lagged effect of reappraisal on NA, always say over what time span it holds (for example, about two hours). With a different prompt schedule, the same underlying process can produce a different number.

"Previous ER predicts later NA" is incomplete without saying how much later. A two-hour association and a 14-hour association need not be the same. A process unfolding over 15 minutes might have disappeared by the next two-hour prompt. The sampling schedule and the lag length are therefore part of the research question. Section 14 shows how much a lag coefficient can change with the length of the interval.

A rule of thumb for design is that the time between prompts should be shorter than the time the process needs to change. Otherwise, for example, a person may fully recover from a stressor between two prompts, and the recovery is never observed (Cloos et al., 2026, p. 70).

Takeaway

Contemporaneous associations characterize co-occurrence at the same occasion. Temporal dependencies characterize relationships between different occasions, often conditional on previous outcomes and other variables. Neither kind of coefficient establishes a causal effect by itself.

3Second distinction: Within-person versus between-person differences

For your researchEMA papers often confuse "people who reappraise a lot" with "moments when a person reappraises more than usual." The answer to your research question depends on which of these two comparisons you mean.

Repeated-measures data contain at least two kinds of variation, and relationships at the two levels can have different signs and meanings.

3.1Between-person differences: "How do people differ from other people?"

For your researchUse this comparison when you want to know whether people who generally reappraise more also generally feel more (or less) NA. It compares people with each other, using each person's average over the whole study.

Imagine that we calculate each participant's average ER and average NA over the full month.

Suppose, for illustration:

Person Mean ER across the month Mean NA across the month
Jayce 65 60
Vi 25 25
Ekko 55 50

These monthly means are computed over all 180 occasions, so they need not resemble the handful of day-1 values shown in Section 1.

A between-person question is:

Do people who generally use more reappraisal also generally experience more negative affect?

In this example, the between-person relationship might be positive. People with more difficult emotional experiences might have more reasons to regulate.

The target is the relationship between people's true mean levels:

Cor(μER,i​,μNA,i​)>0.

In plain EnglishPeople whose true average reappraisal is higher also tend to have a higher true average NA.

The correlation of the observed means, Cor(ERi​,NAi​), estimates this quantity. Because observed means contain sampling error, it tends to be somewhat attenuated, more so when people have few observations (Section 3.5).

The between-person correlation does not describe what happens within Jayce when his ER goes up or down.

3.2Within-person differences: "How does a person differ from their own usual level?"

For your researchUse this comparison when you want to know what happens inside a person: at moments when someone reappraises more than they usually do, is their NA different from their own usual level? Most emotion regulation theories make claims about this within-person comparison.

Now focus only on Jayce. Suppose his mean ER across the month is 65.

  • At one prompt, ER = 80: 15 points above his usual level.
  • At another prompt, ER = 40: 25 points below his usual level.

A within-person question is:

When Jayce reports more ER than is typical for him, does he also report more or less NA than is typical for him?

To construct this deviation using the observed person mean:

ERitc​=ERit​−ERi​.

In plain EnglishEach reappraisal score minus that person's own average. A positive value means more reappraisal than usual for that person, and a negative value means less.

If Jayce's observed mean ER is 65, his ER of 80 becomes ERc=15. This observed deviation is our estimate of the conceptual deviation ERitW​.

Similarly:

NAitc​=NAit​−NAi​.

In plain EnglishThe same for NA: each NA score minus that person's own average NA.

Within-person association concerns how these deviations covary over occasions. Between-person association concerns how people's overall levels covary across individuals.

3.3Why within-person and between-person associations can differ

For your researchThis shows how a study can find that frequent reappraisers have more NA overall, while people tend to feel less NA at moments when they reappraise more than usual. Both findings can be true at the same time, and they mean different things.

It is possible that:

  • Between people: Individuals who use more reappraisal on average also report more NA on average.
  • Within people: At times when an individual uses more reappraisal than usual, they report lower NA than usual, or perhaps lower NA later.

The two findings concern different units of comparison: people versus occasions within people.

Fear and anger provide a hypothetical example. People might rarely feel fear and anger at the very same moment, so the two might be unrelated or even negatively related within persons. Yet it is possible that people who often feel fear also often feel anger, for example because both reflect neuroticism, in which case the two are positively related between persons (Eisele et al., 2026, p. 93).

Inferring a within-person relationship from a between-person one is called the ecological fallacy. The reverse error, inferring a between-person relationship from within-person data, is sometimes called the atomistic fallacy. A coefficient from a regression that mixes both sources of variation can fail to represent either relationship.

3.4Separating the two in a model

For your researchThis gives you a model, and the R code, that estimates the "people" comparison and the "moments" comparison in one analysis, so that neither one contaminates the other.

A common within-between mixed model is:

NAit​=β0​+u0i​+βW​ERitc​+βB​ERi​+εit​.

In plain EnglishNA at a prompt is predicted from three pieces: the person's own baseline (β0​+u0i​), how far their reappraisal at that prompt is from their usual level (weight βW​), and how their usual reappraisal compares with other people's (weight βB​). The term εit​ is what is left over.

Here:

  • βW​ relates occasion-to-occasion ER deviations to NA, for comparisons within people.
  • βB​ relates person-mean ER differences to differences in expected NA between people, subject to the model's covariate and random-effects assumptions.
  • u0i​ lets people have different remaining baseline NA levels after accounting for the predictors.

If we also want the within-person association to vary across people, replace βW​ with βW​+u1i​.

A practical warning about R before any code. NA is a reserved word in R: it is the constant for a missing value. In a formula such as NA ~ ER_cwc, R reads the logical constant NA, not your column, and the call fails. In addition, read.csv() silently renames a column called "NA" to "NA." on import. Use a different name, such as neg_aff, everywhere in code. (The prose of this guide keeps "NA" for negative affect.)

Preparing the variables:

R
library(dplyr)
library(lme4)

ema <- ema |>
  rename(neg_aff = `NA`) |>   # or `NA.` if read.csv() renamed the column
  group_by(id) |>
  mutate(
    ER_pm  = mean(ER, na.rm = TRUE),   # observed person mean
    ER_cwc = ER - ER_pm                # person-mean-centered ER (ER^c)
  ) |>
  ungroup()

The corresponding lmer() specification is:

R
fit_same_time <- lmer(
  neg_aff ~ ER_cwc + ER_pm + (1 + ER_cwc | id),
  data = ema
)

The model separates the ER association into two components and estimates a random intercept and a random within-person ER slope.

The contextual effect: same model, different coefficient. The model above enters person-mean-centered ER together with the person mean. In that parameterization, the coefficient on the person mean is the between-person slope βB​. A second common parameterization enters raw ER together with the person mean:

NAit​=γ0​+u0i​+γ1​ERit​+γ2​ERi​+εit​.

In plain EnglishThe same model, written with raw reappraisal scores instead of deviations. It fits the data exactly as well. Only the meaning of the coefficient on the person's average changes.

Because ERit​=ERitc​+ERi​, the two models are identical, with γ1​=βW​ and γ2​=βB​−βW​. The coefficient γ2​ is called the contextual effect: the expected difference in NA between two people who report the same raw ER at that occasion but whose mean ER differs by one unit. The two parameterizations fit equally well, but the coefficient on the person mean answers a different question in each. Always state which parameterization you used before interpreting that coefficient.

3.5Random intercepts versus within-person centering

For your researchThis explains why adding a random intercept is not enough to isolate the within-person link between reappraisal and NA, and shows that with many prompts per person the practical damage is small. Centering each predictor on the person's own mean remains the safe default.

A random intercept means that people can have different predicted baseline or mean levels. For example, Jayce can have generally higher NA than Vi.

A random intercept alone does not guarantee that the coefficient for raw, uncentered ER cleanly represents a within-person association. In a random-intercept model with raw ER, the fixed slope is a weighted blend of the within-person and between-person slopes. To target within-person and between-person ER associations separately, include an appropriate decomposition or use an equivalent multilevel latent-variable formulation.

Also, observed person means are estimates, not error-free knowledge of the person's underlying long-run mean. With few observations, substantial missingness, trends, or strong temporal persistence, these estimates may be noisy. The resulting bias is largest in models containing lagged outcomes (Section 5.4). MSEM and DSEM can use latent person-level components rather than treating observed averages as perfectly known. A further problem arises when prompts are missed for reasons related to the person's state, for example when NA is high. The observed mean then describes the moments at which the person answered, and it can be biased, not only noisy. Latent centering does not solve this on its own, because it also assumes that prompts are missed at random given the modeled data (Section 10.8).

The size of these two problems in our design. The calculations below assume an intraclass correlation (ICC) of 0.30 for both ER and the NA residuals. The ICC is the proportion of total variance that lies between persons (here, 30% between and 70% within). This is a realistic value: ICCs between 0.2 and 0.4 are typical in ESM studies (Bolger & Laurenceau, 2013, as cited in Eisele et al., 2026, p. 91). In EMA data the ICC is almost always well above zero, so a formal test of "ICC = 0" before fitting a multilevel model is not informative (Viechtbauer, 2026b, p. 166).

  • Reliability of an observed person mean. The reliability of a mean of T independent occasions is often called ICC(2):

    ICC(2)=1+(T−1)⋅ICCT⋅ICC​=1+179×0.30180×0.30​≈0.99.

    In plain EnglishHow well the observed person averages reflect real differences between people, on a scale from 0 to 1: the share of the variation in observed averages that is due to differences in true averages. With 180 prompts and an ICC of 0.30, the observed averages are almost perfectly reliable.

    Positive autocorrelation reduces the amount of independent information (Section 8.4). With an autoregression of 0.70, 180 occasions contain roughly as much information as 32 independent ones, which lowers the reliability to about 0.93, still a high value.

  • Contamination of a raw-ER slope. In a random-intercept model, the between-person information is down-weighted by the factor σe2​/(σe2​+Tσu2​), where σe2​ is the within-person residual variance and σu2​ is the random-intercept variance. With T=180 the factor is about 0.013, and the between-person slope ends up receiving about 0.5% of the weight in the blended estimate. With T=14 (a two-week daily diary) it receives about 6%, and with T=5 panel waves about 12%.

Real data show the same small contamination. In an example dataset with up to 60 prompts per person, the slope of positive affect on raw event pleasantness was 0.194, and the purely within-person slope from the decomposed model was 0.192, even though the between-person slope (0.626) was more than three times larger (Viechtbauer, 2026b, pp. 176-178).

So, in this particular design, both problems are numerically small. Their practical consequences are much larger in designs with few occasions per person. Explicit decomposition is still the right default: it costs nothing, it makes the estimand explicit, and it is required whenever between-person effects or random within-person slopes are of interest.

3.6Why this distinction changes research conclusions

For your researchThis helps you word your conclusions correctly, so that readers know whether your finding is about differences between people or about changes within a person.

Compare two statements:

"People who use more reappraisal experience more NA."

"When a person uses more reappraisal than they usually do, their NA is lower at the same occasion."

The first concerns between-person differences. The second concerns within-person fluctuation. They are different claims and require different estimands. Neither claim describes what happens later, which requires a model of time.

Takeaway

Before interpreting an ER-NA coefficient, state what it compares: different people, or the same person at different occasions.

3.7Ergodicity: when could results across people describe each individual?

For your researchThis explains why results found across people, for example in a cross-sectional survey, may not describe what happens inside any single person, and what you would need to check before claiming that your ER-NA finding holds for each individual.

Typing speed and typing errors illustrate the problem (Hamaker, 2012). Across people, those who type faster make fewer typing errors, because skilled typists are both faster and more accurate. Within any one person, typing faster than usual produces more errors. The relationship is negative between people and positive within every person. A cross-sectional study would therefore suggest the wrong advice: "type faster to make fewer mistakes." Our ER and NA example in Section 3.3 has the same structure. A health example shows the same reversal: older adults who take more steps overall experience less intense pain, but when a person takes more steps than usual, their risk of pain goes up (Davis et al., 2023, as cited in Lachowicz et al., 2026, p. 267).

The formal condition under which results found across people can be transferred to each individual is called ergodicity (Molenaar, 2004). In plain terms, ergodicity requires that there is no structural change over time (so developmental processes are non-ergodic by definition), and that every person has:

  1. the same mean, so there are no stable differences between people,
  2. the same amount of within-person variation,
  3. the same same-occasion covariances between variables, and
  4. the same lagged covariances, that is, the same dynamics,

and that all of these are equal to the values found across people. These conditions are almost never plausible in psychology. People differ in their average NA, in how much their NA fluctuates, and in how strongly their ER and NA go together. Most, if not all, psychological phenomena are likely to be non-ergodic (Hamaker, 2012). Results from cross-sectional or standard panel analyses therefore cannot be taken as descriptions of processes inside individuals without further evidence.

How a cross-sectional correlation mixes the two levels. Suppose both variables have the same intraclass correlation (ICC, the proportion of variance that lies between persons). Then the correlation found in one cross-section of people is a weighted average of the within-person and between-person correlations:

rcross-sectional​=(1−ICC)rwithin​+ICCrbetween​.

In plain EnglishA correlation computed across people at a single moment is a mix of the within-person correlation and the between-person correlation. Each part counts in proportion to how much of the variance lies at its level.

Three scenarios show how the two levels combine (Hamaker, 2012, Figure 5.2):

  • With equal variance at both levels (ICC = 0.5), a within-person correlation of −0.8 and a between-person correlation of 0 give a cross-sectional correlation of −0.4.
  • With ICC = 0.5, a within-person correlation of −0.8 and a between-person correlation of +0.8 cancel out to 0.
  • With four times as much variance between persons as within (ICC = 0.8), the same two correlations give +0.48: the opposite sign of what happens inside every person.

General law, homology, and ergodicity.

  • A general law means that every person has the same within-person relationship, for example the same NA inertia.
  • Homology means that the within-person relationship and the between-person relationship are the same.
  • Ergodicity means that everything matches, including means and variances, so there are no stable differences between people at all.

A general law can hold without homology or ergodicity. Positive and negative affect are an example: they may be negatively related within every person, while people's average PA and average NA are unrelated (Hamaker, 2012). To find out whether a general law holds, a model must allow within-person relationships to differ across people (random slopes) and then check whether they do.

4Third distinction: Can people have different temporal relationships?

For your researchThis section is about whether the link between reappraisal and later NA is the same for everyone. If you suspect that reappraisal predicts later NA more strongly for some people than for others, this section shows how to model that idea and how to test it.

Consider the question:

Does greater-than-usual ER at one occasion predict subsequent NA equally strongly for everyone?

The coefficient may differ across people, and statistical models differ in whether they represent such heterogeneity explicitly.

4.1What is a temporal relationship here?

For your researchThis turns "the link between reappraisal and later NA" into one concrete number, and shows why that number might differ from person to person.

The ER → subsequent NA coefficient describes how much later NA differs, on average, for a difference in earlier ER, after adjusting for the specified covariates.

Suppose the estimated relationship is:

βER→NA​=−0.30.

In plain EnglishTen more points of reappraisal than usual at one prompt go with 3 fewer points of NA at the next prompt, on average, holding earlier NA and the other predictors in the model constant.

But perhaps that relationship is not the same for everyone:

Participant Illustrative ER → subsequent NA coefficient
Jayce -0.40
Vi -0.05
Ekko -0.30
Jynx +0.10
Viktor -0.45

Jayce exhibits a substantial negative lagged relationship, Vi's is close to zero, and Jynx's is slightly positive. These are imagined person-specific values, not reliably estimated individual effects from the small example table.

4.2What does it mean to allow these coefficients to vary?

For your researchThis shows how to give each person their own reappraisal-NA link while still learning about the average link and about how much people differ around it.

A statistical model is a set of equations and assumptions. To allow individual differences in a coefficient, we explicitly include a person-specific coefficient in those equations and specify how it varies across people.

Common-slope model:

NAitW​=ϕNAi,t−1W​+βERi,t−1W​+εit​.

In plain EnglishOne shared carry-over weight (ϕ) and one shared reappraisal weight (β) for everybody in the study.

Here there is one β for the sample. The model assumes the same modeled conditional ER-NA slope applies to all participants (unless interactions or other varying coefficients have been specified). Different people may still have different observed NA trajectories and unexplained outcomes. They do not have distinct fitted ER slopes in this specification.

Random-slope model:

NAitW​=ϕi​NAi,t−1W​+βi​ERi,t−1W​+εit​.

In plain EnglishThe same equation, but now each person i has their own carry-over weight (ϕi​) and their own reappraisal weight (βi​).

In this model, each person's slope can be written, for example, as

βi​=μβ​+uβi​,uβi​∼N(0,τβ2​).

In plain EnglishEach person's reappraisal weight equals the average weight plus that person's own deviation. The deviations follow a bell curve centered on zero, and τβ​ describes how wide that bell curve is.

Now the model contains:

  • μβ​: the mean lagged ER-NA coefficient across the modeled population.
  • τβ2​: the between-person variance in that coefficient. Its square root, τβ​, is the standard deviation of the slopes and is usually easier to interpret.
  • Person-specific slopes βi​, obtained with uncertainty and with partial pooling toward the population distribution (Section 4.5 explains what "obtained" means in frequentist versus Bayesian terms).

If τβ2​ is substantial, the model represents meaningful variation in lagged relationships across people. If it is near zero, little variation is supported under the assumed model.

A quick way to read τβ​. If slopes are roughly normally distributed, about 95% of people's slopes lie within μβ​±1.96τβ​. With μβ​=−0.30 and τβ​=0.15, that range runs from about −0.59 to −0.01: from a strong negative association to almost none. In an example dataset, the average same-prompt slope of positive affect on event pleasantness was 0.19, and the range expected to contain 95% of people's slopes ran from about 0 to 0.40, that is, from no association to one twice as strong as average (Viechtbauer, 2026b, p. 170). This range describes how much people differ. It is not a confidence interval for the average slope, which is far narrower.

Partial pooling. Each person's slope is a compromise between that person's own data and the population average. Approximately,

β^​i​≈λi​bi​+(1−λi​)μ^​β​,λi​=τβ2​+SEi2​τβ2​​.

In plain EnglishEach person's estimated slope is a weighted average of the slope from their own data and the group's average slope. The more precise their own data (small SEi​), the more weight their own slope gets.

Here bi​ is the slope we would get by fitting person i alone and SEi​ is its standard error. A person with many informative observations has a small SEi​, so λi​ is close to 1 and their estimate stays near their own data. A person with few or noisy observations has a large SEi​, so their estimate is pulled ("shrunk") toward the population mean. For this reason, individual slopes from a mixed model are less extreme than slopes from separate per-person regressions. The same pull applies to person means. In an example dataset, three participants with observed average positive affect of 6.45, 2.07, and 3.08 received model-based estimates of 6.41, 2.11, and 3.11, each moved slightly toward the group average of 4.55. With up to 60 prompts per person, the pull is small. It is larger for a person who answered few prompts (Viechtbauer, 2026b, p. 164).

Real EMA data from 129 people show the same shrinkage. Slopes from separate per-person analyses and person-specific slopes from one multilevel model correlated strongly (0.66 to 0.91), but the multilevel estimates varied much less, because extreme per-person values were pulled toward the average. The average autoregression from the per-person analyses (0.36) was also lower than the multilevel average (0.47), a difference consistent with Nickell bias in the short per-person series of at most 60 prompts each (Hamaker et al., 2023).

4.3What does it mean not to allow slope variation?

For your researchA model that gives everyone the same slope assumes that people are alike, so a common slope should be reported as an assumption of the model, not as a finding that people respond alike.

Not allowing slope variation means that we have constrained a parameter to be common across individuals. It does not demonstrate that the true relationship is identical for everyone. We might impose the constraint because of our substantive hypothesis, limited data, computational considerations, or a desire for a parsimonious model.

Conversely, allowing random slopes does not guarantee that the study contains enough information to estimate each person's slope precisely.

4.4"Random" does not mean arbitrary

For your researchA "random" slope is a spread of person-specific values with a shape you can describe. Once you have it, you can ask questions such as "do people whose NA lingers longer show a weaker link between reappraisal and later NA?"

A random slope has a probabilistic distribution. A common assumption is that people's slopes follow an approximately normal distribution. More elaborate models can use other distributions or mixtures.

A model can also estimate covariances among person-specific slopes. For example, the model can estimate whether people whose NA is more persistent show weaker lagged ER-NA associations (Section 10.5).

In an example dataset, people with a high average level of positive affect had flatter slopes of positive affect on event pleasantness (a correlation of −0.44 between intercepts and slopes). This correlation could mean that happy people are less affected by events, or that their ratings were already near the top of the scale, leaving little room to move (a ceiling effect) (Viechtbauer, 2026b, p. 172).

4.5What is a person-specific slope? Frequentist and Bayesian answers

For your researchThis tells you what you can and cannot report about one participant's own reappraisal-NA slope, depending on whether you used lmer() or Bayesian DSEM in Mplus.

The same model gives person-specific slopes a different status in the two inferential frameworks, which changes what you can report or test about them.

  • Frequentist mixed models (lmer()). The parameters are μβ​ and τβ2​ (plus the other fixed effects and variance components). The person-specific deviations uβi​ are treated as random variables, not parameters. Their values are therefore predicted, not estimated. In linear mixed models, these predictions are called best linear unbiased predictors (BLUPs). The lme4 package calls them conditional modes and returns them with ranef(). ranef(fit, condVar = TRUE) also returns the conditional variance of each prediction, so person-specific values come with an uncertainty, which is often large when a person has few prompts. Standard practice does not attach a p-value to each person's slope.
  • Bayesian DSEM (Mplus). All unknowns, including each βi​, are sampled at every iteration of the Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm. Each person's slope therefore has a full posterior distribution, which Mplus can save and plot.

4.6Testing whether slopes vary: a boundary problem

For your researchIf your hypothesis is that people differ in how strongly reappraisal relates to later NA, this explains how to test it without the usual mistakes, both in lmer() and in Mplus.

The natural null hypothesis for "do slopes vary?" is τβ2​=0. That value lies on the boundary of the parameter space, because a variance cannot be negative. As a result, the standard likelihood ratio test (LRT) does not have its usual reference distribution:

  • Adding a single random variance with no covariances: the reference distribution is a 50:50 mixture of χ2(0) and χ2(1). The 5% critical value is 2.71, not 3.84.
  • Adding one random slope together with its covariance with the random intercept (the usual case): the reference distribution is a 50:50 mixture of χ2(1) and χ2(2). The 5% critical value is 5.14, not 5.99 (Self & Liang, 1987; Stram & Lee, 1994).

Using the naive critical value makes the test conservative and lowers its power.

These two reference distributions hold under specific conditions: many persons, and two nested models that differ only in the tested variance (and covariance) and have the same fixed effects. For other comparisons, for example testing several random slopes at once, the mixture weights differ, and a parametric bootstrap is safer: simulate data from the smaller model many times, fit both models to each data set, and use the resulting distribution of the test statistic (pbkrtest::PBmodcomp() does this for lmer() models; Halekoh & Højsgaard, 2014). In lme4, anova() refits REML models with ML before comparing them unless refit = FALSE is given. When the fixed effects are identical, the REML comparison is the usual choice for testing variance components.

In Bayesian DSEM, the analogous shortcut fails in a different way. A variance's posterior distribution only has support on positive values, so its credible interval can never contain zero, and the "one-tailed p-value" Mplus prints for a variance is essentially zero by construction. "The interval excludes zero" therefore provides no evidence about heterogeneity. Practical alternatives include comparing models with and without the random effect, inspecting how much posterior mass lies near zero, and a screening heuristic of adding a random effect only when its variance estimate is large relative to its posterior standard deviation (a ratio above about 3; Muthén & Asparouhov, 2023).

Under a Neyman-Pearson framing, a more informative question is often whether the data can rule out slope variability large enough to matter: pre-specify the smallest standard deviation of slopes that would be of practical interest, and ask whether the estimate and its interval exclude values above it.

Takeaway

The question "Do temporal relationships differ across people?" is about heterogeneity in parameters, not about differences in average ER or NA. Estimating that heterogeneity requires person-specific temporal coefficients in the model, and testing whether it exists requires the boundary-aware procedures described in Section 4.6.

5Ordinary multilevel modeling with lmer()

For your researchThis section shows that the familiar lmer() can already answer many emotion regulation questions, including questions about what happens at the next prompt, and which questions it cannot answer.

Multilevel modeling is a natural starting point because observations are nested within individuals. Measurements from Jayce are likely more similar to one another than measurements from Jayce and Vi, even before modeling specific temporal processes.

5.1A simple contemporaneous multilevel regression

For your researchUse this model when your question is about reappraisal and NA at the same prompt. It gives you the average link and lets each person have their own link.

Consider:

NAit​=β0i​+β1i​ERit​+εit​.

In plain EnglishEach person gets their own intercept (β0i​, the NA expected at a prompt with a reappraisal score of 0) and their own slope linking reappraisal to NA at the same prompt (β1i​).

Here:

  • β0i​ is Jayce's, Vi's, or another person's intercept.
  • β1i​ is that person's ER-NA slope.
  • εit​ is unexplained occasion-specific variation.

This equation permits person-specific intercepts and slopes, but does not automatically separate within-person and between-person ER associations. The centered variables from Section 3 separate the two, which is needed when within-person variation is the target.

For a contemporaneous within-between analysis (with neg_aff standing for NA, as explained in Section 3.4):

R
fit_same_time <- lmer(
  neg_aff ~ ER_cwc + ER_pm + (1 + ER_cwc | id),
  data = ema
)

This model tests whether higher-than-usual ER is associated with higher or lower NA at the same occasion, while also modeling differences in mean ER between individuals. It does not test what happens two hours later.

A simple effect size for within-person predictors. Compare the within-person residual variance of a model without ER (only a random intercept) with that of the model including ER. The proportional reduction is an R2-type measure: the share of moment-to-moment fluctuation in NA that ER accounts for. In an example dataset, event pleasantness accounted for about 12% of the momentary fluctuation in positive affect at the same prompt, but only about 3% as a predictor from the previous prompt (Viechtbauer, 2026b, pp. 173 and 180). In a sample, this proportion can come out slightly negative, and negative values are then reported as 0 (p. 168).

5.2Adding lagged variables

For your researchThis shows how to ask "does reappraisal at one prompt predict NA at the next one?" in lmer(), and how to build lagged variables without common errors such as linking the last prompt of one evening to the first prompt of the next morning.

Multilevel regression can model temporal dependencies. Consider:

NAitW​=​ϕi​NAi,t−1W​+βi​ERi,t−1W​+γi​PAi,t−1W​+εit​.​

In plain EnglishA person's NA (relative to their usual level) is predicted by their own NA, reappraisal, and PA at the previous prompt. Each of the three has its own person-specific weight.

Autoregression, ϕi​. This coefficient describes how strongly previous NA predicts subsequent NA, controlling for earlier ER and PA. Suppose ϕi​=0.70. If a person's NA is 10 points above their own mean at one occasion, it is expected to be 7 points above their mean at the next occasion, with earlier ER and PA held at their usual levels. In that limited sense, "70% of a deviation is expected to remain after one interval" is a correct reading. Three other readings are incorrect:

  • Reading 0.70 as a probability (it is a regression coefficient).
  • Applying it to raw NA levels rather than to deviations from the person's own mean (a person whose NA is 60 does not expect 42 next time).
  • Treating it as standardized when it is not, or forgetting that it is partial, that is, conditional on the other lagged predictors in the equation.

A related quantity is the half-life: the number of intervals after which a deviation is expected to have halved, ln(0.5)/ln(ϕ). For ϕ=0.70 it is about 1.9 intervals, roughly four hours with two-hour prompts. This value assumes that ER and PA stay at their usual levels at every later prompt. In real data, a rise in NA may also change later ER and PA, which then feed back into NA, so the actual return can be faster or slower. A single equation for NA cannot show this. It requires the joint model of Section 10.3, in which NA returns faster than the coefficient 0.70 alone implies.

The same coefficient is described in several ways (Hamaker, 2012; Hamaker et al., 2023):

  • Inertia: the tendency to stay in the current emotional state.
  • Carryover: how much of one occasion's state carries into the next. The term spillover is used both for this coefficient (Hamaker, 2012) and for effects of one variable on another (Hamaker et al., 2023).
  • Regulatory weakness: the inverse of how strongly a person is pulled back to their usual level.
  • Self-predictability: a highly autocorrelated variable is produced by a system that is not much affected by outside influences and is "running its own course." A weakly autocorrelated variable is largely driven by outside influences. A negative autocorrelation signals a zigzag pattern that alternates from one prompt to the next (Kuppens & Myin-Germeys, 2026, p. 30).

The regulatory-weakness description comes from viewing each person as a system with an equilibrium, their own mean, which acts like the bottom of a bowl. When something pushes the person away from it, they roll back. A coefficient close to 0 means a steep bowl: the person returns quickly. A coefficient close to 1 means a shallow bowl: the person stays away from their usual level for a long time.

These labels describe a statistical pattern. "Regulatory" is meant in this dynamical-systems sense of returning to equilibrium: the coefficient does not measure a person's emotion-regulation ability. A high autoregression can also arise when a stressor persists across several prompts, or when a slow process that the model does not include keeps NA high.

Cross-lagged ER coefficient, βi​. This coefficient describes how strongly earlier ER predicts later NA after adjusting for earlier NA and PA. If βi​=−0.30 in unstandardized units, 10 additional ER points predict 3 fewer NA points at the next occasion, other modeled predictors held constant.

Cross-lagged PA coefficient, γi​. This coefficient describes how strongly earlier PA predicts later NA, over and above earlier ER and NA. If γi​=−0.20, greater earlier PA predicts lower subsequent NA.

Constructing lagged variables correctly. A lag must be taken within a person, in the correct temporal order, and it should not silently cross the night or skip over a missed prompt. A sketch with dplyr, assuming day numbers the study days and prompt numbers the prompts 1 to 6 within each day:

R
ema_lagged <- ema |>
  arrange(id, day, prompt) |>
  group_by(id, day) |>                    # lags never cross the night
  mutate(
    gap_ok = (prompt - lag(prompt)) == 1, # previous prompt was answered
    lag_NA = if_else(gap_ok, lag(neg_aff), NA_real_),
    lag_ER = if_else(gap_ok, lag(ER),      NA_real_),
    lag_PA = if_else(gap_ok, lag(PA),      NA_real_)
  ) |>
  group_by(id) |>                         # center on the person's mean
  mutate(
    lag_NA_cwc = lag_NA - mean(neg_aff, na.rm = TRUE),
    lag_ER_cwc = lag_ER - mean(ER,      na.rm = TRUE),
    lag_PA_cwc = lag_PA - mean(PA,      na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  ungroup()

A simplified model:

R
fit_lagged <- lmer(
  neg_aff ~ lag_NA_cwc + lag_ER_cwc + lag_PA_cwc +
            (1 + lag_ER_cwc | id),
  data = ema_lagged
)

Starting the lags afresh each morning is a common rule (Viechtbauer, 2026a, p. 155; 2026b, p. 181). It costs rows: in one example dataset, the lagged analysis could use 23% fewer rows than the same-prompt analysis (10,923 instead of 14,119), with 1,178 rows lost to the night and 2,018 to the prompt after a missed one (Viechtbauer, 2026b, pp. 181-182). Section 10.8 shows how DSEM recovers most of these rows.

In the code, the outcome is entered raw, and the random intercept absorbs each person's mean level. This is equivalent in spirit to modeling NAW and avoids centering the outcome on an estimated mean. As written, the model also allows the ER lag coefficient to vary across people, but not the NA and PA lag coefficients. These are choices of this particular specification, and other MLM specifications can make different ones.

5.3Questions the lagged multilevel model can answer

For your researchLagged lmer() models are dynamic models. If your question concerns one outcome, such as NA, you may not need DSEM at all.

The lagged model can answer a substantive question similar to the one answered by the NA equation in a basic DSEM:

Does higher-than-usual earlier ER predict lower-than-expected later NA, conditional on earlier NA and PA, and does that relationship vary across people?

The claim that MLM cannot model dynamics while DSEM can is therefore false. MLM can incorporate lagged outcomes, lagged predictors, random temporal slopes, and covariances among random slopes.

5.4Limitations of the lagged lmer() model

For your researchA lagged lmer() model does not model ER, PA, and NA jointly, does not offer autocorrelated residuals, can be biased in short series, and does not distinguish uneven time gaps (a problem that discrete-time DSEM shares). If your study needs any of these, consider MSEM or DSEM.

One outcome at a time. The displayed lmer() equation predicts NA. We could fit separate models for ER and PA, but these would not generally estimate a joint cross-outcome innovation covariance. Other multivariate mixed-model frameworks can do so.

Limited within-person residual covariance options in lmer(). The lme4::lmer() implementation does not offer an AR(1) or other time-series residual correlation structure. Other R software does:

  • nlme::lme() accepts correlation = corAR1() for equally spaced occasions and correlation = corCAR1() for a continuous-time AR(1), which uses the actual elapsed time between observations and therefore handles unequal spacing.
  • glmmTMB offers ar1() and an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck ou() covariance structure (the continuous-time analogue of AR(1)).

A lagged outcome may explain some serial dependence, but it does not guarantee independent residuals. A model that includes both a lagged outcome and autocorrelated residuals is a richer (ARMA-type) structure. Most analyses use one or the other.

Dynamic-panel bias (Nickell bias). When a lagged outcome is centered on the observed person mean, the estimated autoregressive coefficient is biased downward in finite series. The reason is that the observed mean is computed from the same observations, including the current innovation, which induces a small negative correlation between the centered lagged predictor and the error. For an AR(1) with coefficient ϕ and T occasions per person, the bias is approximately

bias(ϕ^​)≈−T−11+ϕ​

In plain EnglishWhen each person's lagged NA is centered on their observed average, the estimated carry-over comes out too small, on average, by roughly (1+ϕ)/(T−1): a lot with few prompts per person, very little with many, and somewhat more when the true carry-over is strong.

Values of this approximation (Hamaker & Grasman, 2015; Nickell, 1981) for ϕ=0.70:

Occasions per person, T Approximate bias Expected estimate
10 -0.19 0.51
20 -0.09 0.61
50 -0.035 0.67
180 -0.009 0.69

A simulation with 300 persons per study agreed: across 100 simulated studies, the average estimates were 0.60 for T=20 and 0.69 for T=180 (Monte Carlo standard errors of 0.001 or less; R code in Section 21.1). In this study's design the bias is therefore negligible, but it is substantial for short series, and it can also distort cross-lagged coefficients. Latent centering, as used by DSEM, avoids Nickell bias because the person mean is estimated as part of the model rather than plugged in. This removes the specific plug-in mechanism behind Nickell bias. It does not remove every small-sample problem: with short series, the treatment of the first observation (see "Initial conditions" below) and the priors (Section 13.3) can still affect the estimates. The same mechanism becomes severe if one centers on day means with only six prompts per day (Section 15).

Centering the lagged outcome in lmer(). Published examples differ on this choice. Some enter the lagged outcome uncentered, with a random intercept (e.g., Viechtbauer, 2026b, p. 183). In simulations, person-mean centering the lagged outcome biased the average autoregressive effect downward, which is a problem mainly when the question is whether there is an autoregressive effect on average. When the question is whether a person-level variable predicts individual differences in autoregression (a cross-level interaction), person-mean centering performed better. The choice should therefore follow the main question (Hamaker & Grasman, 2015). Latent centering in DSEM removes the need for this choice, and with 180 prompts per person, as here, the practical difference is small.

When a lagged dependent variable, person-specific effects, and observed person means appear together, the results also depend on finite-sample bias and on how the first observation of each series is treated.

Initial conditions. The first observation of each person (or each day) has no preceding observation. Models differ in how they treat it: dropping it, treating its missing lag as data to be imputed within the model (as Mplus does), or modeling it from the stationary distribution. With 180 occasions the choice makes little difference, but with short series it can change the estimates.

Unequal time intervals. Ordinary "previous observation" lags do not automatically distinguish two-hour gaps from overnight gaps. This problem applies to discrete-time DSEM too. Section 14 discusses the options, including TINTERVAL and continuous-time models in Mplus.

5.5When would lmer() be sufficient?

For your researchIf you only need the average lagged link between reappraisal and NA, and you have many prompts per person, lmer() is usually enough.

If the question is modest, for example, whether earlier ER predicts later NA on average, and a carefully specified single-outcome mixed model represents the temporal dependencies adequately, lmer() or another mixed-model approach may be sufficient. There is no methodological requirement to use a framework labeled DSEM.

6Multilevel structural equation modeling (MSEM)

For your researchThis section shows what multilevel SEM adds to an emotion regulation study: it treats each person's usual level as something to estimate rather than a known average, and it can model measurement error in reappraisal and affect, either with several items per construct or, under extra assumptions, with single items.

6.1What is structural equation modeling?

For your researchSEM lets you write several connected equations at once, and lets a construct such as reappraisal be measured by several questionnaire items instead of one.

Structural equation modeling (SEM) is a framework for specifying relationships among observed or latent variables, often using multiple connected equations. It can also include a measurement model: a description of how observable questionnaire items reflect less directly observable psychological constructs.

Multilevel SEM (MSEM) extends these ideas to hierarchical data, for example, EMA observations within individuals. MSEM is a broad family of models, not one fixed statistical equation.

6.2MSEM can estimate the same within-between relationships as MLM

For your researchFor the basic questions ("within a person, does more reappraisal go with less NA?" and "do people who reappraise more have less NA?"), MSEM and a well-built lmer() model give nearly the same answer. MSEM's advantage is that it treats each person's average as estimated, not as known exactly.

A simple two-level SEM decomposes each variable into a latent between-person component (superscript B, the person's true mean) and a latent within-person component (superscript W). It might specify, at the within-person level:

NAitW​=βW​ERitW​+γW​PAitW​+εit​.

In plain EnglishWithin each person, NA at a prompt is predicted by reappraisal and PA at the same prompt, each measured relative to the person's usual level.

At the between-person level, it might specify:

NAiB​=βB​ERiB​+γB​PAiB​+ζi​.

In plain EnglishBetween people, a person's usual NA is predicted by their usual reappraisal and their usual PA. The term ζi​ is what makes this person's usual NA differ from that prediction.

The first equation compares occasions within the same person. The second compares people who differ in their typical levels.

A simple MSEM and a correctly specified multilevel regression can express nearly equivalent within-between relationships. The main technical difference is that MSEM treats the person means as latent (the multilevel latent covariate approach; Lüdtke et al., 2008), whereas the lmer() model plugs in observed means. The psychological quantity being estimated is the same in both.

6.3What does measurement error mean?

For your researchEach EMA rating of reappraisal or NA contains some measurement error, which can make real links look weaker in your results or distort them in other ways.

Measurement error means that an observed score is not a perfect representation of the construct or quantity we care about.

Suppose Jayce's actual level of cognitive reappraisal at a prompt is conceptually 60 on some latent scale. He might select a response equivalent to 50 because he misunderstands an item, forgets part of the relevant interval, answers hurriedly, or the item captures only one aspect of the strategy.

An intuitive decomposition is:

observed score=construct-related signal+measurement error.

In plain EnglishWhat a person selects on the screen equals the part that reflects their real experience plus an error.

The decomposition is a simplification: error can be random, systematic, person-specific, context-dependent, or shared across items.

When variables are measured unreliably, the statistical relationships among them can be distorted. Under classical measurement-error assumptions, error in a single predictor attenuates its regression coefficient toward zero. With multiple variables, correlated errors, autocorrelated measurement errors, or more complicated assumptions, the direction of the bias is harder to predict. In time-series models specifically, ignoring measurement error biases autoregressive coefficients toward zero, so observed affect appears less persistent than the underlying affective state, and cross-lagged coefficients can shrink, disappear, reverse sign, or appear spuriously (Schuurman & Hamaker, 2019).

6.4Example: ER measured with three items

For your researchIf you ask about reappraisal with several items, this shows how to combine them into one latent reappraisal score that keeps what the items share and sets aside what is specific to each item, which includes measurement error but can also include meaningful item-specific content.

Instead of asking a single ER question, we might use:

  1. "I tried to reinterpret what happened."
  2. "I tried to think about the situation differently."
  3. "I tried to change how I understood the situation."

A latent-factor model could be:

ER1,it​ER2,it​ER3,it​​=ν1​+λ1​ηER,it​+e1,it​,=ν2​+λ2​ηER,it​+e2,it​,=ν3​+λ3​ηER,it​+e3,it​.​

In plain EnglishEach of the three reappraisal items reflects one shared, unobserved reappraisal level at that prompt (ηER,it​), rescaled by its loading λ and shifted by its intercept ν, plus its own noise e.

Here:

  • ηER,it​ represents the latent ER construct at that occasion.
  • λ1​,λ2​,λ3​ are factor loadings, describing how strongly each item relates to the factor.
  • ν1​,ν2​,ν3​ are item intercepts.
  • e1,it​,e2,it​,e3,it​ are item-specific residuals, which may include measurement error and item-specific meaningful content.

We could construct analogous latent PA and NA variables. The temporal model could then relate the latent constructs, rather than treating noisy questionnaire averages as exact measures.

Many conventional latent-variable specifications need multiple indicators. A factor model also makes assumptions about dimensionality and the structure of residuals. Repeated measurement raises measurement invariance questions: whether items have comparable meanings and loadings across occasions and people. In a multilevel factor model there is also a within-person factor and a between-person factor, and their loadings need not be equal. Equal loadings across the two levels (cross-level invariance) are required before the between-person factor can be read as the person mean of the within-person factor. The reliability of a scale can also differ greatly between levels. A latent factor removes only the error that is unique to each item, not error shared by all items.

The two levels can differ considerably: in one ESM dataset, two factors were enough to describe affect between persons, but five were needed within persons (Eisele et al., 2021, as cited in Eisele et al., 2026, p. 93). Newer methods, such as latent Markov factor analysis and DSEM, can let the factor structure itself change across moments and across people, which is one way to study measurement invariance over time (Eisele et al., 2026, pp. 92-93).

6.5Measurement error versus a process innovation

For your researchA real surge in NA, for example after an argument, carries over to the next prompts, whereas a careless answer affects only the prompt at which it was given. Models that tell the two apart give more accurate estimates of how long NA lingers.

Measurement error and process innovations are different quantities:

  • Measurement error: The discrepancy between an observed item response and the latent or intended measured quantity.
  • Process innovation: A real, new departure in the psychological process that the dynamic model did not predict from earlier observations.

Imagine Jayce has a real increase in NA because of an unexpected argument. That can be a process innovation. If he accidentally selects 80 when his underlying NA would correspond more closely to 60, the discrepancy may reflect measurement error.

The two differ in what happens at later prompts. An innovation enters the psychological process itself, so the dynamics carry it forward. With ϕ=0.70, a +30 innovation in NA at 2 p.m. is still expected to be +21 at 4 p.m. and +14.7 at 6 p.m. A measurement error affects only the recorded response at the occasion where it occurs. It is not carried forward, because the underlying state did not change. A model that confuses the two can misrepresent temporal persistence and cross-lagged associations.

This difference makes measurement error estimable even with a single item. In the AR(1) plus white noise model (AR(1)+WN; Schuurman & Hamaker, 2019), each observed score is a latent AR(1) process plus independent measurement error. Its autocorrelation function has a characteristic form. For lags k≥1,

ρk​=Rϕk.

In plain EnglishWith measurement error, the correlation between two ratings k prompts apart equals the reliability R times the carry-over ϕ multiplied by itself k times. The one-time drop by the factor R is the pattern that identifies measurement error.

Here R is the within-person reliability: the proportion of within-person observed variance due to the latent process rather than to error. The autocorrelation drops by the factor R immediately after lag 0 and then decays at the true rate ϕ. A pure AR(1) process, by contrast, decays smoothly from 1. Because of this pattern, DSEM can estimate the measurement-error variance with one indicator per construct. Identification requires nonzero dynamics: if ϕ=0, innovations and measurement errors cannot be told apart. For the same reason, the separation is weak when the autoregression is close to zero or the series are short, and the reliability estimate can then be imprecise. If the measurement errors are themselves correlated from one prompt to the next, the model mistakes them for dynamics, and the reliability estimate is biased.

Many EMA constructs are measured with a single item, and the usual internal-consistency reliability (such as Cronbach's alpha or omega) needs several items. The (test-retest) reliability of single items can be assessed with estimates based on components of multilevel (vector-)autoregressive models (Schuurman & Hamaker, 2019), or by presenting the same item twice at or near the same moment (Dejonckheere et al., 2022; see also Eisele et al., 2026, p. 96).

6.6Does MSEM have to be contemporaneous?

For your researchMSEM can also include lagged effects, so it can also test whether reappraisal predicts later NA. At that point it is already close to DSEM.

MSEM can include lagged effects, for example:

NAitW​=ϕNAi,t−1W​+βERi,t−1W​+γPAi,t−1W​+εit​.

In plain EnglishWithin each person, NA is predicted from their own NA, reappraisal, and PA at the previous prompt.

With analogous equations for ER and PA, the model becomes a dynamic multilevel SEM.

Takeaway

MSEM's main contribution is the flexible, joint representation of between-person and within-person structures, potentially with multiple outcomes and latent measurement models. With temporal dependencies added, MSEM becomes very similar to DSEM.

7Fourth distinction: What is a "dynamic system"?

For your researchThis section explains what it means to call ER, PA, and NA a "dynamic system," and when you need a model that predicts all three together rather than NA alone.

7.1What does dynamic mean?

For your researchA model is "dynamic" when it uses earlier prompts to predict later ones. Even a model of NA alone, with NA's own carry-over, is dynamic.

A process is dynamic when we explicitly model how its state evolves over time. The present is related to the past, and we want to characterize that temporal evolution.

For example:

A person who feels unusually high NA at noon may still feel unusually high NA at 2 p.m.

That persistence is a dynamic feature: previous NA helps predict current NA.

A process can be dynamic even if it contains only one variable. An autoregressive NA model is dynamic because NA changes over time in a statistically structured way.

7.2What does system mean?
