For your researchCalling ER, PA, and NA a "system" means that you care about how they predict one another over time, not only about one of them.

A system is a set of components that are considered together because their relationships matter to the behavior of the whole.

For our study, the components are ER, PA, and NA.

We might hypothesize:

  • Elevated NA is followed by more ER use.
  • Greater ER is followed by lower NA.
  • Greater ER is followed by higher PA.
  • Greater PA is followed by less NA.
  • PA and NA also persist from one occasion to the next.

Because of these connections, a model of one component alone cannot describe how the variables evolve together.

7.3What does a dynamic system mean in our study?

For your researchOne everyday sequence (distress, then reappraisal, then relief) illustrates what a dynamic system looks like in daily life.

A dynamic system is a collection of variables whose values evolve over time in ways that may depend on their own past and on the past of other variables in the collection.

Think of a sequence:

  1. Jayce's NA is unusually high at noon.
  2. This elevated NA predicts greater ER use at 2 p.m.
  3. Greater ER at 2 p.m. predicts lower NA at 4 p.m.
  4. Lower NA at 4 p.m. may change the predicted ER and PA levels at 6 p.m.

The example is a set of hypothesized predictive relationships, not a claim that these influences are established or causal.

7.4Modeling one outcome versus modeling the system jointly

For your researchIf you want to know not only what predicts later NA but also what predicts later reappraisal (for example, whether high NA predicts more reappraisal at the next prompt), you need an equation for each of the three variables.

A single-equation model might predict NA using earlier ER, PA, and NA:

NAitW​=βERi,t−1W​+γPAi,t−1W​+ϕNAi,t−1W​+εNA,it​.

In plain EnglishNA at this prompt is predicted from reappraisal, PA, and NA at the previous prompt.

This single equation is a dynamic model of NA, but it does not estimate what predicts later ER or later PA.

A joint system also models the other outcomes:

ERitW​PAitW​NAitW​​=a11​ERi,t−1W​+a12​PAi,t−1W​+a13​NAi,t−1W​+εER,it​,=a21​ERi,t−1W​+a22​PAi,t−1W​+a23​NAi,t−1W​+εPA,it​,=a31​ERi,t−1W​+a32​PAi,t−1W​+a33​NAi,t−1W​+εNA,it​.​

In plain EnglishThree equations, one per variable. Each of reappraisal, PA, and NA at this prompt is predicted from all three at the previous prompt. The nine a weights describe every carry-over and every cross-influence.

Now every variable may help predict itself and the others. This is a vector autoregressive model of order 1, or VAR(1). "Order 1" means that only the immediately preceding occasion is used as a predictor.

7.5Why is joint modeling useful?

For your researchA joint model lets you test feedback loops, such as "high NA predicts more reappraisal, which in turn predicts lower NA," in one analysis.

Joint modeling lets us describe reciprocity and feedback. For example:

  • NAt−1​→ERt​: distress may be followed by greater regulation use.
  • ERt−1​→NAt​: prior regulation use may predict later distress.

Those are two different lagged coefficients. Both can be nonzero, and they need not be equal or even have the same sign. When they have opposite signs, as in this example (NA raises later ER, ER lowers later NA), they form a negative feedback loop, which tends to pull the system back toward its usual state and can produce damped oscillations (Section 10.3).

A joint model also permits correlations among same-occasion innovations (Section 8.6). It also supports questions about how an earlier departure in one variable propagates through the system over several occasions (Section 10.3).

7.6Is joint estimation the only way to study a system?

For your researchYou can often get the same cross-lagged numbers from separate models. The joint model is needed mainly for quantities that depend on all equations at once, and it is worth its cost only when your question requires it.

Separate regressions can also be useful and, under particular assumptions, can even produce the same point estimates for equation-specific slopes as joint estimation. In single-level linear regression, when every equation contains the same predictors, equation-by-equation least squares gives the same coefficients as joint estimation (the seemingly unrelated regressions result; Zellner, 1962). Nevertheless, separate regressions do not ordinarily furnish the full joint innovation model, all cross-equation restrictions, and parameter uncertainty for functions of the complete system in one integrated fit. Multivariate mixed models and SEM approaches offer other ways to do this.

A larger model is not automatically a better description. In a comparison of how well models predicted new, unseen data from typical ESM datasets, person-specific VAR(1) models predicted worst, and multilevel VAR(1) models did not outperform simpler multilevel AR(1) models in which each variable is predicted only by its own past (Bulteel et al., 2018, as cited in Lafit, 2026a, p. 216). Cross-lagged effects in affect data are often small, so a full system model is worth its cost when the question is about the cross-influences themselves, not as a default.

7.7"Dynamic system" does not mean "causal system"

For your researchA model can show that NA predicts later reappraisal without showing that NA causes reappraisal. Keep the word "predicts" in your conclusions unless your design supports a stronger claim.

A VAR equation can accurately describe predictability without identifying a mechanism of influence.

If earlier NA predicts later ER, that does not prove that manipulating NA would change ER. Unmeasured situations, stressors, anticipation, trends, and other variables might explain the statistical association. Arrows in a predictive VAR diagram are not automatically causal arrows.

Takeaway

Dynamic refers to evolution over time. System refers to related components studied together. A dynamic system model describes how those components' current values depend on their earlier values, often with reciprocal relationships.

8Fifth distinction: What is a temporal covariance structure?

For your researchThis section explains why prompts that are close in time resemble each other, and how that resemblance affects both your standard errors and the meaning of your reappraisal coefficients.

A temporal covariance structure describes two facts: observations close together in time may be more similar than observations far apart, and different variables may share unexpected changes.

8.1What does covariance mean?

For your researchCovariance describes whether two things go up and down together, and the rest of this section builds on that definition.

Covariance describes how two quantities vary together.

  • Positive covariance: When one variable is above its expected level, the other tends to be above its expected level as well.
  • Negative covariance: When one is above its expected level, the other tends to be below its expected level.
  • Near-zero covariance: There is little linear co-movement, although other kinds of dependence could remain.

Unlike correlation, covariance depends on the variables' measurement scales. Correlation standardizes covariance to a scale between -1 and +1.

8.2What makes a covariance structure temporal?

For your researchYour NA ratings from the same afternoon are not independent pieces of information, and the temporal covariance structure describes how they are linked.

Consider Jayce's NA at noon, 2 p.m., and 4 p.m. These measurements are not three independent draws. Noon NA may be associated with 2 p.m. NA; 2 p.m. NA may be associated with 4 p.m. NA; and noon NA may even be associated with 4 p.m. NA.

The temporal covariance structure specifies the expected variances and covariances across times, potentially for several variables.

For one person, it concerns quantities such as:

Cov(NAt​,NAt−1​),Cov(NAt​,NAt−2​).

In plain EnglishHow much NA at one prompt varies together with NA one prompt earlier, and with NA two prompts earlier.

In a multivariate model, it also concerns quantities such as:

Cov(ERt​,NAt−1​)

In plain EnglishHow much reappraisal at one prompt varies together with NA at the previous prompt.

It also concerns the same-occasion covariance between PA and NA.

8.3A simple AR(1) illustration

For your researchThis shows with simple numbers how NA's carry-over makes ratings a few hours apart resemble each other. It also explains why "NA fluctuates a lot" and "NA changes abruptly" are two different properties of a person.

Suppose a centered NA process follows:

NAtW​=0.70NAt−1W​+εt​.

In plain English70% of the previous prompt's deviation in NA (NAt−1W​) is expected to remain at this prompt, and a new surprise (εt​) is added.

Assume that the innovations are independent over time and that the process is stationary, meaning its mean, variance, and autocorrelations do not change over time.

Then the lag-one autocorrelation is 0.70. The lag-two autocorrelation is:

0.702=0.49.

In plain EnglishTwo prompts apart, the carry-over is applied twice: 0.70 times 0.70.

And the lag-three autocorrelation is:

0.703=0.343.

In plain EnglishThree prompts apart, it is applied three times, so the resemblance keeps fading.

In this simple example, observations become less correlated as their separation grows:

Time separation Correlation in this AR(1) illustration
One interval 0.70
Two intervals 0.49
Three intervals 0.343

This pattern is one possible temporal correlation structure. The corresponding covariance values additionally depend on the stationary variance of NA, which for an AR(1) process is

Var(NAtW​)=1−ϕ2σε2​​.

In plain EnglishHow widely a person's NA swings around their own usual level: the size of the new surprises (σε2​), enlarged because past surprises pile up through the carry-over.

With ϕ=0.70, the total within-person variance is about twice the innovation variance (1/0.51≈1.96). Persistence accumulates past innovations, so a persistent process fluctuates more widely than its individual shocks.

Real data may require other structures: AR(2), moving-average components, trends, periodicity (for example, daily cycles), time-varying variances, or continuous-time models.

A slow trend can also make NA look more persistent than it is. If NA drifts slowly over the study, successive prompts look more alike than the moment-to-moment process alone would make them, and an autoregressive coefficient estimated without accounting for the trend is typically too large (Viechtbauer, 2026b, p. 184). One common trend in EMA data is the initial elevation bias: many participants report higher values in their first few assessments, followed by a slight decrease that then stabilizes. Its cause is unknown, and it is one reason why some researchers set aside the first few assessments (Kuppens & Myin-Germeys, 2026, p. 29, citing Shrout et al., 2018). Section 13.5 includes checking for trends in the model-building sequence.

Variability and instability are different properties. A person's within-person variance is sometimes used as a measure of emotional instability. However, a strongly persistent process (high ϕ) can wander far from its mean, and so have a large variance, while changing only a little from one prompt to the next (Jahng et al., 2008). As a measure of moment-to-moment instability, Jahng and colleagues proposed the mean squared successive difference (MSSD), the average squared change between consecutive prompts. For a stationary AR(1) process with total variance σ2:

MSSD=2σ2(1−ϕ).

In plain EnglishThe average squared jump between consecutive prompts. It grows with the overall spread σ2 and shrinks when the carry-over ϕ is high.

Two people can therefore have the same variance and very different instability. For example, a person who feels good during the first half of the week and bad during the second half shows the same variability as a person who alternates between feeling good and bad all week, but a very different pattern of change (Kuppens & Myin-Germeys, 2026, p. 30). The MSSD is useful, and it also works for data with trends, but it does not provide a model of the actual process (Hamaker, 2012). A dynamic model, by contrast, separates persistence (ϕ) from the size of new shocks (the innovation variance).

8.4Why does temporal covariance matter for inference?

For your researchThis explains why 180 prompts from one person are worth less than 180 independent answers, and when that makes your p-values too small or your intervals too narrow.

If 180 observations from Jayce are strongly correlated, they do not contain the same information as 180 independent observations. The effective sample size summarizes this loss: it is the number of independent observations that would contain the same information. For estimating a mean from an AR(1) series, it is approximately

Teff​≈T1+ϕ1−ϕ​.

In plain EnglishHow many fully independent answers a person's correlated answers are worth when estimating their average. The stronger the carry-over ϕ, the fewer.

With T=180 and ϕ=0.70, Teff​≈32. Jayce's 180 prompts contain roughly as much information about his mean NA as 32 independent ones.

Whether this dependence biases the standard errors depends on the model. If the model's lagged terms capture the dependence, so that the innovations are uncorrelated over time, the regression standard errors are valid. The problem arises when dependence remains in the residuals, for example in a purely contemporaneous model that ignores temporal structure while both predictor and outcome are autocorrelated. Treating the observations as independent then makes standard errors too small, intervals too narrow, and p-values too small.

The temporal structure also changes the substantive interpretation of the coefficients. If NA has strong persistence, an apparent association between ER and later NA may partly reflect the fact that people use ER during episodes that were already changing. Incorporating relevant lagged variables changes what an ER coefficient is conditioned on (Section 2.4).

8.5Three related but different sources of covariance

For your researchThree kinds of "going together" can occur in the same data: people who are high on both variables, moments that resemble nearby moments, and surprises that hit two variables at the same prompt.

(a) Stable between-person covariance. People who generally have higher ER may also generally have higher NA. This is covariance between people's typical levels.

(b) Temporal covariance within a person. Jayce's NA at 2 p.m. may resemble his NA at noon. This is covariance between occasions.

(c) Contemporaneous innovation covariance. Jayce may experience a sudden rise in NA and a sudden fall in PA at the same prompt, beyond what the model predicted from earlier measurements. These unexpected deviations may be correlated.

A model may represent one, two, or all three of these covariances.

8.6What is an innovation?

For your researchAn innovation is the surprise part of NA at a prompt: what the earlier prompts could not predict. This section explains what such surprises contain, why some people have bigger surprises than others, and where the word comes from.

In a dynamic model, an innovation is the part of an outcome at the current time that the model did not predict from earlier information and the other included predictors.

Imagine the model predicts Jayce's NA at 4 p.m. will be 35, but he reports NA = 65 after an unexpected conflict. His NA innovation is +30 on this simplified interpretation.

At the same occasion, perhaps his PA is 25 points below its predicted value and his ER is 15 points above its predicted value.

Those departures might be correlated:

  • NA innovation: +30.
  • PA innovation: -25.
  • ER innovation: +15.

A joint dynamic model may specify:

εit​∼MVN(0,Σi​).

In plain EnglishAt each prompt, the surprises in reappraisal, PA, and NA are drawn together from a bell-shaped distribution centered on zero. The matrix Σi​ describes, for person i, how large the surprises tend to be and how they move together.

The matrix Σi​ is:

Σi​=​σER,i2​σER,PA,i​σER,NA,i​​σER,PA,i​σPA,i2​σPA,NA,i​​σER,NA,i​σPA,NA,i​σNA,i2​​​.

In plain EnglishA three-by-three table. The diagonal cells are the variances of each variable's surprises (how large they tend to be). The other cells are covariances: they say whether, at the same prompt, a surprise in one variable tends to come with a surprise in the same direction (positive) or in the opposite direction (negative) in another variable. The table is symmetric because "PA with NA" is the same as "NA with PA."

The diagonal elements are innovation variances: how much unexplained fluctuation each variable has. The off-diagonal elements are innovation covariances: how those unexpected fluctuations co-occur.

For example, a negative σPA,NA​ would mean that occasions with unexpectedly elevated PA tend to have unexpectedly reduced NA, after conditioning on the model's predictors.

The subscript i on Σi​ means that each person may have their own innovation variances and covariances. Mplus has long allowed random innovation variances, modeled on the log scale so they stay positive. Since Mplus 8.9 (2023), it also allows random innovation correlations: each person's correlation is modeled through the Fisher z transformation, zi​=atanh(ρi​), which is normally distributed across persons, and the median person-level correlation is recovered as tanh of the mean of zi​. Before version 8.9, this required workarounds.

The content of an innovation. The innovation is the combined effect of everything that happened between two prompts and influenced the process: conversations with colleagues or family, a stressful email, coffee or alcohol, news, a memory that came to mind, a worry about tomorrow (Hamaker, 2012). The model does not need to name these influences. It only describes how large their combined impact tends to be (the innovation variance) and how it carries forward over time (through the dynamics).

People can differ in innovation variance for two reasons (Jongerling et al., 2015): some people are exposed to more or larger events, and some people react more strongly to the same events. For this reason, DSEM allows the innovation variance to differ between people.

Origin of the word "innovation." The term comes from engineering and the mathematics of prediction, not from psychology. An innovation is the part of the current observation that is new: the part that could not have been predicted from everything observed before.

  • Origin. The idea goes back to Wold (1938), who showed that any well-behaved stationary series can be written as a weighted sum of past unpredictable shocks (the Wold decomposition), and to work on predicting stationary processes by Kolmogorov (1939-1941) and Wiener (1942, published 1949). Bode and Shannon (1950), and independently Zadeh and Ragazzini (1950), simplified Wiener's prediction theory by first turning a signal into the series of its unpredictable parts. Each of those parts is new information that arrives at that moment, hence the later name "innovation." The name itself was apparently first used by Wiener and Masani in the mid-1950s (Kailath, 1974).
  • Spread. The "innovations approach" papers by Kailath (from 1968 onward) made the term standard in filtering. In the Kalman filter, the innovation is the gap between a new measurement and its prediction: the "compare" step in Section 10.8.
  • In time-series models. Because the lagged terms already capture what the past predicts, the residual of a model such as NAt​=ϕNAt−1​+εt​ is exactly this unpredictable new part. That is why time-series texts call it the innovation. Econometricians also call it a shock. Other names include random shock, disturbance, residual, and dynamic error (Hamaker, 2012; Hamaker et al., 2017).
  • What the name conveys. Calling it an innovation rather than just an error signals the point of Section 6.5: an innovation enters the process and is carried forward by the dynamics, whereas a measurement error is not.

A note on sources: Wikipedia's entry Innovation (signal processing) credits Bode and Shannon (1950) with the word itself, but the word does not appear in their paper. So we do not know for certain who coined the term. The account above follows Kailath (1974), "A view of three decades of linear filtering theory" (doi.org/10.1109/TIT.1974.1055174), who says only that the name was "apparently" first used by Wiener and Masani. The later mathematical theory of "innovation representations" is reviewed in a 1989 survey in the Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society.

8.7Are contemporaneous innovation covariance and contemporaneous ER-NA association identical?

For your research"Reappraisal and NA go together at the same prompt" can mean three different things, depending on what has been removed first. This helps you say which one your model estimated.

A raw contemporaneous association relates measured ER and NA at the same occasion and can reflect stable person differences, predictable temporal evolution, and occasion-specific co-movement.

A within-person contemporaneous association removes stable person differences but may still reflect predicted temporal structure.

A contemporaneous innovation covariance concerns what remains associated after the model has accounted for earlier information.

These three quantities are different estimands. A residual innovation covariance does not determine the direction of an instantaneous causal relationship.

8.8Residual autocorrelation: A diagnostic warning

For your researchAfter fitting a dynamic model, check whether the leftovers still show a pattern over time. If they do, the model has missed part of how NA changes.

Even after including NAt−1​ and other lagged predictors, the residuals might still be temporally correlated. Remaining autocorrelation suggests that the specified dynamics have not captured all temporal dependence, or that the innovation assumptions are incomplete. Plotting the autocorrelation function (ACF) of the residuals is the standard check. Mplus provides ACF and partial autocorrelation (PACF) plots for time-series models.

Takeaway

Temporal covariance describes the dependence among observations across time. Modeling it is needed for valid uncertainty estimates, for separating persistent processes from new shocks, and for interpreting the model's conditional relationships.

9The random-intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM)

For your researchThis section is for the case where you have a few waves of data months apart rather than daily prompts, for example ER and depressive symptoms measured four times over a year. It shows how the RI-CLPM separates "who is generally high" from "who is higher than usual at a given wave," and how it relates to DSEM.

The RI-CLPM separates stable between-person differences from within-person temporal processes.

9.1The problem with a traditional cross-lagged panel model

For your researchA traditional cross-lagged panel model can make stable differences between people look like effects of reappraisal over time.

A conventional cross-lagged panel model can mix stable individual differences with within-person dynamics. For example, a finding that people with generally high ER later tend to have high NA does not establish that increases in ER within a person predict later increases in that person's NA.

The RI-CLPM addresses this problem by explicitly separating trait-like or stable person-specific components from within-person deviations. The distinction was motivated by a methodological critique of the traditional model (Hamaker et al., 2015).

9.2Decomposing an observed score

For your researchEach person's score at a wave is split into three parts: the average of everyone at that wave, the person's stable difference from that average, and the person's temporary deviation at that wave. Only the temporary deviations are used to study change within people.

For ER and NA, write:

ERit​=μER,t​+κER,i​+erit​.

In plain EnglishA person's reappraisal score at wave t equals the group average at that wave, plus the person's stable difference from the group, plus a temporary deviation at that wave.

NAit​=μNA,t​+κNA,i​+nait​.

In plain EnglishThe same three-part split for NA.

Here:

  • μER,t​ and μNA,t​ are the population means at wave t.
  • κER,i​ and κNA,i​ are stable person-specific deviations from those means: the random intercept factors. In the SEM, each is a latent factor whose loadings on that variable's observed scores are all fixed to 1.
  • erit​ and nait​ are the within-person deviations at occasion t. They are latent variables too. With a single indicator per wave, they also absorb any measurement error.

For example, Jayce may generally experience higher NA than Vi, represented by his stable NA component. On a particular day he may feel unusually distressed relative to himself, represented by a positive nait​.

9.3Modeling the within-person temporal process

For your researchThe within-person part of the RI-CLPM answers the question: when a person reappraises more than usual at one wave, is their NA lower than expected at the next wave, given their NA at the earlier wave?

A simple two-variable RI-CLPM specifies:

erit​=ϕER​eri,t−1​+γNA→ER​nai,t−1​+εER,it​.

In plain EnglishA person's temporary reappraisal deviation at this wave is predicted by their own reappraisal deviation and their NA deviation at the previous wave.

nait​=ϕNA​nai,t−1​+γER→NA​eri,t−1​+εNA,it​.

In plain EnglishA person's temporary NA deviation at this wave is predicted by their own NA deviation and their reappraisal deviation at the previous wave.

Read the second equation as:

Jayce's deviation in NA at the current occasion is predicted by his deviation in NA at the previous occasion and his deviation in ER at the previous occasion.

The RI-CLPM can also allow:

  • Covariance between the two stable random intercept factors.
  • Covariance between within-person innovations at the same wave.
  • Time-specific means and, in conventional specifications, time-specific dynamic parameters or variances.

9.4Why is it called random-intercept rather than random-slope?

For your researchA standard RI-CLPM lets people differ in their usual levels, but it gives everyone the same reappraisal-NA link over time. If you expect that link to differ between people, you need an extended model.

The random intercepts let people have different stable levels of ER and NA. They do not automatically give each person their own lagged ER-NA coefficient.

A conventional RI-CLPM might estimate one common cross-lagged coefficient for a given interval:

γER→NA​=−0.25.

In plain EnglishOne shared number for everyone: a reappraisal deviation 10 points higher at one wave predicts an NA deviation 2.5 points lower at the next wave, holding the earlier NA deviation constant.

The model therefore does not estimate a separate coefficient for each person, such as -0.40 for Jayce and -0.05 for Vi. To represent random temporal slopes, we would need an extended model with that additional structure.

As in Section 4, random intercepts and random slopes answer different questions: random intercepts describe differences in stable levels, and random slopes describe differences in temporal relationships.

9.5RI-CLPM versus DSEM: Similarities

For your researchFor the core within-person question about reappraisal and later NA, the RI-CLPM and DSEM can write down the same lagged equations.

Both can describe:

  • Within-person autoregressive relationships.
  • Within-person cross-lagged relationships.
  • Stable between-person differences.
  • Covariance among stable person-level components.
  • Same-occasion innovation covariance.

A constrained RI-CLPM and a corresponding simple DSEM can express the same lagged within-person equations (Section 9.7).

9.6RI-CLPM versus DSEM: Usual differences

For your researchIn practice, the choice usually follows from your design: a few waves months apart point to the RI-CLPM, many prompts per day point to DSEM. The other differences concern time-specific parameters, random slopes, richer time-series structures, and estimation.

Typical sampling designs. RI-CLPMs are commonly used for panel studies with a relatively small number of waves, for example, baseline, 3 months, 6 months, and 9 months. DSEM is particularly oriented toward intensive longitudinal data, such as 180 EMA occasions per person. The difference lies in common application. Mathematically, either model can be specified for either design, subject to the practical limits described in Section 9.7.

Some studies combine both time scales. A measurement-burst design repeats a week or so of EMA several times, months apart. One study used three one-week bursts spread over a year (Dejonckheere et al., 2018, as cited in Cloos et al., 2026, pp. 39-40). DSEM suits the moment-to-moment dynamics within each burst, and panel models suit the change between bursts. The pre-post model in Part 3 of the walkthrough tab shows one way to model two EMA periods together.

Time-specific parameters. Traditional RI-CLPM implementations often allow wave-specific means and other wave-specific parameters. Analysts can constrain paths to be equal if stationarity is plausible. Basic intensive longitudinal DSEM formulations often use time-invariant dynamic parameters and stable person-specific means, while allowing extensions for trends and other nonstationarity.

Random dynamic coefficients. DSEM accommodates hierarchical variation in autoregressive or cross-lagged coefficients. Conventional RI-CLPM random intercepts account for stable level differences, not necessarily person-specific slopes. Extended RI-CLPMs relax some of these restrictions, for example with multiple indicators, multiple groups, and time-invariant predictors and outcomes (Mulder & Hamaker, 2021).

Richer time-series structures. DSEM frameworks are designed for features such as higher-order lags, dynamic latent variables, and subject-specific innovation variances. SEM can also be extended to contain many of these structures, although some of these extensions are less convenient computationally.

Parameterization and estimation. Different software may use different constraints, latent-variable parameterizations, priors, treatments of initial observations, and estimators. Those differences can affect results even when the conceptual questions are similar.

Both models share a further limitation: cross-lagged panel models can fail to recover cross-lagged effects, for example when the true process involves feedback at a faster time scale than the measurement interval (Muthén & Asparouhov, 2024). A cross-lagged coefficient is always relative to the chosen interval and model.

9.7When could RI-CLPM and DSEM be effectively equivalent?

For your researchIn theory, an RI-CLPM fitted to your EMA data could give the same answer as a simple DSEM. In practice, with 180 prompts per person, the RI-CLPM is impractical to estimate in its usual form, which is the main practical reason for using DSEM with EMA data.

Suppose we fit a three-variable RI-CLPM to all 180 occasions, constrain corresponding lagged coefficients to be equal across intervals, and use an appropriate treatment of stable person differences and innovation covariances.

Now suppose we fit a DSEM with the same dynamic equations, the same initial-condition assumptions, compatible variance structures, and no random temporal slopes. The two models can then encode the same substantive process and may imply the same population covariance structure. With latent centering, the DSEM person means play exactly the role of the RI-CLPM random intercepts, and the DSEM within-person components play the role of the RI-CLPM within-person deviations.

Equivalent structural equations do not guarantee numerically identical estimates if the actual likelihoods, prior distributions, missing-data assumptions, or initialization differ.

The wide-format RI-CLPM is not practical with 180 occasions. An RI-CLPM is usually estimated in wide format, with one column per variable per wave. With 3 variables and 180 occasions that is 540 observed variables for 150 persons: more variables than people, so the sample covariance matrix cannot be of full rank. A heavily constrained model can in principle still be fitted to the raw data, but the unrestricted covariance matrix cannot be estimated, so the usual chi-square test of fit is unavailable, and estimation becomes difficult. Wide format also requires that "occasion 37" means the same moment for everyone, which EMA schedules with random prompts and missed beeps rarely satisfy. DSEM avoids both problems by working in long format, with occasions as rows and a model whose number of parameters does not grow with the number of occasions. This practical limit, and not a difference in the processes the two models can describe, is the main reason DSEM is used for intensive longitudinal data.

Takeaway

The RI-CLPM is a dynamic SEM formulation closely related to DSEM. It explicitly separates stable between-person levels from within-person fluctuations, and it is the natural choice for a handful of widely spaced waves.

10Dynamic structural equation modeling (DSEM)

For your researchThis section explains what DSEM adds to an emotion regulation study: one model in which ER, PA, and NA predict each other over time, each person can have their own dynamics, missed prompts are handled within the model, and the person-specific results can be related to other variables such as depression.

Dynamic structural equation modeling (DSEM) integrates three modeling traditions:

  1. Time-series modeling: Describe dependence across occasions, including autoregressive and cross-lagged processes.
  2. Multilevel modeling: Describe variation between people in levels and, when specified, temporal coefficients or variances.
  3. Structural equation modeling: Represent multiple equations, covariances, latent variables, and measurement models within an integrated framework.

The name does not imply that every DSEM automatically has latent questionnaire factors, correlated innovations, random slopes, or multiple outcomes. Those are modeling choices.

10.1The ordinary multivariate DSEM baseline

For your researchThis writes the whole three-variable system for one person in compact form. You can read it as: each person has usual levels, and their moment-to-moment departures from those levels follow a set of carry-over and cross-influence rules.

Collect our three variables into a vector:

yit​=​ERit​PAit​NAit​​​.

In plain EnglishThe three scores of person i at prompt t, stacked into one column so they can be handled together.

Decompose each person's observed scores into their characteristic levels and within-person departures:

yit​=μi​+wit​.

In plain EnglishEach score equals the person's usual level plus their departure from that level at this prompt.

The vector of person means is:

μi​=​μER,i​μPA,i​μNA,i​​​

In plain EnglishThe person's three usual levels: one for reappraisal, one for PA, and one for NA.

The vector μi​ represents person-specific expected levels under this simplified stationary model, and wit​ represents deviations from those levels. In DSEM, μi​ is latent: it is estimated as part of the model (latent centering), not computed beforehand as an observed average. The elements of wit​ are the ERitW​, PAitW​, and NAitW​ from the notation guide.

A multilevel VAR(1) model is:

wit​=Ai​wi,t−1​+εit​​.

In plain EnglishThe departures at this prompt equal a table of weights (Ai​) applied to the departures at the previous prompt, plus new surprises. This one equation describes the whole dynamic system.

The lag matrix is:

Ai​=​a11,i​a21,i​a31,i​​a12,i​a22,i​a32,i​​a13,i​a23,i​a33,i​​​.

In plain EnglishA three-by-three table of weights for person i. Each row is an outcome at this prompt, and each column is a predictor at the previous prompt.

Rows correspond to later outcomes, and columns correspond to earlier predictors. The matrix therefore contains nine potential lagged relationships.

10.2Expanding the three equations

For your researchThis spells out the compact form as three ordinary-looking regressions, so you can see which number answers "does reappraisal predict later NA?" and which answers "does NA predict later reappraisal?"

ERitW​=PAitW​=NAitW​=​a11,i​ERi,t−1W​+a12,i​PAi,t−1W​+a13,i​NAi,t−1W​+εER,it​,a21,i​ERi,t−1W​+a22,i​PAi,t−1W​+a23,i​NAi,t−1W​+εPA,it​,a31,i​ERi,t−1W​+a32,i​PAi,t−1W​+a33,i​NAi,t−1W​+εNA,it​.​

In plain EnglishThe same system written out as three regressions, one per variable. Each uses all three variables from the previous prompt, with person-specific weights.

For example:

  • a11,i​: Earlier ER → later ER (ER autoregression).
  • a22,i​: Earlier PA → later PA (PA autoregression).
  • a33,i​: Earlier NA → later NA (NA autoregression, often called emotional inertia).
  • a31,i​: Earlier ER → later NA.
  • a13,i​: Earlier NA → later ER.
  • a21,i​: Earlier ER → later PA.

Other off-diagonal entries similarly describe cross-lagged relationships.

10.3A hypothetical lag matrix and its interpretation

For your researchThis interprets a full set of example numbers and shows how to see what the system does over several prompts: for example, how a spike in NA is followed by more reappraisal and then fades away.

Suppose, for illustration, that the modeled population-average coefficients are:

A=​0.400.25−0.30​0.050.60−0.15​0.30−0.100.70​​.

In plain EnglishExample weights, with rows and columns in the order reappraisal, PA, NA. For instance, the bottom-left cell (−0.30) says that reappraisal at one prompt predicts lower NA at the next, and the top-right cell (0.30) says that NA at one prompt predicts more reappraisal at the next.

The row and column order is ER, PA, NA. Interpret four examples:

NA → later ER = +0.30. Occasions with greater-than-usual NA predict greater-than-expected ER at the following occasion, adjusting for the other earlier variables. This is consistent with people deploying strategies when distressed, but not proof of that mechanism.

ER → later NA = -0.30. Greater-than-usual ER predicts lower later NA, conditional on the modeled prior state.

ER → later PA = +0.25. Greater-than-usual ER predicts higher later PA, conditional on the modeled prior state.

NA → later NA = +0.70. NA exhibits substantial conditional persistence over one interval.

All of these are partial predictive coefficients. They are not automatically standardized. Their interpretation in units depends on whether the data were standardized and on the measurement scales used.

These invented values are deliberately large so that the dynamics are easy to see. For comparison, a multilevel VAR(1) model fitted to a synthetic illustration dataset (200 people, 10 prompts a day for 6 days) gave autoregressions of 0.38 for PA and 0.27 for NA and cross-lagged coefficients of only −0.04 (NA to later PA) and −0.11 (PA to later NA) (Lafit, 2026a, pp. 211-214). Small cross-lagged effects are typical of affect data (Section 7.6), which is one reason why EMA studies need many prompts and many people.

The behavior of the system over time. Individual coefficients do not show how the system behaves as a whole, but two tools do: the impulse response and the eigenvalues of the lag matrix.

The first is the impulse response: start from everyone at their usual levels, add a one-time departure to one variable, and apply the lag matrix repeatedly to see how the departure spreads to the other variables over the following occasions. Suppose NA is 10 points above its usual level at occasion 0, while ER and PA are at their usual levels. Multiplying by A step by step gives the expected departures:

Occasions later ER PA NA
0 0.00 0.00 10.00
1 +3.00 -1.00 +7.00
2 +3.25 -0.55 +4.15
3 +2.52 +0.07 +2.01
4 +1.61 +0.47 +0.64
5 +0.86 +0.62 -0.10
6 +0.34 +0.60 -0.42
7 +0.04 +0.49 -0.49

After the NA spike, expected ER rises, NA falls faster than its autoregression alone would imply, expected PA rises a few occasions later, and NA briefly undershoots its usual level around five to seven occasions later before returning. These are implications of the invented matrix, not data. This simple impulse also assumes that a shock to NA arrives alone. When innovations are correlated, a realistic NA shock comes with simultaneous ER and PA shocks, and impulse responses then depend on how that correlation is handled.

The second tool is the set of eigenvalues of A. Eigenvalues are numbers that summarize how strongly the system as a whole amplifies or damps departures from the usual state. If every eigenvalue has a modulus (absolute size) below 1, departures die out and the system is stable. Complex eigenvalues indicate oscillation. For this matrix the eigenvalues are 0.44 and 0.63±0.22i, with moduli 0.44 and 0.67. The system is stable, and the complex pair produces the damped oscillation seen in the table. The oscillation comes from the negative feedback loop described in Section 7.5: NA → later ER is positive while ER → later NA is negative.

10.4What makes this DSEM specifically multilevel?

For your researchThe multilevel part lets each participant have their own set of dynamics, so that you can learn how much people differ in, for example, how strongly reappraisal predicts later NA.

The matrix can differ between participants:

Ai​=Aj​.

In plain EnglishTwo different people, i and j, can have different tables of weights.

Consider these illustrative values:

Participant ER → later NA NA → later ER NA autoregression
Jayce -0.40 +0.35 +0.60
Vi -0.05 +0.10 +0.85
Ekko -0.30 +0.50 +0.45
Jynx +0.10 +0.15 +0.75

One possible random-effect equation is:

a31,i​=γ31​+u31,i​,u31,i​∼N(0,τ312​).

In plain EnglishEach person's reappraisal-to-later-NA weight equals the average weight (γ31​) plus that person's own deviation. The deviations follow a bell curve centered on zero with variance τ312​. Its standard deviation, τ31​, describes how much people differ.

The model estimates the population-average ER → NA slope, the between-person variance in that slope, and person-specific slopes with uncertainty.

Other entries can also vary by person if data and model complexity permit.

Normally distributed random coefficients have one technical side effect: nothing prevents a particular person's matrix, in a particular MCMC draw, from being nonstationary (an eigenvalue with modulus of 1 or more). Mplus reports a warning in such cases and excludes those draws when computing standardized estimates. Occasional warnings are usually harmless. Frequent warnings indicate that, for some persons, a substantial share of the sampled lag matrices is unstable.

10.5Can we relate individual differences in two dynamic parameters?

For your researchThis lets you ask questions such as "do people whose NA lingers longer show a weaker link between reappraisal and later NA?" or "does baseline depression predict how long a person's NA lingers?"

Suppose we ask:

Do individuals with stronger NA persistence tend to show weaker negative ER → later NA associations?

The statistical quantity could be:

Cov(a31,i​,a33,i​).

In plain EnglishAcross people, this covariance says whether a stronger NA carry-over goes together with a stronger or weaker reappraisal-to-later-NA weight.

  • a31,i​ is person i's ER → subsequent NA coefficient.
  • a33,i​ is person i's NA autoregressive coefficient.

A covariance between them describes a between-person relationship between two within-person dynamic parameters. The parameters summarize within-person processes, and the covariance describes how those summaries co-vary across individuals.

An appropriately specified multilevel random-effects model can also estimate a covariance among random slopes, so this covariance is not exclusive to DSEM. DSEM estimates it within a multivariate time-series model, together with the other dynamic parameters.

Using person-specific parameters as predictors and outcomes. The SEM part of DSEM treats each person's mean, inertia, slopes, and innovation variance as latent variables at the between level. These latent variables can then enter any between-level structural model (Hamaker et al., 2023):

  • Predicting the parameters: does baseline depression predict higher mean NA, stronger NA inertia, or a weaker ER → NA slope?
  • A common factor: do several person-specific parameters share one underlying dimension, for example a general affective vulnerability? Indices of affect dynamics tend to cluster into a few dimensions across people (Dejonckheere et al., 2019, as cited in Kuppens & Myin-Germeys, 2026, p. 33).
  • Mediation through dynamics: does baseline depression predict later depression through NA inertia?

An example of the third type used daily NA from 101 young adults in the COGITO study (Hamaker et al., 2017). In standardized terms, baseline depressive symptoms predicted mean NA (0.43) and NA inertia (0.38). Controlling for baseline symptoms, inertia predicted depressive symptoms at follow-up (0.44), but mean NA did not (0.04, with a credible interval that included zero). When each person's innovation variance was added as a third mediator, the pattern was the same (inertia to later symptoms 0.37; mean NA −0.02). In this sample, the persistence of NA, and not its average level, predicted later depressive symptoms. The walkthrough tab shows how such models are specified in Mplus.

10.6Correlated innovations in DSEM

For your researchCorrelated innovations describe surprises that affect several variables at the same prompt, such as a conflict that raises NA, lowers PA, and is met with more reappraisal, all at the same prompt.

The three current outcomes can contain correlated unexpected changes:

εit​∼MVN(0,Σi​).

In plain EnglishThe surprises in the three variables at each prompt come from one joint bell curve, so they can be correlated with each other.

For instance, a surprising conflict might coincide with higher-than-expected NA, lower-than-expected PA, and higher-than-expected ER, even after accounting for the previous occasion. The innovation covariance matrix describes these conditional same-occasion associations. As noted in Section 8.6, current Mplus versions allow both the innovation variances and the innovation correlations to vary across persons.

An innovation is distinct from measurement error: it can reflect a real, unforeseen psychological event. A DSEM can represent measurement error separately in two ways: with item-level latent factors when several items per construct are available (Section 6.4), or with a single indicator per construct through the AR(1)+WN structure, which is identified by the dynamics (Section 6.5).

10.7Extensions of DSEM

For your researchA list of extensions you may need later, for example to handle trends, daily cycles, skewed NA ratings, yes/no items, or effects that span more than one prompt.

Depending on the specification and software, DSEM frameworks can also incorporate:

  • Higher-order lags, such as AR(2): NAt​=ϕ1​NAt−1​+ϕ2​NAt−2​+εt​.
  • Dynamic latent factors, such as a time-varying latent PA construct measured by several indicators.
  • Person-specific innovation variances and correlations, allowing some individuals to have more unpredictable, or more tightly coupled, moment-to-moment affect than others.
  • Covariates and trends, including context, time of day, stressors, and other predictors.
  • Residual DSEM (RDSEM), in which the autoregressive structure is placed on the residuals rather than on the outcomes themselves. In RDSEM, covariate effects are purely "direct" (a lagged outcome does not carry a covariate's effect forward), which makes it convenient for modeling time trends as covariates. Without covariates, RDSEM and DSEM coincide (Asparouhov & Muthén, 2020).
  • Cycles such as daily or weekly rhythms (Muthén, Asparouhov, & Keijsers, 2025), floor effects in skewed symptom ratings (Muthén, Asparouhov, & Shiffman, 2025), missing-not-at-random mechanisms (McNeish, 2025), and intensive longitudinal mediation (McNeish & MacKinnon, 2025).
  • Non-normal outcomes. NA ratings are often skewed, with many low values, and some EMA items are yes/no or counts. In Mplus, binary and ordinal items can be declared categorical in DSEM. For mixed models in R, options include logistic models for yes/no items (such as "Are you alone?"), Poisson models for counts (such as the number of stressful events since the last prompt), Gamma models for positively skewed scores, and negative binomial, zero-inflated, hurdle, and two-part models (Lafit, 2026a, pp. 189-205 and 216-217). Emotion regulation items raise the same issue. An item such as "Since the last prompt, how much did you use reappraisal?" often has many zeros, because at many prompts no regulation was attempted, and a normal model can then fit poorly. Options include the floor-effects approach for DSEM (Muthén, Asparouhov, & Shiffman, 2025) or splitting the item into two parts: whether the strategy was used, and how much when it was. Check the distribution of each item before choosing a model.
  • Complex time-series dependence, when justified and supported by the available information.

In a multivariate VAR(1), stability depends on the eigenvalues of the lag matrix, not on whether each coefficient lies between -1 and +1. A matrix whose individual entries are all modest can still be unstable, and vice versa. Parameter plausibility and system stability should be assessed jointly, as illustrated in Section 10.3.

10.8How DSEM handles missing and unevenly spaced prompts: the Kalman filter idea

For your researchYour participants will miss prompts, and every night creates a long gap. This explains in everyday terms how DSEM fills those gaps using the surrounding answers instead of throwing data away, and why that gives better estimates of how long NA lingers and of what reappraisal predicts.

Real EMA data contain gaps. People miss prompts, and prompts are not equally spaced: two hours during the day, fourteen hours overnight. Lagged models need "the previous occasion," so every gap leaves a lagged predictor missing. DSEM handles these gaps in a way that ordinary lagged regression cannot. Its approach can be understood through the Kalman filter, a method engineers have used since 1960 (Kalman, 1960; Harvey, 1989).

The Kalman filter in plain words

Imagine you want to know Jayce's true level of negative affect at every moment. You never see it directly. You only have two imperfect sources of information:

  1. A prediction. From Jayce's NA at the previous prompt and his inertia, you can predict where his NA should be now. With ϕ=0.70, if he was 10 points above his usual level two hours ago, you predict about 7 points above it now. The prediction is uncertain, because new things may have happened since then (innovations).
  2. A measurement. Jayce's new self-report. It is also imperfect, because of measurement error.

The Kalman filter combines the two, giving more weight to whichever source is more precise. At every prompt it repeats three steps:

  1. Predict. Move the previous best guess forward with the model (multiply its deviation by ϕ) and widen the uncertainty, because innovations may have occurred.
  2. Compare. See how far the new report is from the prediction.
  3. Update. Move the guess part of the way toward the report. The fraction moved is called the Kalman gain:
K=uncertainty of the prediction+measurement-error varianceuncertainty of the prediction​.

In plain EnglishThe Kalman gain is the weight given to the new report. The more uncertain the prediction is compared with the report, the further the guess moves toward the report.

If the self-reports are very precise, K is close to 1 and the guess jumps almost all the way to the report. If the reports are noisy, K is small and the guess moves only a little. The updated guess is also more certain than either source alone, because two independent pieces of information have been combined.

Missing prompts. When a prompt is missing, there is nothing to compare, so the filter skips steps 2 and 3. It keeps the prediction and lets the uncertainty grow. At the next observed prompt it compares and updates again. The information from before the gap is therefore carried across it, discounted by the dynamics (ϕ2 for a two-step gap), with correspondingly larger uncertainty.

A companion tool, the Kalman smoother, goes back over the whole series afterwards and also uses the prompts that came after a gap. The estimate for a missing prompt then uses information from both sides of the gap.

What DSEM does

DSEM turns an unequal-interval problem into a missing-data problem. TINTERVAL places the prompts on a regular time grid, empty grid cells become missing values, and these are handled with "a discrete-time Kalman filter approach, which is known to perform well in case of data missing at random" (Hamaker et al., 2023, p. 580).

Strictly speaking, Mplus does the equivalent work inside its Bayesian sampler. Missing values are treated like unknown parameters: at every iteration, the sampler draws new values for them given the model, the current parameter values, and the surrounding data (Asparouhov et al., 2018). Over many iterations, for a linear model with normally distributed errors and given the parameters, these draws follow the same distribution that a Kalman smoother computes. The sampler also averages over uncertainty in the parameters. For missing prompts, the plain-words description above therefore describes what DSEM achieves, even though Mplus does not run a separate filter. The grid approach "tends to work quite well up to 80% of missing data" (Hamaker et al., 2023, p. 581). Here the missing data are mainly the empty grid cells that TINTERVAL inserts, not prompts that participants skipped, and the figure comes from simulations under specific conditions (Asparouhov et al., 2018). It is not a general tolerance for nonresponse. Inserting too many missing values between observations can also destabilize the estimation (Asparouhov et al., 2018).

Which part of the filter applies depends on the model. The plain-words description assumed that each report contains measurement error. A DSEM without a measurement-error term, such as the main input in Section 13.2, assumes instead that each report is the person's exact state at that moment. Its measurement-error variance is 0, so K=1: the model takes every observed report at face value and uses the prediction step only to fill in missing prompts. The weighting between prediction and report happens only when a measurement-error term is added (Section 6.5). Filling in missing prompts, separating measurement error from the true state, and handling unequal gaps are therefore three different problems. DSEM can address all three, but the default model addresses only the first, and the third when TINTERVAL is used.

This approach assumes that prompts are missed "at random." This means that, once the observed data are taken into account, whether a prompt is missed does not depend on the unobserved values themselves. Missed prompts can follow a pattern, for example when a participant consistently misses the first prompt of the day, or depend on the very phenomenon under study, as when a patient skips prompts during panic (Cloos et al., 2026, p. 62). Time-of-day patterns can be handled by including time in the model. In a study that recorded short audio snippets at missed prompts, there was little evidence that missing a prompt was related to emotions or social interactions (Sun et al., 2021, as cited in Cloos et al., 2026, p. 62). When missingness depends on the unobserved NA itself, models for data missing not at random are needed (McNeish, 2025; Section 10.7).

What ordinary lagged regression cannot do

Consider an ordinary lagged multilevel regression in lmer(). Each row needs an observed outcome and an observed lagged predictor, which creates three problems.

  1. Every missed prompt removes two pieces of information. A missed 2 p.m. prompt removes the pair (noon, 2 p.m.) and the pair (2 p.m., 4 p.m.). With 30% of prompts missing at random, only about half of the consecutive pairs remain (0.70×0.70=0.49). The noon report still contains information about 4 p.m., but lagged regression cannot use it. DSEM can, because the model links the noon report to 4 p.m. through the dynamics. (In the example dataset described in Section 5.2, this rule and the overnight rule cost the lagged analysis 23% of its rows.)
  2. Using the last available prompt silently changes the lag. If the analyst lags to the previous available row, some "one-step" lags span four or six hours. The coefficient then blends different intervals. In this example, with positive inertia that fades over time, the blend pulls the coefficient toward zero. For cross-lagged coefficients, which can rise and then fall as the interval grows (Section 14.1), the direction of the bias can differ. Filling a missing lag with an earlier prompt "would again require further adjustments to the model" for the longer lag (Viechtbauer, 2026b, p. 182).
  3. A lagged predictor measured with error is treated as error-free. Regression takes the predictor at face value, so measurement error in NA at t−1 attenuates the estimated inertia. A state-space model (the Kalman framework, or DSEM with a measurement-error term) separates the latent state from the noisy report and estimates the inertia of the latent state.

A simulation shows the size of all three problems. 150 simulated persons each had 180 prompts and a true NA inertia of 0.50. "Within-person reliability" is the share of within-person variance in the reports that comes from the true state rather than measurement error. Each cell is the average estimate over 20 simulated studies. Because each simulated study is large, the estimates varied little from study to study: the Monte Carlo standard error of each cell (the uncertainty that comes from averaging a limited number of studies) is between 0.001 and 0.004. The R code is in Section 21.2.

Condition Lagged regression, complete pairs Lagged regression, last available prompt Model-based, no measurement-error term Model-based, with measurement-error term
Complete data, no measurement error 0.49 0.49 0.50 0.50
30% of prompts missing 0.49 0.40 0.50 0.50
Within-person reliability 0.70, complete data 0.34 0.34 0.35 0.50
Within-person reliability 0.70, 30% missing 0.34 0.28 0.36 0.50

"Model-based" means maximum likelihood with a Kalman filter and a latent person mean, which targets the same quantities as DSEM with latent centering.

  • Missing at random, complete pairs only: lagged regression remains approximately unbiased but is less precise. In a separate set of 200 simulated studies with 40% of prompts missing, the standard deviation of the complete-pair estimates across studies was about 1.25 times that of the model-based estimates (bootstrap 95% interval 1.15 to 1.35). Since precision grows with sample size, complete-pair regression would need roughly 1.5 times as many persons to be as precise.
  • The large biases come from lagging to the last available prompt and from ignoring measurement error. The Kalman approach removes the first bias without further specification. The second requires the model to include a measurement-error term (Section 6.5).
  • The small difference in the first row (0.49 versus 0.50) is Nickell bias, which is small with 180 prompts per person (Section 5.4).

Comparison with other approaches.

  • lmer() has all three problems above and uses observed rather than latent person means.
  • Lagged regression with the interval as a moderator. One can compute the time since the previous prompt and let it interact with the lagged predictor, so that the lagged association can weaken over longer gaps (Selig et al., 2012; suggested in Viechtbauer, 2026b, p. 181). This takes unequal spacing into account, but it still drops the pairs around missed prompts and treats the lagged predictor as error-free.
  • nlme or glmmTMB with continuous-time residual structures (corCAR1(), ou()) handle unequal spacing in the residuals. The lagged predictors, however, must still be observed, and measurement error in them is not separated.
  • RI-CLPM in wide format uses full-information maximum likelihood, which also uses all available data. It requires the same waves for everyone, which EMA schedules do not provide.
  • Continuous-time models, such as ctsem in R (which uses the Kalman filter directly) or continuous-time RDSEM in Mplus, use the exact time stamps instead of a grid. They are "the most truthful way to handle unequal intervals" (Hamaker et al., 2023, p. 580), although the grid-with-missing-data approach performed about equally well in simulations (De Haan-Rietdijk et al., 2017).

The Kalman approach is therefore not unique to DSEM. DSEM combines it with random effects for every person, latent centering, optional measurement-error terms, and a between-level SEM in one model.

11Comparison of the four approaches

For your researchThis section puts the four approaches side by side, so that you can match your emotion regulation question to the simplest approach that answers it.

This table concerns common implementations, not absolute mathematical limits. Whether a capability is present depends on the actual model specified.

Capability MLM via lmer() MSEM Conventional RI-CLPM Multilevel DSEM
Handles repeated observations Yes Yes Yes Yes
Separates within- and between-person associations If specified appropriately (observed person means) Yes, with latent person means Core design feature Core feature (latent centering)
Estimates same-occasion ER-NA association Yes Yes Can represent within-wave association/covariance Yes
Estimates lagged ER → NA association With lagged predictors With lagged structure Yes Yes
Estimates NA autoregression With lagged NA (Nickell bias in short series) With lagged structure Yes Yes (no Nickell bias)
Estimates random lagged ER → NA slopes Yes, if specified Possible Not in a conventional RI-CLPM Yes, if specified
Estimates ER, PA, and NA jointly Not with three ordinary separate lmer() fits Yes Yes Yes
Estimates cross-outcome innovation covariance Not with ordinary separate lmer() fits Possible Yes Yes, including person-specific (random) correlations
Represents item-level latent measurement models Not natively Yes With an appropriate measurement extension Yes; also single-indicator AR(1)+WN
Separates day-level from moment-level variation Three-level random intercepts, e.g., (1 | id/day) Three-level SEM No Three-level DSEM (Mplus 9 and later)
Handles unequal spacing directly With nlme corCAR1() or glmmTMB ou() residuals No No (wave-based) TINTERVAL approximation; continuous-time RDSEM for two-level observed-variable models
Naturally oriented toward very dense EMA Less specialized Depends on specification Less commonly used for dense EMA (wide format) Yes
Accommodates rich time-series structures Limited in lmer() itself With extensions With extensions A central design goal
Bayesian estimation required? No No No Not mathematically; in Mplus, yes (ESTIMATOR = BAYES); the R package mlts is also Bayesian

A "yes" in the table means the framework can represent it, not that every analysis automatically does. A "no" or "not conventional" does not mean that an equivalent model is impossible through extensions or other software.

The table should not be read as a ranking in which DSEM is always best. A simpler model that answers the intended question under defensible assumptions is preferable to an unnecessarily complex model.

11.1When the four approaches agree and when they differ

For your researchIf your question is "on average, does reappraisal predict lower NA at the next prompt?", all four approaches can give the same answer. Their answers differ when you ask about differences between people, volatility, measurement error, or gaps.

When the four approaches give the same answer. Suppose the question is: "On average, when a person's ER is higher than usual at one prompt, is their NA lower than expected at the next prompt, holding their previous NA constant?" The estimand is one fixed within-person cross-lagged coefficient β, with stable person means removed. Suppose also that the data are complete, the prompts are equally spaced, measurement error is negligible, each person has many occasions, and the same equation is fitted. Then a lagged MLM, a dynamic MSEM, a constrained RI-CLPM, and a DSEM without random slopes all estimate the same β. In the analogous simulation for inertia in Section 10.8, run under exactly these conditions, lagged regression gave 0.49 and the model-based estimate 0.50 (true value 0.50). The small differences that remain come from Nickell bias, priors, and the handling of the first observation.

When they give different answers. The approaches give different answers when the question concerns a quantity that only some of them estimate in their usual form:

  • Do people differ in how strongly ER predicts later NA? A random-slope MLM or DSEM gives the average slope and the spread of slopes, whereas a conventional RI-CLPM gives one slope for everyone.
  • Does NA also predict later ER, and do the two variables share surprises? A joint model (MSEM, RI-CLPM, DSEM) estimates both directions and the innovation covariance, whereas two separate lmer() fits do not estimate the covariance.
  • Are some people more emotionally volatile? Only DSEM routinely gives each person their own innovation variance.
  • Is inertia underestimated because of measurement error? DSEM can include a measurement-error term even with single items, whereas a lagged MLM cannot.
  • How are missed prompts and overnight gaps handled? DSEM carries information across them through the model, whereas a lagged MLM drops the affected pairs.
  • What if the data are four waves, months apart? The RI-CLPM is the natural choice, because DSEM needs many occasions per person.

11.2Practical requirements of each approach

For your researchBefore choosing DSEM, check what it will cost you in data, decisions, computing time, software, and learning, compared with simpler options that may already answer your question.

Each gain in flexibility requires more data, assumptions, decisions, time, or money. The table summarizes typical costs for a design like ours. The thresholds are rough rules of thumb from the sources cited in Sections 5, 9, and 13, not hard limits.

Cost MLM via lmer() MSEM RI-CLPM DSEM (Mplus)
Data format Long format; lagged variables built by hand Long format Wide format; the same waves for everyone Long format; a time variable for the grid
How much data Contemporaneous models: modest. Lagged models: many occasions per person, or Nickell bias grows Tens to hundreds of persons for stable between-level estimates At least 3 waves; usually hundreds of persons Roughly 50 or more persons and 20 or more observed occasions each; 25 or more for random slopes and variances
Missing prompts Rows with a missing outcome or lag are dropped Maximum likelihood or Bayes uses available data Full-information maximum likelihood Handled within the Bayesian sampler (Section 10.8)
Unequal spacing Ignored unless coded (or continuous-time residuals in nlme) Usually ignored Each interval gets its own parameters, or equal intervals are assumed Time grid (TINTERVAL) or continuous-time RDSEM
Key assumptions Linear, normal residuals; observed person means and lagged predictors treated as error-free Linear, normal; measurement model correct Stable trait plus within-person process; comparable measurement across waves Linear, normal at both levels; stationarity unless trends are modeled; normal random effects; priors
Estimation REML or ML ML or Bayes ML (FIML) Bayesian MCMC only (in Mplus)
Decisions to make and report Centering, lag construction, which slopes are random Latent or observed covariates, measurement model Equality constraints across waves, invariance Time grid, priors, iterations, convergence checks, which effects are random
Computing time (our design) Seconds Seconds to minutes Not feasible with 180 waves Minutes to hours
Software lme4, free lavaan (free; random intercepts only) or Mplus (commercial) lavaan (free) or Mplus Mplus (commercial) or mlts in R (free, Stan-based)
