12Statistical model versus estimation method

For your researchThis section separates two things that are often confused: the model (what you assume about how reappraisal and NA relate) and the estimation method (how the computer finds the numbers). It also shows how to read Bayesian output if you are used to p-values.

A statistical model describes the mathematical relationships and probability assumptions. For example:

NAitW​=ϕi​NAi,t−1W​+βi​ERi,t−1W​+εit​.

In plain EnglishThe model: each person's NA departure is predicted from their own previous NA and previous reappraisal, with person-specific weights. How the numbers are found from the data is a separate choice.

A complete statistical specification also states how the random effects are distributed, how innovations behave, what conditions apply to initial observations, how missing data are handled, and so forth.

An estimation method describes how we use data to learn the model's parameters. Examples include:

  • Maximum likelihood.
  • Restricted maximum likelihood (REML, for appropriate mixed-model settings). Plain maximum likelihood treats the fixed effects as known when it estimates the variance components, so with few persons the variance estimates are biased. REML reduces this bias (Lafit, 2026b, p. 226). The ML bias is downward: the variances come out too small.
  • Bayesian estimation with Markov chain Monte Carlo.

R's lmer() is a software implementation for particular mixed models; MSEM and DSEM are modeling frameworks; and "Bayesian" describes an inferential approach, not a unique psychological model.

If two implementations specify the same likelihood and parameter restrictions, they can represent the same underlying process even if one is called a mixed model and another is called SEM. Bayesian results can differ because of priors and uncertainty conventions. Frequentist implementations can differ because of estimators, approximation, and finite-sample behavior.

The estimation method also changes what the output means, even for the same model:

Output Frequentist (e.g., lmer()) Bayesian (e.g., Mplus DSEM)
Point estimate Maximum likelihood (or REML) estimate Posterior median (Mplus default) or mean
Uncertainty Standard error; confidence interval with a long-run coverage guarantee Posterior standard deviation; credible interval containing 95% of posterior probability
"p-value" Probability of data at least as extreme under H0​ Mplus prints a one-tailed p-value: the proportion of posterior draws on the other side of zero. It is a posterior probability, not a frequentist p-value
Person-specific slopes Predictions (BLUPs, conditional modes) Posterior distributions

With diffuse priors and large samples, the Bayesian one-tailed value is often numerically close to half of a two-sided frequentist p-value, but the two answer different questions and should not be used interchangeably in a Neyman-Pearson decision rule without saying so.

The choice among the four approaches should follow from the assumptions and estimands implied by the fitted equations.

13Estimating DSEM in Mplus in practice (as of Mplus 9.1.1)

For your researchThis is the hands-on part: which Mplus version to use, a starting model for ER, PA, and NA, how to read the output, how much data you need, and a safe order in which to build up your model.

This section collects practical information that the conceptual sections leave out. It reflects the Mplus documentation and methodological papers available in October 2026. Software changes, so check the version history on the Mplus website before relying on any detail.

13.1Mplus versions and DSEM-related changes

For your researchCheck your Mplus version before running DSEM: one recent version had a bug that can distort results under a common setting.

The current release is Mplus 9.1.1 (September 16, 2026). It is a corrective release: in Mplus 9.1, two-level DSEM models with lagged observed variables gave distorted results when PROCESSORS exceeded the number of MCMC chains (for example, PROCESSORS = 8 without a matching CHAINS setting). If you ran such models in 9.1, rerun them in 9.1.1.

DSEM-relevant milestones:

13.2A minimal two-level DSEM for our three variables

For your researchA ready-to-adapt Mplus input for the three-variable ER-PA-NA model, with notes on its main parts.

The input below sketches the ER-PA-NA VAR(1) from Section 10 with two random dynamic coefficients. It is illustrative: check it against the DSEM examples in the Mplus User's Guide and a primer on DSEM in Mplus (McNeish & Hamaker, 2020) before use. As in R, the variable is renamed negaff to avoid any confusion with missing-value codes.

Check the time grid before you run it. With TINTERVAL = hours(2) and time counted in hours since the start of the study, this input places all of a person's prompts on one two-hour grid that runs through the nights. Each night becomes six missing grid rows, and the model carries the same dynamics through them, which implies an overnight carryover of about ϕ7 (Section 14.2). The process does not start afresh each morning. If your question concerns only consecutive prompts within a day, use three-level DSEM (Section 15) or one of the other options in Section 14.2.

Mplus input (illustrative)
TITLE:     ER-PA-NA multilevel VAR(1) with two random coefficients;
DATA:      FILE = ema.dat;
VARIABLE:  NAMES = id day prompt hours er pa negaff;
           USEVARIABLES = er pa negaff;
           MISSING = ALL (-999);      ! missing-value code in ema.dat
           CLUSTER = id;
           LAGGED = er(1) pa(1) negaff(1);
           TINTERVAL = hours(2);      ! hours since study start
ANALYSIS:  TYPE = TWOLEVEL RANDOM;
           ESTIMATOR = BAYES;
           CHAINS = 2;
           PROCESSORS = 2;            ! never more than CHAINS in 9.1
           BITERATIONS = (5000);      ! minimum number of iterations
MODEL:     %WITHIN%
           s31 | negaff ON er&1;      ! random ER -> later NA
           s33 | negaff ON negaff&1;  ! random NA inertia
           negaff ON pa&1;
           er ON er&1 pa&1 negaff&1;
           pa ON er&1 pa&1 negaff&1;
           er WITH pa negaff;         ! innovation covariances
           pa WITH negaff;
           %BETWEEN%
           er WITH pa negaff s31 s33;
           pa WITH negaff s31 s33;
           negaff WITH s31 s33;
           s31 WITH s33;              ! Cov(a31_i, a33_i), Section 10.5
OUTPUT:    TECH1 TECH8 STANDARDIZED;
PLOT:      TYPE = PLOT3;

Notes on the main pieces:

  • MISSING declares the code that marks missing values in the data file. Change it to the code your file uses.
  • LAGGED creates the lagged versions of observed variables (er&1, and so on). For a latent variable, the lag is declared in its BY statement with (&1) and then used as f&1, as in the measurement-error model below.
  • TINTERVAL places observations on a regular time grid (here, two-hour bins) and inserts missing rows where no observation falls. If two observations fall in the same bin, Mplus moves one of them to an adjacent bin (Hamaker et al., 2023). Section 14.2 explains what the grid implies for overnight gaps.
  • On the between level, the person means of er, pa, and negaff are latent variables (latent centering), and s31 and s33 are the person-specific coefficients.
  • Mplus computes standardized coefficients for each person and averages them across persons when the model contains random slopes or variances. For significance statements about the average of a random slope, use the unstandardized mean.

A single-indicator measurement-error model (AR(1)+WN, Section 6.5) for NA alone has this core:

Mplus input (illustrative)
MODEL:     %WITHIN%
           f BY negaff@1(&1); ! latent NA state; (&1) creates its lag f&1
           f ON f&1;          ! latent autoregression
           negaff;            ! measurement-error variance
           %BETWEEN%
           negaff;

13.3Reading Bayesian output as a Neyman-Pearson statistician

For your researchHow to translate Mplus's Bayesian output (posterior medians, credible intervals, one-tailed p-values) into the terms you would use in a frequentist analysis, and which checks to report in your paper.

  • Point estimates are posterior medians by default. Posterior standard deviations play the role of standard errors.
  • 95% credible intervals are the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the posterior draws. They are probability statements about the parameter given the data and prior, not long-run coverage statements, although with diffuse priors and adequate data they often behave similarly.
  • The one-tailed p-value is the proportion of posterior draws on the opposite side of zero from the estimate (Section 12). For variances it is always close to zero by construction (Section 4.6).
  • Convergence is judged with the potential scale reduction factor (PSRF), which compares variability between chains to variability within chains. Values close to 1 indicate that independent chains agree. Mplus 9 also reports the effective sample size (ESS) of the posterior draws: how many independent draws the autocorrelated chain is worth. Inspect trace plots (PLOT: TYPE = PLOT3) and, as a robustness check, rerun with a fixed, larger number of iterations to confirm that the estimates do not change.
  • Priors. Mplus defaults are intended to be diffuse: flat or very wide normal priors for intercepts, slopes, and loadings; an inverse-gamma prior IG(-1, 0), equivalent to a uniform prior on (0, infinity), for single variances; and inverse-Wishart priors for covariance matrices. With many persons and many occasions, as here, the data usually dominate the estimates of fixed effects. Random-effect variances are a partial exception: the inverse-Wishart prior "tends to be informative when variances are close to zero" (Schuurman, Grasman, & Hamaker, 2016), which is typical for the variance of an autoregressive or cross-lagged coefficient across persons, and its influence grows as the number of persons falls. Run a prior sensitivity analysis and preregister priors and the sensitivity set, which limits researcher degrees of freedom.
  • Model comparison. The main index Mplus reports for DSEM is the deviance information criterion (DIC). DIC is known to be unstable in models with many random effects, so combine it with convergence checks, substantive plausibility, and sensitivity analyses rather than treating small DIC differences as decisive.
  • Standardized estimates. A recommended approach standardizes each person's coefficients with that person's own within-person standard deviations (Schuurman, Ferrer, et al., 2016). Mplus does this within every MCMC iteration and reports "Within-Level Standardized Estimates Averaged Over Clusters." The posterior SD of this average describes uncertainty about the average, not how much people differ. In addition, standardized and unstandardized person-specific slopes can rank people differently, so correlations among random effects can change, or even disappear, after standardization. In one EMA study, a clear negative correlation between the unstandardized slopes linking events and negative affect disappeared after standardization. Which version is more informative depends on the purpose (Hamaker et al., 2023).
  • Overall model fit. Unlike ordinary SEM, DSEM has no saturated model to compare against, so there is no overall fit test like the chi-square. The practical checks are: residual autocorrelation (any that remains means the dynamics are not fully captured), comparison of rival models with DIC (which can be unstable), the Bayesian Wald test for sets of parameters, and credible intervals for individual parameters. Bayes factors exist but are sensitive to the priors (Hamaker et al., 2023). A useful additional check is predictive: simulate data from the fitted model (in R, or with Mplus's Monte Carlo facility using the estimates as population values) and compare features that matter for your question, such as each person's autocorrelations, standard deviations, and share of responses at the scale floor, between the simulated and the observed data. Convergence diagnostics (PSRF, ESS, trace plots) only show whether the sampler has settled; they say nothing about whether the model fits.

13.4How much data does DSEM need?

For your researchRough numbers for how many participants and answered prompts you need for the model you have in mind, and how to plan your sample size more precisely.

Simulation studies and practical guidance can be summarized as follows (McNeish, 2019; Muthén & Asparouhov, 2023; Schultzberg & Muthén, 2018). These are rough benchmarks, not guarantees.

  • Occasions per person: at least about 15 to 20 observed occasions for basic models; at least about 25 for random slopes and random innovation variances; around 50 for good single-person (N = 1) performance.
  • Persons: about 50 at a minimum, and precise estimates of between-person variances and covariances may require several hundred.
  • Trade-off: more persons compensate for fewer occasions more effectively than the reverse.
  • Inserted rows do not count: rows inserted by TINTERVAL are missing data and contain no information. Count observed occasions per person.

Our design (150 persons, up to 180 occasions each) exceeds these benchmarks for random dynamic coefficients, provided compliance is reasonable. Exceeding them does not guarantee precise estimates of every parameter: the variance of the random ER-NA slope and its covariance with inertia are the parameters most likely to remain uncertain, and a simulation of the planned model (below) is the way to check.

Planning by simulation. For a specific hypothesis, simulation-based power analysis is recommended: generate many datasets from the model you expect, fit the planned model to each, and count how often the effect is detected (Lafit, 2026b, pp. 221-222). The free PowerAnalysisIL app (Lafit et al., 2021) covers common multilevel questions, including multilevel autoregressive models, group differences in autoregression, and person-level predictors of autoregression, and it builds in the autocorrelation of EMA data. Practical points (Lafit, 2026b):

  • The app assumes equally spaced prompts and no missing data, so enter the number of prompts you expect people to answer, not the number you plan to send (p. 235).
  • Whether more persons or more prompts helps more depends on the hypothesis. For a difference between groups of people, adding prompts helped little: with 20 persons per group, power rose only from about 0.49 to about 0.57 when the number of prompts went from 20 to 200 (p. 234, Table 11.3).
  • When the expected effect is uncertain, compute power over a range of plausible values (a sensitivity power analysis), or use safeguard power analysis (Lafit et al., 2025; Lafit, 2026b, p. 236).

For DSEM itself, the same logic can be applied with Mplus's Monte Carlo facility (Schultzberg & Muthén, 2018).

13.5Building the model step by step

For your researchA safe order in which to build up your DSEM, so that problems are caught early and your final model is not the result of undisclosed trial and error.

  1. Look at the data first. Plot each person's ER, PA, and NA over time (Viechtbauer, 2026a, pp. 155-157). Check for trends over the study and over the day, and for an initial elevation in the first prompts (Section 8.3). Model trends as covariates when present. RDSEM is convenient for this (Section 10.7).
  2. Start with random intercepts only (person means) and fixed dynamic coefficients.
  3. Add random slopes one at a time, retaining those whose variance is supported by the data (for example, a variance estimate that is large relative to its posterior standard deviation, Section 4.6). Avoid estimating all covariances among random effects at once.
  4. Keep the number of random effects well below the number of observed occasions per person.
  5. Remove persons with no within-person variation on an outcome, because they contribute nothing to within-person dynamics and can impede convergence. If you also exclude participants with low compliance, remember that any such cutoff is arbitrary, and a sensitivity analysis can check whether the conclusions change with a different cutoff (Viechtbauer, 2026a, p. 151). State the cutoff in advance (step 6).
  6. Preregister the sequence and the decision rules, so that the final model is not the product of undisclosed specification search. A preregistration template written specifically for ESM studies is available, with a tutorial (Kirtley et al., 2021), and post-registration is an option when the data already exist (Kirtley, 2026, pp. 102-103).

13.6Alternatives in R

For your researchFree R alternatives if you do not have Mplus, with what each one can and cannot do.

  • mlts (version 2.0.1, CRAN, December 2025) fits multilevel manifest and latent time-series models, including DSEM-type models, using Stan.
  • brms can fit multivariate multilevel models with manually created lagged predictors (using observed centering unless latent centering is coded explicitly).
  • ctsem and dynr fit continuous-time and state-space dynamic models.
  • nlme and glmmTMB provide AR(1) and continuous-time residual structures for single-outcome mixed models (Section 5.4).
  • mlVAR and graphicalVAR estimate multilevel and person-specific VAR models and display them as networks (Lafit, 2026a, p. 215). With its default lmer estimator, mlVAR centers on observed person means, so Nickell bias applies to short series. Its estimator = "Mplus" option instead runs Bayesian DSEM in Mplus. Network "centrality" indices computed from such models have been criticized as unstable and hard to interpret for psychological variables (Bringmann et al., 2019, as cited in Lafit, 2026a, p. 215).
  • Data preparation. R code for the data checks and analyses in Chapters 8 and 9 of Myin-Germeys and Kuppens (2026) is available at www.real-leuven.be, and a step-by-step preprocessing framework with an R package and tutorial website is available at preprocess.esmtools.com (Revol et al., 2024, as cited in Viechtbauer, 2026a, p. 147).

14Time spacing, missing prompts, and the meaning of a lag

For your researchThis section explains why the time between prompts is part of your result. A link between reappraisal and NA two hours later need not equal the same link across a night, and missed prompts can silently change the lag.

Our example uses six prompts per day. Suppose they arrive at 10 a.m., noon, 2 p.m., 4 p.m., 6 p.m., and 8 p.m.

  • The gap from 2 p.m. to 4 p.m. is 2 hours.
  • The gap from 8 p.m. to 10 a.m. is 14 hours.

A naive discrete-time equation:

NAt​=ϕNAt−1​+βERt−1​+εt​

In plain EnglishNA at a prompt is predicted from NA and reappraisal at the previous prompt, with the same weights whether that prompt was two hours ago or the evening before.

This equation uses the same parameters for every "one-step" transition unless differences in spacing are represented explicitly. It therefore makes a substantive assumption: a two-hour prediction and a 14-hour prediction are treated as equal. For emotion processes, this assumption is often implausible.

14.1How much can a lag coefficient depend on the interval?

For your researchThis shows how quickly a carry-over or cross-lagged effect can change with the length of the gap, so that you choose, and report, the time scale of your reappraisal effects deliberately.

A continuous-time model describes the process as evolving smoothly between measurements, so that the lag coefficient depends on the elapsed time Δt. For a single variable, the continuous-time AR(1) (an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process) implies

ϕ(Δt)=e−θΔt.

In plain EnglishThe carry-over shrinks smoothly as the gap grows. The gap in hours is Δt, and θ sets how fast the carry-over fades.

Here θ>0 is the rate at which deviations decay. Mplus calls the corresponding parameter the drift. It follows that doubling the interval squares the coefficient.

Suppose the two-hour coefficient is ϕ(2)=0.70. Then:

  • The one-hour coefficient is 0.701/2≈0.84.
  • The 14-hour overnight coefficient is 0.707≈0.08.

If both kinds of transitions are pooled into a single discrete-time ϕ, the estimate is a blend of roughly 0.70 and 0.08 and describes neither interval. In multivariate continuous-time models, cross-lagged coefficients need not be monotone in Δt: they often rise, peak at some interval, and then fall. A cross-lagged effect can therefore look strong at one sampling interval and negligible at another.

Smaller differences between daytime intervals. With semi-random prompting, daytime intervals also vary, for example between 20 and 160 minutes in one example dataset (Viechtbauer, 2026a, p. 146). Treating semi-random intervals as equal is "relatively safe" "because the differences in the intervals will generally equal out" (Cloos et al., 2026, p. 51). For a rough average coefficient, and once the overnight gap is handled separately, this is often a workable assumption, but it is not exact. Because ϕ(Δt) is curved, a mix of shorter and longer intervals does not average out to the coefficient for the average interval. In simulations, a discrete-time model accounting only for the night was biased by as much as 60% of the true parameter when the true autocorrelation was small (below 0.3), with the size and direction of the bias depending strongly on the true values. A time-grid approach (the analogue of Mplus's TINTERVAL) performed about as well as the exact continuous-time model, although coarser grids would likely perform less well, and continuous-time modeling is recommended whenever possible (De Haan-Rietdijk et al., 2017). When the precise size of a lagged effect is of interest, use one of these two options.

14.2Strategies for handling overnight gaps and unequal intervals

For your researchPractical options for handling nights and uneven gaps in your data, from the simplest (start the lags afresh each morning) to the most complete (continuous-time or three-level models).

Possible strategies include:

  1. Treat overnight transitions separately, or exclude them from the within-day lag process when theoretically justified. In R, compute lags within days (Section 5.2). In two-level Mplus models, inserting an empty record between days does not work as a reset. Mplus imputes every missing value at every iteration from the model, so the empty record is filled in from the previous evening, and the night becomes a two-step transition (a carryover of about ϕ2, which is 0.49 for ϕ=0.70, more than the ϕ7 of strategy 2). Inserting many empty records makes the overnight carryover close to zero (the two-level model in the smoking example of Asparouhov & Muthén, 2026, had at least 24 missing rows between days), at the cost of more missing data and slower convergence. Three-level DSEM (strategy 4) handles the night directly.
  2. Discretize time with TINTERVAL (Mplus). Observations are placed on a regular grid, and empty grid cells become missing rows. With two-hour bins and prompts from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m., each night inserts six missing rows, so even perfect compliance produces 50% missing rows. The model then treats a night as seven two-hour steps, implying an overnight coefficient of about ϕ7. This assumes that the process evolves overnight exactly as it does during the day. Whether sleep is better treated as a "reset" is a substantive question. If two prompts fall in the same grid cell, Mplus moves one of them to an adjacent cell (Hamaker et al., 2023), which changes the intervals slightly. With semi-random prompting, check how the prompts were assigned to cells and whether the results change with the bin width. Smaller bins approximate continuous time better but create more missing rows and slower convergence. In one example, data coverage was 17% with one-unit bins, 34% with two-unit bins, and 51% with three-unit bins (Muthén & Asparouhov, 2023).
  3. Use a continuous-time model. Mplus 8.11 and later offer continuous-time RDSEM (CTIME option), which uses the actual time stamps, inserts no rows, and estimates a drift. Current limitations: two-level models, observed variables only, lag-1 dynamics only. In R, ctsem offers general continuous-time SEM, and nlme::corCAR1() and glmmTMB's ou() provide continuous-time residual structures.
  4. Model the day as its own level with three-level DSEM (Section 15). Each day becomes its own within-day series, the overnight gap is never treated as a lag, and day-to-day carryover is modeled separately at the day level.
  5. Include sensible time-of-day, day-level, or contextual predictors when nonstationarity is plausible, for example daily cycles (Muthén, Asparouhov, & Keijsers, 2025).
  6. Let the time since the previous prompt moderate the lagged effect in a mixed model (Selig et al., 2012; Section 10.8). This is easy in lmer(), but it is an approximation, and it still drops the pairs around missed prompts.

14.3Missing prompts

For your researchA missed prompt can turn a two-hour lag into a four-hour lag without you noticing, unless the lags are constructed as described below.

Missing prompts can also create accidental "longer lags": if the 2 p.m. assessment is missing, the prior observed prompt for 4 p.m. may be noon, not 2 p.m. Taking the preceding available row may therefore change the estimand. The R code in Section 5.2 sets such lags to missing. TINTERVAL and continuous-time models handle them by construction.

These problems are not automatically solved by DSEM. They arise from the temporal structure of the study and must be addressed in model construction.

14.4Additional design issue: What time interval does an ER item refer to?

For your researchIf your reappraisal item asks about the time "since the last prompt" and your NA item asks about "right now," this explains what your coefficients measure and which model matches your question.

Consider two EMA questions:

  • "How much have you used reappraisal since the previous assessment?"
  • "How much negative affect do you feel right now?"

These questions cover different temporal windows. The coefficient connecting their responses is harder to interpret, because reappraisal could have occurred at any point during the preceding interval.

The meaning of a purported "ER at t" score depends on the questionnaire's recall window. It should not be assumed that all variables reflect instantaneous measurements. In this example, a "contemporaneous" ER-NA association partly reflects ER that occurred before the NA rating, so it combines the contemporaneous and lagged questions of Sections 2.2 and 2.3.

Recall windows for emotion regulation. Emotion regulation typically unfolds over minutes to hours rather than at one instant, so asking about it "since the last prompt" is often more natural than asking about "right now" (Eisele et al., 2026, p. 79). The disadvantage is that the timing within the interval is unknown. Applied to our design with two-hour intervals:

  • The lags are longer than they look. If reappraisal occurred at a random point in the preceding interval, it occurred on average about one hour before the NA rating at the same prompt (less, if people mainly recall recent episodes). The "same-prompt" coefficient therefore describes a lag of roughly one hour, and the "lagged" coefficient (ER reported at t−1 predicting NA at t) a lag of roughly three hours. With 90-minute intervals, the same reasoning gives 45 and 135 minutes (Viechtbauer, 2026b, pp. 180-181).
  • A natural model for regulation questions. Predicting NA at t from ER reported at t (which covers the interval since t−1), while controlling for NA at t−1, tests whether regulation during an interval predicts the change in NA over that interval. This model has been used for emotion regulation strategies (Brans et al., 2013) and is a simple version of the vector-autoregressive model (Kuppens & Myin-Germeys, 2026, p. 32). In Mplus it is written negaff ON er negaff&1;. Because NA at t−1 is held constant, the coefficient for ER no longer reflects only the fact that people regulate when NA is already high. Section 2.4's caution still applies, however: if NA rose during the interval and prompted the regulation, the coefficient mixes both directions.
  • For a concurrent association, match the time references. If the question is whether two states co-occur, both items should refer to the same moment (Eisele et al., 2026, p. 80).

15A third level: moments within days within persons (three-level DSEM)

For your researchThis section deals with the fact that your prompts come in days. Some days are worse than others, and ignoring that can make NA look more persistent from one prompt to the next than it is.

15.1Day-level variation

For your researchThis splits each NA rating into three parts: the person's usual level, how that day differed from usual, and how that moment differed from the rest of the day.

A workday, an argument, a poor night's sleep, or a weekend can shift a person's affect for the whole day. For this reason, the study period should cover both weekdays and weekend days for every participant (Cloos et al., 2026, p. 46). Our data therefore contain three sources of variation. For person i, day d, and prompt t within that day:

NAidt​=μNA,i​+δNA,id​+NAidtW​.

In plain EnglishA rating equals the person's usual NA, plus how far that day was from usual, plus how far that moment was from the day's level.

  • μNA,i​: the person's long-run mean (level 3, person).
  • δNA,id​: how much that day's level departs from the person's mean (level 2, day).
  • NAidtW​: how much the moment departs from that day's level (level 1, moment).

In two empirical examples, day-level variance was about 5% of the total for positive affect in one study, but about 30% for smoking urge and 33% for negative affect in another (Asparouhov & Muthén, 2026).

15.2What goes wrong if the day level is ignored?

For your researchIf good and bad days are ignored, the model mistakes "a bad day" for "NA that lingers from prompt to prompt."

In a two-level model, the day component δid​ is not modeled, so it remains in the within-person part. Because all prompts on the same day share it, it makes consecutive prompts more similar than the moment-to-moment process alone would. An autoregressive coefficient then absorbs this shared day-level variance and tends to overstate moment-to-moment inertia. How much depends on the size of the day component and on how the overnight transitions are handled, as the simulation below shows.

In a simulation, data were generated for 150 persons, 30 days, and 6 prompts per day, with a true within-day autoregression of 0.30 (innovation standard deviation 1), a day-level component with standard deviation SDday​, and no carryover between days. A two-level analysis that ignores days (person-mean centering, lags taken across consecutive rows including overnight) gave the following average estimates over 50 simulated studies per row (Monte Carlo standard errors of about 0.001; R code in Section 21.3):

SDday​ Estimated autoregression (true value 0.30)
0.0 0.24
0.5 0.35
0.7 0.42
1.0 0.52

With no day-level variance, the estimate is slightly too low, because the uncorrelated overnight transitions are pooled with the within-day ones (Section 14.1). As day-level variance grows, the estimate becomes increasingly too high.

Centering on observed day means also fails. Centering each prompt on its observed day mean and taking lags within days removes the day component, but each day has only six prompts. That is a series of length 6, and Nickell bias (Section 5.4) is then approximately −(1+0.30)/5=−0.26. In the same simulation, this approach estimated the autoregression at about 0.01 instead of 0.30. The day component therefore has to be estimated as part of the model, as a latent component. Three-level DSEM does this. Other hierarchical models can too, provided they also separate the day component from the lagged predictor. Adding a day random intercept to an lmer() model with a lagged outcome does not, because the lagged outcome contains the same day component.

Empirical results show the same pattern. In an EMA study of smoking urge, moving from two-level to three-level DSEM reduced the within-person autoregressions from 0.75 to 0.57 (smoking urge) and from 0.46 to 0.09 (negative affect), and increased one cross-lagged effect from 0.18 to 0.28 (Asparouhov & Muthén, 2026). In simulations, two-level DSEM overestimated the within-day autocorrelation by about 0.16 when day-level variance was present (Asparouhov & Muthén, 2026).

15.3The three-level DSEM model

For your researchThis describes the model that keeps moments, days, and persons apart, and that can also estimate whether a bad day carries over into the next one.

Three-level DSEM (Asparouhov & Muthén, 2026), available in Mplus 9 and extended in 9.1, has the following structure:

  • Level 1 (moments within a day). A within-day time-series model, such as the VAR(1) of Section 10, with lags within the day only. Lags that would reach before the first prompt of a day are treated as missing, so the overnight gap is never treated as a lag.

  • Level 2 (days within a person). Day-level components with their own structural model. Since Mplus 9.1, the day components can also follow a (non-random) day-to-day autoregression:

    δid​=ρδi,d−1​+ζid​.

    In plain EnglishHow far today's level is from the person's usual level (δid​) is partly predicted by how far yesterday's level was (δi,d−1​), weighted by ρ, plus something new today (ζid​).

    A bad day can therefore spill over into the next day, separately from moment-to-moment inertia.

  • Level 3 (persons). Person means and person-specific coefficients, with their variances and covariances.

  • Random effects. Intercepts can vary at levels 2 and 3. Within-day coefficients, including autoregressions, can vary across persons (level 3) and, in principle, across days (level 2). Since 9.1, residual variances and correlations can also be random.

  • Latent centering at every level. The person and day components are latent variables, which avoids Nickell bias and the bias from treating observed day means as error-free.

15.4Practical recommendations for three-level DSEM

For your researchWhat the data must provide for three-level DSEM to give reliable estimates.

Recommendations from Asparouhov and Muthén (2026):

  • DSEM3 is limited to continuous, normally distributed variables and is available for DSEM, not RDSEM. Mplus 9 introduced it as an experimental feature (Muthén & Muthén, n.d.).
  • The number of persons drives the accuracy of person-level estimates. In simulations, 50 persons with 10 days and 10 prompts per day recovered the parameters well, whereas with only 5 persons a person-level parameter was strongly biased.
  • Time-series models at both the moment and the day level need substantial data: more than 5 observations at each of these two levels, more than 2% of the total variance at each level, and autocorrelations that differ clearly from 0 and 1 at both levels.
  • With many small days (few prompts per day), avoid day-specific random slopes and autoregressions, and keep only random day intercepts.
  • A random effect is worth adding only if it replaces at least 5 to 10 fixed parameters.
  • High autocorrelation combined with few units at any level makes estimation more difficult and can lead to non-convergence.
  • The person-level and day-level random effects are likely to be strongly correlated in the posterior, which can slow convergence. Mplus 9.1 implements a joint updating algorithm for some three-level models.

The Mplus input files for all examples are included in Asparouhov and Muthén (2026). In Mplus three-level models, the CLUSTER statement lists the higher level first (for example, CLUSTER = id day;).

15.5When is the day level worth modeling?

For your researchA short checklist for deciding whether your emotion regulation study needs the day level at all.

  • When day-level variance is non-trivial: check the three-level variance decomposition first, for example with a three-level random-intercept model in R, lmer(neg_aff ~ 1 + (1 | id/day), data = ema). The result can be turned into two ICCs: the share of total variance due to days and the share due to persons (Hedges et al., 2012). In a synthetic illustration dataset on momentary affective valence, days accounted for about 4% and persons for about 23% of the variance (Lafit, 2026a, pp. 206-209).
  • When the research question involves daily processes (spillover between days, day-level stressors) alongside moment-level dynamics.
  • When within-day inertia is the focal estimand, because that is the quantity most distorted by ignoring days.

For purely contemporaneous questions, three-level random intercepts in lmer() may be sufficient. Cross-classified time-series models (persons crossed with time points) are a different extension: they let the mean vary across calendar time, for example a common trend shared by all participants.

16Choosing a model for different research questions

For your researchFind the scenario that matches your research question. Each one names a suitable starting model and what it estimates, and some also note what it cannot tell you.

No single model is best for every question. The appropriate model follows from the estimand and the scientific theory.

Scenario A. Same-occasion ER and affect

For your researchChoose this if your hypothesis is about how reappraisal and affect go together at the same prompt.

Question:

When people engage in more cognitive reappraisal than usual, do they report lower NA and higher PA at the same assessment?

Suitable starting point: A within-between mixed model or MSEM, perhaps with random contemporaneous ER slopes.

For example:

NAit​=β0​+u0i​+βW​ERitc​+βB​ERi​+εit​.

In plain EnglishNA at a prompt is predicted from the person's baseline, their reappraisal relative to their own usual level (within-person part), and their usual reappraisal compared with other people (between-person part).

Estimand: Within-person contemporaneous association, with a separate between-person component.

Not answered: what happens two hours afterward, and what causes the association.

Scenario B. Does earlier ER predict later NA?

For your researchChoose this if your hypothesis is that reappraising more than usual is followed by lower NA at the next prompt.

Question:

When someone reports more reappraisal than usual, is their NA lower two hours later after accounting for their earlier NA?

Suitable starting point: A carefully specified lagged mixed model, a dynamic MSEM, or DSEM.

NAitW​=ϕNAi,t−1W​+βERi,t−1W​+εit​.

In plain EnglishNA (relative to the person's usual level) is predicted from NA and reappraisal at the previous prompt. The coefficient β is the number your hypothesis is about.

Estimand: A within-person lagged partial predictive relationship at the defined lag, equivalently the association of earlier ER with change in NA conditional on earlier NA (Section 2.3).

Not answered: Whether manipulating reappraisal would lower NA.

Scenario C. Reciprocal links among ER, PA, and NA

For your researchChoose this if you expect links in both directions, for example distress predicting later reappraisal and reappraisal predicting lower later distress.

Question:

Does ER predict later affect, and do PA and NA also predict subsequent ER use?

Suitable starting point: A multivariate VAR-type model, estimated through DSEM or another appropriate joint dynamic modeling framework.

Estimands: The nine lagged coefficients in the 3×3 lag matrix, together with any specified innovation covariances, and system-level summaries such as impulse responses and stability (Section 10.3).

Advantage: We can examine both directions of the predictive relationships and characterize the joint process.

Scenario D. Different temporal relationships across people

For your researchChoose this if you expect that reappraisal is followed by lower NA for some people but not for others.

Question:

Does the ER → later NA association differ substantially between participants?

Suitable starting point: A model with a random cross-lagged ER slope, implemented through MLM or DSEM.

Estimands: The average slope, the between-person slope variance (or standard deviation), and possibly predictors or correlates of that heterogeneity. Test the variance with a boundary-corrected test or an equivalent Bayesian procedure (Section 4.6).

Scenario E. Is affective inertia related to ER-NA coupling?

For your researchChoose this if you want to relate two person-level dynamic features to each other, such as how long NA lingers and how strongly reappraisal predicts later NA.

Question:

Do people whose NA is more persistent tend to have weaker or stronger lagged ER-NA associations?

Suitable starting point: A multilevel dynamic model with person-specific NA autoregression and ER → NA slopes and an estimated covariance among those random parameters.

Estimand: Cov(a31,i​,a33,i​) or the corresponding correlation.

Advantage of DSEM: The relationship is estimated as part of a joint ER-PA-NA dynamic system, although appropriately constructed random-effects models can address related questions.

Scenario F. Do we need a questionnaire-level measurement model?

For your researchChoose this if you worry that measurement error in your reappraisal or affect items distorts the dynamics you estimate.

Question:

Can we separate the latent ER, PA, and NA constructs from item-specific variation while analyzing within-person temporal relationships?

Suitable starting point: A dynamic latent-variable model within MSEM or DSEM, given enough items and suitable assumptions. With single items, an AR(1)+WN measurement-error model in DSEM is an alternative (Section 6.5).

Estimands: Relationships among latent construct fluctuations rather than only relationships among observed sum or mean scores.

Scenario G. Do we have only four widely separated waves?

For your researchChoose this if your data are a few waves months apart rather than many daily prompts.

Question:

Do within-person departures in ER predict later departures in NA over several months, after separating stable differences between individuals?

Suitable starting point: The RI-CLPM, subject to model identification, measurement comparability, timing, and the research design.

Estimands: Within-person autoregressive and cross-lagged coefficients, plus stable between-person covariance.

Scenario H. Do days add variation beyond moments?

For your researchChoose this if you expect whole good and bad days, or a carry-over from one day to the next, in addition to moment-to-moment changes.

Question:

Is moment-to-moment NA inertia distinct from day-to-day carryover, and does a stressful day shift affect for the whole day?

Suitable starting point: Three-level DSEM with moments within days within persons (Section 15), after checking the size of the day-level variance.

Estimands: The within-day autoregression and cross-lagged coefficients, the day-level variance, the day-to-day autoregression of day components, and person-level heterogeneity.

Scenario I. Did an intervention change the dynamics?

For your researchChoose this if you run an emotion regulation training and want to know whether it changed people's daily emotional dynamics, not only their average mood.

Question:

After an emotion regulation training, do people's mean NA, NA inertia, and sensitivity to events change more than in a control group?

Suitable starting point: A DSEM with two EMA bursts, one before and one after the intervention. Each person gets separate parameters for each burst, and the change in each parameter is regressed on the group dummy (Hamaker et al., 2023; see Part 3 of the walkthrough tab).

Estimands: Initial group differences (which should be near zero after randomization), time effects (change in the control group), and treatment effects (additional change in the treated group). Each is estimated separately for the means, the inertia, the slopes, and the innovation variance.

In a randomized mindfulness trial, the trained group showed larger decreases than the control group in mean NA, in the rated unpleasantness of events, and in NA inertia. The NA innovation variance decreased over time in the control group (a time effect), and the change in the trained group did not differ from it (the credible interval for the difference included zero; Hamaker et al., 2023).

17ER → later NA does not establish emotion regulation effectiveness

For your researchA common overstatement in emotion regulation research reads "reappraisal predicts lower NA later" as "reappraisal works." This section lists what else could produce the same number and which designs can support stronger conclusions.

Suppose we estimate:

βER→NA​=−0.30.

In plain EnglishTen more points of reappraisal than usual at one prompt go with 3 fewer points of NA at the next prompt, on average, holding earlier NA constant. This number alone does not show that reappraisal caused NA to be lower.

A lagged association alone, whether estimated with lmer(), MSEM, RI-CLPM, or DSEM, does not justify the conclusion:

"Using reappraisal reduces negative affect."

Several alternative explanations remain:

  • Confounding by context: People may use reappraisal in situations that are already becoming less stressful.
  • Selection into strategy use: People may use reappraisal when they think a situation is manageable, and perceived manageability could itself predict later NA.
  • Unmeasured time-varying factors: Social interactions, stressor severity, fatigue, sleep, or anticipated events could affect both ER and subsequent affect.
  • Temporal ambiguity within prompts: Strategy use may refer to an interval rather than an instant, and the process may unfold faster than the sampling frequency. In addition, a person's current mood can influence how they rate what happened earlier in the interval, so even an item about the past can be influenced by the present (Viechtbauer, 2026b, pp. 179-180).
  • Measurement error and misspecification: Noisy responses, missing nonlinear relationships, or incorrect lag assumptions can distort estimates.

Controlling for prior NA and PA does not guarantee that these problems disappear.

A worked example of confounding. Suppose an unmeasured variable, "the situation is starting to resolve," makes reappraisal more likely at one prompt and lowers NA at the next. If reappraisal itself has no effect at all, the lagged ER coefficient will still be negative, and its size will grow with the strength of the confounder's two paths. Adjusting for prior NA does not remove this bias, because the confounder acts after prior NA was measured.

There is also a construct distinction:

  • ER strategy use concerns whether and how much someone engaged in a particular strategy.
  • ER strategy effectiveness concerns how successfully the strategy altered an emotional response.

Observed strategy use is not the same quantity as strategy effectiveness. Lagged associations may provide evidence relevant to effectiveness hypotheses, but stronger causal designs and assumptions are required to estimate effects of interventions on strategy use, for example micro-randomized prompts that instruct reappraisal at randomly chosen moments.

The main ways to add such "non-natural" variation to daily life are following people around a predictable event (such as receiving exam grades), introducing a manipulation in daily life (such as a public-speaking task), or delivering an intervention through the phone (Kuppens & Myin-Germeys, 2026, pp. 34-35). The decision rules of just-in-time adaptive interventions are evaluated and optimized in micro-randomized trials (Beames et al., 2026, p. 252). In such a trial, whether a brief intervention is delivered is randomized at many moments for each person, so its momentary effects can be estimated without the confounding discussed above. Randomizing when a person is prompted to reappraise is the most direct design for estimating whether reappraisal lowers NA, and not only whether it predicts lower NA.

Further cautions (Hamaker et al., 2023):

  • Lagged coefficients are specific to the interval. At other intervals they can shrink, grow, or even change sign (Section 14.1).
  • A changed parameter is not a causal parameter. If a training changes people's ER → NA coefficient, the training had a causal effect on that coefficient. The coefficient itself is still not a causal effect of ER on NA, because time-varying confounders may still be involved.
  • Neither unstandardized nor standardized coefficients tell how much change an intervention could produce. A variable with a small coefficient may still be a valuable target if it can be changed far beyond its natural range of variation. Judging this requires substantive knowledge of the domain.

DSEM can also serve as a step between developing a theory and running an intervention study, because it can show whether the predicted within-person pattern exists before an experiment is run.

18Summary of the main conceptual lessons

For your researchThis section gathers the guide's main lessons into one checklist that you can use when you plan, run, or review an EMA analysis of emotion regulation.

The approaches form an overlapping family rather than a strict hierarchy:

Multilevel regression handles clustered observations and can estimate contemporaneous or lagged within-person associations and random slopes.

MSEM adds jointly specified relations and latent measurement structures, with explicit within-person and between-person levels. It can also contain dynamics.

RI-CLPM is a particular longitudinal SEM that separates stable between-person differences from within-person autoregressive and cross-lagged processes. Conventional random intercepts do not imply random temporal slopes.

DSEM integrates intensive time-series relationships, multilevel heterogeneity, and SEM structures in one modeling framework. The specific model determines which components are included. Three-level DSEM adds a day level between moments and persons.

Across the comparisons in this guide:

  1. DSEM is not automatically more informative than a lagged MLM. If both implement the same relevant dynamic structure and assumptions, they may answer the same substantive question.
  2. RI-CLPM and DSEM can be closely related mathematically. Their differences often reflect usual data designs, parameter constraints, varying-slope capabilities, and estimation or implementation choices.
  3. MSEM becomes dynamic when we add temporal relationships. The distinction between "MSEM" and "DSEM" is not a clean separation between methods that can and cannot model lagged relationships.

Before choosing a model, answer these questions in order:

Bottom line: Choose the model by its estimands and assumptions, not by its name. For our EMA example, the main distinction is whether we want contemporaneous ER-affect co-occurrence, a lagged ER-affect predictive relationship, a complete reciprocal dynamic system, or heterogeneity in that system across individuals and days.

19Glossary

For your researchA quick lookup for the main technical terms used in the guide, explained in terms of the emotion regulation study.

Term Plain-language meaning in our EMA study
Estimand The exact population quantity we want to estimate, such as a same-occasion within-person ER-NA slope or a two-hour lagged slope.
Contemporaneous association Whether ER and NA co-vary at the same assessment occasion.
Temporal dependency Whether earlier ER, PA, or NA contains information that predicts a later variable.
Granger-type predictability Earlier values of one variable improve the prediction of another variable beyond that variable's own past. A statement about prediction, not intervention.
Within-person Comparing someone's observation with that same person's usual level.
Between-person Comparing one person's typical levels or parameters with another person's.
True (latent) person mean, μi​ The long-run level a person's scores fluctuate around; unobserved and estimated.
Observed person mean, xi​ The average of a person's observed scores; an estimate of μi​ that contains sampling error.
Person-mean centering (CWC) Subtracting the observed person mean from each score ("centering within cluster").
Latent centering Decomposing scores into latent between and within components inside the model, as MSEM and DSEM do.
Contextual effect The between-person slope minus the within-person slope; the coefficient on the person mean when raw (uncentered) predictors are also in the model.
Ecological fallacy Inferring a within-person relationship from a between-person one.
Intraclass correlation (ICC) The proportion of total variance that lies between persons (or, in a three-level model, between days or persons).
ICC(2) The reliability of an observed person mean, which increases with the number of occasions.
Random intercept A model component allowing people to differ in stable or expected levels of an outcome.
Random slope A model component allowing a regression relationship to differ across people.
Partial pooling (shrinkage) Person-specific estimates are pulled toward the population mean, more strongly when a person's own data are less informative.
BLUP / conditional mode The frequentist prediction of a person's random effect in a mixed model.
Boundary problem Testing whether a variance is zero, where zero lies at the edge of the parameter space, so the usual chi-square reference distribution is wrong.
Autoregression A variable's previous value predicts its own later value, such as NA → later NA.
Cross-lagged coefficient An earlier value of one variable predicts a later value of another, such as ER → later NA.
Half-life The number of intervals after which a deviation is expected to have halved: ln(0.5)/ln(ϕ), for a single-variable AR(1) process.
Nickell bias Downward bias in an autoregressive coefficient when the lagged outcome is centered on an observed mean computed from a short series; about −(1+ϕ)/(T−1).
Dynamic Explicitly describing how values evolve over time.
System A set of connected variables studied together; here, ER, PA, and NA.
Dynamic system Connected variables whose current states depend on earlier states of themselves and one another.
VAR(1) A system in which current variables are predicted from all modeled variables one occasion earlier.
Lag matrix The matrix of all autoregressive and cross-lagged coefficients in a VAR; rows are later outcomes, columns are earlier predictors.
Impulse response The expected path of all variables after a one-time departure in one variable.
Eigenvalues (of the lag matrix) Numbers summarizing whether the system as a whole damps (modulus below 1) or amplifies departures; complex eigenvalues indicate oscillation.
Feedback loop Two variables predicting each other over time; with opposite signs it is a negative (stabilizing) loop.
Measurement error The part of an observed score that does not faithfully represent the intended latent quantity. It is not carried forward in time.
AR(1)+WN A latent AR(1) process observed with independent measurement error ("white noise"); estimable with a single indicator.
Within-person reliability The share of within-person observed variance due to the latent process rather than measurement error.
Latent factor An unobserved construct inferred from multiple indicators, such as reappraisal inferred from three items.
Innovation A new, conditionally unpredictable departure in the process after accounting for prior modeled information. It is carried forward by the dynamics.
Innovation covariance How unexpected same-occasion changes in two variables co-occur.
Random innovation variance / correlation Person-specific innovation variances (log scale) and correlations (Fisher z scale).
Temporal covariance structure The pattern of variances and covariances of measurements across time, within and possibly across variables.
Effective sample size The number of independent observations containing the same information as a set of correlated ones; for an AR(1) mean, about T(1−ϕ)/(1+ϕ). In Bayesian output, ESS also refers to the number of independent posterior draws.
Affective inertia Persistence of affect from one occasion to the next, commonly operationalized using an autoregressive coefficient.
Stationarity Roughly, the relevant statistical properties of the process do not systematically change over time; precise definitions depend on what properties are assumed constant.
RDSEM Residual DSEM: the autoregressive structure is placed on residuals rather than on the outcomes.
TINTERVAL An Mplus option that places observations on a regular time grid and inserts missing rows for empty grid cells.
Continuous-time model / drift A model in which lag coefficients depend on elapsed time; the drift governs how fast deviations decay.
Three-level DSEM (DSEM3) DSEM with moments within days within persons (or other three-level nestings), with latent centering at every level.
PSRF Potential scale reduction factor: a Bayesian convergence diagnostic comparing variability between and within MCMC chains.
One-tailed p-value (Mplus Bayes) The proportion of posterior draws on the opposite side of zero; a posterior probability, not a frequentist p-value.
Causal effect How an outcome would differ under an intervention on a variable, under specified assumptions; not automatically given by observational lagged coefficients.
Cattell's data box A picture of all possible data as a box with three sides: persons, variables, and occasions. Designs differ in which slice of the box they use.
Ergodicity The condition under which results across people also describe each individual: all persons share the same means, variances, and (lagged) covariances. Almost never plausible in psychology.
General law Every person has the same within-person relationship.
Homology The within-person and between-person relationships are the same.
Equilibrium (attractor) The level a person returns to after being pushed away; in a stationary model, the person's mean.
MSSD Mean squared successive difference: the average squared change between consecutive prompts; a descriptive index of moment-to-moment instability.
Kalman filter A step-by-step method that combines a model-based prediction with a noisy new measurement, weighting each by its reliability; when a measurement is missing, it carries the prediction forward with growing uncertainty.
Kalman gain The fraction of the gap between prediction and new measurement by which the Kalman filter updates its estimate.
Kalman smoother A backward pass after the filter that also uses later observations, so estimates for any moment, including gaps, use the whole series.
State-space model A model with an unobserved (latent) state that evolves over time and is observed with error; the framework in which the Kalman filter operates.
Replicated N = 1 analysis Fitting the same time-series model to each person separately and summarizing the results across persons.
Partial autocorrelation (PACF) The correlation between a variable and itself k occasions earlier, after removing what the occasions in between explain.
ESM (experience sampling method) Another name for EMA. The two terms are used largely interchangeably.
Compliance The share of planned prompts that a participant answered; about 79% on average across studies.
Initial elevation bias The tendency for the first few reports in a study to be higher than later ones, which then stabilize.
Measurement-burst design Several EMA periods (bursts) separated by longer gaps, for example three one-week bursts over a year.
Missing at random (MAR) Whether a prompt is missed may depend on observed information (such as time of day) but not on the unobserved value itself.
Lag as moderator Letting the time since the previous prompt interact with a lagged predictor, so the lagged effect can weaken over longer gaps.
Micro-randomized trial A design that randomizes, at many moments for each person, whether a brief intervention is delivered.
