21Appendix: R code for the simulations

For your researchIf you want to check or extend a simulation result reported in this guide, the complete code is here. It runs in base R, without extra packages.

The simulation results reported in the text of Sections 5.4, 10.8, and 15.2 come from the three R scripts below. Each script sets its random seed, so running it should reproduce the reported numbers (they were produced with R 4.3). Each script prints the average estimate across the simulated studies and its Monte Carlo standard error: the uncertainty in that average that comes from running a limited number of simulated studies, computed as the standard deviation of the estimates divided by the square root of the number of studies.

The interactive figures are separate. Each draws one simulated data set in your browser from a fixed seed, so its values can differ slightly from the averages reported in the text.

21.1Nickell bias (Section 5.4)

Simulates studies of 300 persons with a true autoregression of 0.70 and estimates it after centering each person's series on its observed mean, for series of 20 and 180 prompts.

Show the R code (01_nickell_bias.R)R
# Nickell bias when the lagged outcome is centered on the observed person mean
# (Section 5.4 of "Analyzing the relationships between variables in EMA data").
# Base R only; runs in a few seconds.

set.seed(2026)
n_persons <- 300    # simulated persons per study
phi       <- 0.70   # true autoregression
n_reps    <- 100    # simulated studies per series length
T_values  <- c(20, 180)

# One study: each person has a stationary AR(1) series of length T.
simulate_study <- function(n_persons, T, phi) {
  y <- matrix(0, n_persons, T)
  y[, 1] <- rnorm(n_persons, 0, 1 / sqrt(1 - phi^2))
  for (t in 2:T) y[, t] <- phi * y[, t - 1] + rnorm(n_persons)
  y
}

# Pooled within-person estimate: center every series on its observed mean,
# then regress each centered score on the previous centered score.
within_ar <- function(y) {
  yc <- y - rowMeans(y)
  T  <- ncol(y)
  sum(yc[, -1] * yc[, -T]) / sum(yc[, -T]^2)
}

results <- t(sapply(T_values, function(T) {
  est <- replicate(n_reps, within_ar(simulate_study(n_persons, T, phi)))
  c(T             = T,
    mean_estimate = mean(est),
    mc_se         = sd(est) / sqrt(n_reps),   # Monte Carlo standard error
    approximation = phi - (1 + phi) / (T - 1))
}))
print(round(results, 3))

21.2Missing prompts and measurement error (Section 10.8)

Simulates studies of 150 persons with 180 prompts each and a true inertia of 0.50, with or without missing prompts and measurement error. It compares lagged regression (complete pairs, or lagging to the last available prompt) with a model-based estimator: maximum likelihood with a Kalman filter and a latent person mean, with or without a measurement-error term. The second part compares the precision of complete-pair regression and the model-based estimator with 40% of prompts missing.

Show the R code (02_missing_and_measurement_error.R)R
# Missing prompts and measurement error: lagged regression versus a model-based
# (Kalman filter) estimator (Section 10.8 of "Analyzing the relationships between
# variables in EMA data"). Base R only; runs in about 10 to 15 minutes.

set.seed(2026)
n_persons <- 150
n_prompts <- 180
phi       <- 0.50                   # true inertia of the latent NA state
var_state <- 1 / (1 - phi^2)        # within-person variance of the state (innovation SD = 1)

# One study. reliability = share of within-person report variance that comes
# from the true state; p_missing = probability that a prompt is missed (at random).
simulate_study <- function(reliability, p_missing) {
  var_error <- var_state * (1 - reliability) / reliability
  state <- matrix(0, n_persons, n_prompts)
  state[, 1] <- rnorm(n_persons, 0, sqrt(var_state))
  for (t in 2:n_prompts) state[, t] <- phi * state[, t - 1] + rnorm(n_persons)
  y <- rnorm(n_persons, 5, 1) + state +
       matrix(rnorm(n_persons * n_prompts, 0, sqrt(var_error)), n_persons)
  y[matrix(runif(n_persons * n_prompts) < p_missing, n_persons)] <- NA
  y
}

# Lagged regression on person-mean-centered reports.
# last_available = FALSE: use only pairs of consecutive prompts that were both answered.
# last_available = TRUE:  lag each answer to the previous *answered* prompt.
lagged_regression <- function(y, last_available = FALSE) {
  num <- 0; den <- 0
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(y))) {
    yc <- y[i, ] - mean(y[i, ], na.rm = TRUE)
    if (last_available) yc <- yc[!is.na(yc)]
    now <- yc[-1]; before <- yc[-length(yc)]
    ok  <- !is.na(now) & !is.na(before)
    num <- num + sum(now[ok] * before[ok]); den <- den + sum(before[ok]^2)
  }
  num / den
}

# Model-based estimator: maximum likelihood with a Kalman filter. The state of each
# person is (person mean, within-person deviation); the person mean is latent, the
# deviation follows an AR(1), and the report may contain measurement error.
# theta = (atanh(phi), log innovation variance, log error variance, grand mean,
#          log variance of person means)
kalman_negloglik <- function(theta, y, with_error) {
  f  <- tanh(theta[1]); s2 <- exp(theta[2])
  e2 <- if (with_error) exp(theta[3]) else 0
  g  <- theta[4]; t2 <- exp(theta[5])
  n  <- nrow(y)
  a_m <- rep(g, n); a_w <- rep(0, n)                      # predicted state
  P00 <- rep(t2, n); P01 <- rep(0, n); P11 <- rep(s2 / (1 - f^2), n)
  loglik <- 0
  for (t in seq_len(ncol(y))) {
    yt <- y[, t]; obs <- !is.na(yt)
    F  <- P00 + 2 * P01 + P11 + e2                        # variance of the predicted report
    v  <- yt - (a_m + a_w)                                # prediction error
    K0 <- (P00 + P01) / F; K1 <- (P01 + P11) / F          # Kalman gains
    loglik <- loglik - 0.5 * sum(log(2 * pi * F[obs]) + v[obs]^2 / F[obs])
    h0 <- P00 + P01; h1 <- P01 + P11
    # update with the report (only where the prompt was answered)
    a_m[obs] <- a_m[obs] + K0[obs] * v[obs]; a_w[obs] <- a_w[obs] + K1[obs] * v[obs]
    P00[obs] <- P00[obs] - K0[obs] * h0[obs]
    P01[obs] <- P01[obs] - K0[obs] * h1[obs]
    P11[obs] <- P11[obs] - K1[obs] * h1[obs]
    # predict the next prompt: the person mean stays, the deviation decays by phi
    a_w <- f * a_w; P01 <- f * P01; P11 <- f^2 * P11 + s2
  }
  -loglik
}

model_based <- function(y, with_error) {
  start <- c(atanh(0.3), 0, -1, mean(y, na.rm = TRUE), 0)
  if (with_error) {
    fit <- optim(start, kalman_negloglik, y = y, with_error = TRUE, method = "L-BFGS-B")
    tanh(fit$par[1])
  } else {
    fit <- optim(start[-3], function(th) kalman_negloglik(append(th, 0, 2), y, FALSE),
                 method = "L-BFGS-B")
    tanh(fit$par[1])
  }
}

# ---- Table in Section 10.8: 20 simulated studies per condition ----
n_reps <- 20
conditions <- expand.grid(p_missing = c(0, 0.3), reliability = c(1, 0.7))
table_rows <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(conditions)), function(k) {
  est <- replicate(n_reps, {
    y <- simulate_study(conditions$reliability[k], conditions$p_missing[k])
    c(pairs          = lagged_regression(y),
      last_available = lagged_regression(y, last_available = TRUE),
      model_no_error = model_based(y, with_error = FALSE),
      model_error    = model_based(y, with_error = TRUE))
  })
  data.frame(reliability = conditions$reliability[k], p_missing = conditions$p_missing[k],
             estimator = rownames(est), mean = rowMeans(est),
             mc_se = apply(est, 1, sd) / sqrt(n_reps))
})
print(do.call(rbind, table_rows), digits = 4, row.names = FALSE)

# ---- Precision with 40% missing: 200 simulated studies ----
n_reps <- 200
est <- replicate(n_reps, {
  y <- simulate_study(reliability = 1, p_missing = 0.4)
  c(pairs = lagged_regression(y), model = model_based(y, with_error = FALSE))
})
sd_ratio <- sd(est["pairs", ]) / sd(est["model", ])
boot_ratio <- replicate(4000, { b <- sample(n_reps, replace = TRUE)
  sd(est["pairs", b]) / sd(est["model", b]) })
cat(sprintf("40%% missing, %d studies: complete-pair mean %.3f (SD %.4f), model-based mean %.3f (SD %.4f)\n",
            n_reps, mean(est["pairs", ]), sd(est["pairs", ]), mean(est["model", ]), sd(est["model", ])))
cat(sprintf("SD ratio %.2f, bootstrap 95%% interval %.2f to %.2f\n",
            sd_ratio, quantile(boot_ratio, 0.025), quantile(boot_ratio, 0.975)))

21.3Ignoring the day level (Section 15.2)

Simulates studies of 150 persons with 30 days of 6 prompts, a true within-day autoregression of 0.30, a day component of varying size, and no carryover between days. It compares a two-level analysis that ignores days with centering on observed day means.

Show the R code (03_day_level.R)R
# Ignoring the day level, and centering on observed day means
# (Section 15.2 of "Analyzing the relationships between variables in EMA data").
# Base R only; runs in under a minute.

set.seed(2026)
n_persons <- 150
n_days    <- 30
n_prompts <- 6       # prompts per day
phi       <- 0.30    # true within-day autoregression
sd_days   <- c(0, 0.5, 0.7, 1.0)   # SD of the day component
n_reps    <- 50      # simulated studies per condition

# One study. Each day starts afresh from the stationary distribution
# (no carryover between days) and is shifted by its own day component.
simulate_study <- function(sd_day) {
  y <- array(0, c(n_persons, n_days, n_prompts))
  person_mean <- rnorm(n_persons)
  for (d in 1:n_days) {
    day_shift <- rnorm(n_persons, 0, sd_day)
    w <- rnorm(n_persons, 0, 1 / sqrt(1 - phi^2))
    for (k in 1:n_prompts) {
      if (k > 1) w <- phi * w + rnorm(n_persons)
      y[, d, k] <- person_mean + day_shift + w
    }
  }
  y
}

# (a) Two-level analysis that ignores days: center on the person mean and
#     take lags across consecutive rows, including the overnight transition.
two_level_ar <- function(y) {
  flat <- matrix(aperm(y, c(1, 3, 2)), n_persons)  # rows = persons, columns in time order
  yc <- flat - rowMeans(flat)
  n  <- ncol(yc)
  sum(yc[, -1] * yc[, -n]) / sum(yc[, -n]^2)
}

# (b) Center on the observed day mean and take lags within days only.
day_mean_ar <- function(y) {
  yc <- y - as.vector(apply(y, c(1, 2), mean))
  sum(yc[, , -1] * yc[, , -n_prompts]) / sum(yc[, , -n_prompts]^2)
}

results <- t(sapply(sd_days, function(s) {
  est <- replicate(n_reps, { y <- simulate_study(s); c(two_level_ar(y), day_mean_ar(y)) })
  c(sd_day          = s,
    two_level       = mean(est[1, ]), two_level_mc_se = sd(est[1, ]) / sqrt(n_reps),
    day_mean        = mean(est[2, ]), day_mean_mc_se  = sd(est[2, ]) / sqrt(n_reps))
}))
print(round(results, 3))

A practical walkthrough for DSEM in Mplus

This walkthrough is adapted from the supplementary materials for the DSEM chapter by Hamaker et al. (2023) in the Handbook of Structural Equation Modeling (2nd ed.). The original materials are at ellenhamaker.github.io/DSEM-book-chapter.

It covers the same models in simplified form, with a figure and a nontechnical explanation for each step. The Mplus input is rewritten for our emotion regulation example, and the original output is reproduced unchanged with an interpretation. Section 6 lists small errors in the original materials and how they are corrected here.

Under construction: the R version

This walkthrough currently shows every step in Mplus only. A version that shows how to do all of this in R is under construction, and this tab will be updated with it soon.

1Overview

For your researchThe walkthrough shows how to run DSEM in Mplus for an emotion regulation study, using the published models of Hamaker et al. (2023) as templates.

1.1Relation to the original materials

For your researchEach model on this tab comes with Mplus input written for reappraisal and NA, the original output from Hamaker et al.'s study of unpleasant events and NA, and an interpretation of that output.

This tab is a simplified, step-by-step version of the supplementary website for the chapter Dynamic structural equation modeling as a combination of time series modeling, multilevel modeling, and structural equation modeling by Hamaker et al. (2023; website dated July 2021). The original website shows the Mplus input and output for every model in the chapter. This tab differs from the website as follows:

  1. Each step is explained in nontechnical language and illustrated with a figure.
  2. All Mplus input is rewritten for the variables of our emotion regulation example.
  3. Every output block is the original output from Hamaker et al., copied unchanged, because we have no ER data from which to produce new output. The text explains how to read each block. Their data concern negative affect and unpleasant events, so the signs and sizes of the estimates describe their study, not ER.

Section 6 lists small errors in the original materials that we found while checking the numbers, and how they are corrected on this tab.

1.2The original study and our example

For your researchThe table shows which variable in our example takes the role of each variable in Hamaker et al.'s study.

Hamaker et al. studied how unpleasant events and negative affect predict each other in daily life. Our guide addresses the same kind of question about emotion regulation (ER) and negative affect (NA), and the variables of the two studies correspond as follows:

Hamaker et al. (2023) Our version on this tab
Outcome y Momentary negative affect (na_pre) Momentary negative affect (negaff)
Predictor x Unpleasantness of events since the previous beep (ue_pre) Use of reappraisal since the previous prompt (er)
Persons 129 150
Schedule 10 beeps a day, at random times within 90-minute blocks, for 6 days 6 prompts a day, every 2 hours from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m., for 30 days
Time variable TimeHours: hours since the start of day 1 hours: hours since the start of day 1
Time grid TINTERVAL = TimeHours(1); (1-hour grid) TINTERVAL = hours(2); (2-hour grid)
Person-level predictor Depression score before the EMA period (ham_pre) Depression score before the EMA period (dep_pre)
Person-level outcome Depression score after the EMA period (ham_post) Depression score after the EMA period (dep_post)
Intervention (Part 3) Mindfulness training versus control ER training versus control

ER reported "since the previous prompt." In both studies, the predictor asks about the interval since the previous prompt, while NA asks about right now. The predictor therefore refers to things that happened before the NA rating, even though both are recorded at the same prompt. This is called an implicit lagged relation (Hamaker et al., 2023). For this reason, the models below regress NA on the predictor measured at the same prompt.

The same applies to ratings of the most important event since the previous beep: if such an event happened at a random point in a 90-minute interval, it happened on average about 45 minutes before the affect rating (Eisele et al., 2026, pp. 79-80; Viechtbauer, 2026b, pp. 180-181). With our 2-hour intervals, reappraisal reported at a prompt happened on average about one hour before the NA rating.

Expected signs. Unpleasant events should raise NA, so Hamaker et al.'s coefficient from events to NA is positive. In our study, if reappraisal lowers NA, the coefficient from ER to NA would be negative. However, reactive regulation (Section 2.4 of the "Concepts and models" tab) can make it positive. The coefficient from earlier NA to later ER is expected to be positive: distress prompts regulation.

1.3Notation

For your researchThe symbols used on this tab, and the names of the corresponding random effects in the Mplus input and output.

  • yt​: NA at prompt t. xt​: ER reported at prompt t, about the interval since prompt t−1.
  • ϕy​: NA inertia, how much NA carries over from one prompt to the next.
  • βy​: ER → NA, how NA changes with ER since the previous prompt.
  • ϕx​: ER autoregression, whether high ER tends to follow high ER.
  • βx​: NA → later ER, whether high NA at one prompt is followed by more ER.
  • ψy​, ψx​: innovation (residual) variances: how large the unexplained moment-to-moment changes are.
  • Superscripts: yit(w)​ is the within-person part (the deviation from the person's own mean), and yi(b)​ is the between-person part (the person's own mean).

In the Mplus input, these random effects are called phi_na, b_na, phi_er, b_er, psi_na, and psi_er. Hamaker et al.'s output uses PHI_NA, BETA_NA (or B_AE), PHI_UE, BETA_UE (or B_EA), PSI_NA (or VAR_NA), and PSI_UE (or VAR_UE).

1.4Structure of the walkthrough

For your researchThe walkthrough moves from separate models for each person to one multilevel model for all persons, and then to person-level predictors and outcomes such as depression.

The walkthrough introduces the three components of DSEM in turn:

  1. Time-series modeling (Part 1): each person is analyzed separately, as a study with one participant. This gives each person's dynamics, but the results of different persons cannot be related to each other within the model.
  2. Multilevel modeling (Part 2, Models 0 to 3): all persons are analyzed in one model. Each person has their own parameters, and these parameters can be correlated with each other and predicted from person-level variables.
  3. Structural equation modeling (Part 2, Models 4 to 6): the person-specific parameters are used in factor models and path models.

Part 3 applies the same models to a pretest-posttest design, to test whether an intervention changed people's means and dynamics.

2Data format and Bayesian estimation settings

For your researchThe data layout, estimation settings, and convergence checks described here apply to every model on this tab.

2.1Data file layout

For your researchHow to arrange an EMA data file for Mplus, including the coding of missed prompts and of time.

Mplus needs the data in long format: one row per prompt, with the rows of all persons stacked. The first rows of our data file could look like this:

id day prompt hours er negaff dep_pre dep_post
1 1 1 0 20 80 14 11
1 1 2 2 70 75 14 11
1 1 3 4 -999 -999 14 11
1 1 4 6 40 25 14 11
1 2 1 24 35 50 14 11

In this layout:

  • hours keeps counting across days. Prompt 1 of day 2 is at 24 hours, not 0. Mplus uses this variable to place prompts on a time grid and to recognize gaps, including the night.
  • Missing prompts are coded -999, and the input tells Mplus so with MISSING = ALL(-999);.
  • Person-level variables (dep_pre, dep_post) repeat on every row of the same person. Mplus is told that they only vary between persons.
  • Variable names should be short. We use at most 8 characters, which is safe in every Mplus version.

Hamaker et al. needed one extra step: their raw item ran from unpleasant (negative) to pleasant (positive), so they reversed it with DEFINE: ue_pre = -1*U2P_pre; so that higher scores mean more unpleasant events. Our ER item already runs in the intended direction, so we need no such step.

2.2Estimation settings in the ANALYSIS command

For your researchThe estimation settings below appear in every DSEM input on this tab. Each line is explained so that the settings can be adapted to other models.

DSEM in Mplus always uses Bayesian estimation. Every model on this tab uses a version of this ANALYSIS block:

Mplus input, our ER version
ANALYSIS:  ESTIMATOR = BAYES;   ! Bayesian estimation (required for DSEM)
           PROC = 2;            ! use 2 processors (one per chain)
           BITER = (5000);      ! at least 5000 iterations per chain
           THIN = 10;           ! keep every 10th draw
           BSEED = 9371;        ! starting seed, so the results can be reproduced

What each line does:

  • ESTIMATOR = BAYES requests Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) estimation. Mplus runs two chains by default. Each chain is a long sequence of random draws that should settle into the posterior distribution of the parameters.
  • PROC = 2 runs the two chains in parallel on two processors, which shortens the computation time. Mplus 9.1 produced distorted results in some DSEM models when PROCESSORS exceeded the number of chains. Version 9.1.1 fixed this (Section 13.1 of the "Concepts and models" tab). With two processors and two chains, the problem does not arise.
  • BITER = (5000) sets a minimum number of iterations. Mplus continues beyond it if the chains have not yet converged. The first half of each chain is discarded as burn-in (the warm-up period), and the estimates come from the second halves of both chains. FBITER = 5000 would instead fix the number exactly.
  • THIN = 10 keeps only every 10th draw. Consecutive draws are similar to each other, and thinning reduces this autocorrelation. With THIN = 10, each chain runs 10 × 5000 iterations.
  • BSEED fixes the random starting point, so running the same input again gives the same results.

2.3Convergence checks

For your researchChecks of convergence to run on every DSEM before interpreting or reporting its results.

Mplus can report estimates even when the chains have not converged, so convergence should be checked for every model. The original materials illustrate three checks for Model 0.

Check 1: the PSR (potential scale reduction). Requesting OUTPUT: TECH8; prints the PSR every 100 iterations. The PSR compares the spread of the draws between the two chains with the spread within each chain. If both chains sample from the same distribution, the PSR is close to 1. Mplus reports the largest PSR among all parameters, and which parameter it belongs to:

Original Mplus output from Hamaker et al. (negative affect and unpleasant events)
TECHNICAL 8 OUTPUT

   TECHNICAL 8 OUTPUT FOR BAYES ESTIMATION

     CHAIN    BSEED
     1        6974
     2        534401

                     POTENTIAL       PARAMETER WITH
     ITERATION    SCALE REDUCTION      HIGHEST PSR
     100              1.000               1
     200              1.015               2
     300              1.015               2
     400              1.020               8
     500              1.012               8
   (...)
     2600             1.000               5
     2700             1.000               5
     2800             1.000               2
     2900             1.000               5
     3000             1.000               5

Here the PSR reaches 1.020 at iteration 400 and is 1.000 at the end, which indicates that the two chains agree.

Check 2: trace plots. PLOT: TYPE = PLOT3; makes plots of the draws of each chain over the iterations. When the chains have converged, the trace plots show two overlapping horizontal bands, with no upward or downward trend and no isolated extreme values. The figure in Section 13.3 of the "Concepts and models" tab shows what this looks like.

Check 3: autocorrelation of the draws. The same plot menu shows how strongly each draw resembles the previous draws. These autocorrelations should drop to zero quickly. If they stay high, increase THIN or the number of iterations.

The priors. The output also lists the prior for every parameter. With the Mplus defaults, means get a flat normal prior, N(0,∞), and variances and covariances get an inverse-Wishart prior, here IW(0,−3), which is also non-informative:

Original Mplus output from Hamaker et al. (negative affect and unpleasant events)
     PRIORS FOR ALL PARAMETERS            PRIOR MEAN      PRIOR VARIANCE     PRIOR STD. DEV.

     Parameter 1~IW(0.000,-3)              infinity            infinity            infinity
     Parameter 2~IW(0.000,-3)              infinity            infinity            infinity
     Parameter 3~IW(0.000,-3)              infinity            infinity            infinity
     Parameter 4~N(0.000,infinity)           0.0000            infinity            infinity
     Parameter 5~N(0.000,infinity)           0.0000            infinity            infinity
     Parameter 6~IW(0.000,-3)              infinity            infinity            infinity
     Parameter 7~IW(0.000,-3)              infinity            infinity            infinity
     Parameter 8~IW(0.000,-3)              infinity            infinity            infinity

The parameter numbers match the TECH1 output, which lists the position of each parameter in the model.

3Part 1: Separate models for each person (replicated N = 1)

For your researchEach participant is analyzed separately here. The results show how much people differ in the relation between reappraisal and NA, without assuming that the parameters of different people come from a common distribution.

3.1Fitting one model per person in Mplus

For your researchHow to fit the same model to each participant's data in one Mplus run, and how to read the resulting output.

The most direct way to study within-person dynamics is to fit a time-series model to each person separately and then summarize the results across persons, which is called a replicated N = 1 analysis. Each person's parameters are estimated from that person's data only, with no assumption that different people have similar parameters.

Mplus has no option for fitting a model to each person separately. The facility that Mplus provides for simulation studies can be used instead (Hamaker et al., 2023):

  • Save each person's data in a separate file, for example person001.dat to person150.dat.
  • Make one more file, IDlist.dat, that lists the 150 file names.
  • Tell Mplus that these are Monte Carlo replications. Mplus then fits the model to each file in turn and reports the average results.
Mplus input, our ER version
DATA:      FILE = IDlist.dat;     ! a list of 150 file names, one per person
           TYPE = MONTECARLO;     ! fit the model to each file, then summarize
VARIABLE:  NAMES = id day prompt hours er negaff dep_pre dep_post;
           USEVARIABLES = negaff er;
           MISSING = ALL(-999);
DEFINE:    STANDARDIZE(negaff);   ! standardize within each file,
           STANDARDIZE(er);       ! that is, within each person

Standardizing within each file. Because each file contains one person, STANDARDIZE here standardizes each person's data with that person's own mean and standard deviation. The coefficients then become effect sizes on a common scale for everyone. (The alternative, OUTPUT: STDYX;, standardizes with model-implied variances. For models with lags, the two can differ considerably.)

Reading the output of a replicated analysis. The output has the format of a simulation study, and some of its columns do not apply here:

Column Meaning here
Population Ignore. Only meaningful in a real simulation.
Average The estimate averaged across all persons.
Std. Dev. How much the person-specific estimates differ across persons.
S. E. Average The average posterior standard deviation (uncertainty) of a person's estimate.
M. S. E., 95% Cover Ignore. Only meaningful in a real simulation.
% Sig Coeff The proportion of persons whose 95% credible interval excludes zero.

3.2N = 1 Model 1: NA regressed on ER at the same prompt

For your researchThis model estimates each participant's association between reappraisal and NA at the same prompt, and the spread of these associations across participants.

Question. For a given person, is NA higher or lower at prompts where more reappraisal was reported for the preceding interval?

yt​=ν+βxt​+ζt​

In plain EnglishFor one person: NA at a prompt equals a baseline (ν), plus a weight (β) times the reappraisal reported for the preceding interval, plus a part the model does not explain (ζt​).

Here ν is an intercept, β is the ER → NA coefficient (also called the person's responsiveness, or stress sensitivity when the predictor is events; Hamaker et al., 2023), and ζt​ is the part of NA the model does not explain. There are no lags yet, so the timing of prompts does not matter.

Mplus input, our ER version
MODEL:     negaff ON er;     ! NA now, regressed on ER since the previous prompt
           er;               ! mention ER's variance (see below)
OUTPUT:    TECH1 TECH8;

The line er;. Without it, Mplus treats ER as a fixed predictor, and any prompt with ER missing is dropped entirely. Mentioning its variance brings ER into the model, so prompts with missing ER can still contribute.

Original output (events → NA, averaged over 129 persons):

Original Mplus output from Hamaker et al. (negative affect and unpleasant events)
MODEL RESULTS

                              ESTIMATES              S. E.     M. S. E.  95%  % Sig
                  Population   Average   Std. Dev.   Average             Cover Coeff

NA_PRE     ON
  UE_PRE              0.000     0.3040     0.1735     0.1487     0.1222 0.496 0.504

Means
  UE_PRE              0.000     0.0016     0.0122     0.1586     0.0002 1.000 0.000

Intercepts
  NA_PRE              0.000     0.0013     0.0073     0.1477     0.0001 1.000 0.000

Variances
  UE_PRE              0.500     1.0936     0.0287     0.2617     0.3531 0.000 1.000

Residual Variances
  NA_PRE              0.500     0.9760     0.1178     0.2329     0.2404 0.062 1.000

Interpretation. The standardized coefficient from unpleasant events to NA averages 0.30 across persons, with a standard deviation of 0.17 across persons, so people differ considerably. For about half of the persons (0.504), the credible interval excludes zero.

3.3N = 1 Model 2: Adding NA inertia

For your researchThis model adds NA inertia (the carryover of NA from one prompt to the next) and shows whether each person's reappraisal-NA association changes when inertia is included.

Question. Does NA carry over from one prompt to the next, and does the ER → NA coefficient change once that carryover is taken into account?

yt​=ν+βxt​+ϕyt−1​+ζt​

In plain EnglishThe same, plus NA carried over from the previous prompt with weight ϕ (the inertia).

The new parameter ϕ is NA inertia. Because the model now includes a lagged variable, the input needs two additional lines:

Mplus input, our ER version
VARIABLE:  ...
           LAGGED = negaff(1);      ! create negaff&1, NA at the previous grid point
           TINTERVAL = hours(2);    ! place prompts on a 2-hour grid
MODEL:     negaff ON negaff&1;      ! inertia
           negaff ON er;            ! ER -> NA
           er;
  • LAGGED = negaff(1); creates a new variable, negaff&1: NA one grid step earlier.
  • TINTERVAL = hours(2); places each prompt in a 2-hour slot and inserts empty slots wherever no prompt fell, for example overnight. Each lag then always means "two hours earlier." Hamaker et al. used a 1-hour grid because their beeps came at random times within 90-minute blocks. Our prompts are fixed every 2 hours, so a 2-hour grid fits exactly. Because the grid runs through the night, the model also applies the same dynamics across each night, as seven two-hour steps. Section 14.2 of the "Concepts and models" tab discusses the alternatives. (Section 10.8 of that tab explains how the empty slots are handled.)

Original output:

Original Mplus output from Hamaker et al. (negative affect and unpleasant events)
MODEL RESULTS

                               ESTIMATES              S. E.     M. S. E.  95%  % Sig
                  Population   Average   Std. Dev.   Average             Cover Coeff

NA_PRE     ON
  NA_PRE&1            0.000     0.3620     0.2764     0.1693     0.2069 0.504 0.496
  UE_PRE              0.000     0.2668     0.1614     0.1410     0.0970 0.496 0.504

Means
  UE_PRE              0.000     0.0025     0.0187     0.1572     0.0004 1.000 0.000

Intercepts

Interpretation. Average NA inertia is 0.36, and the events → NA coefficient drops from 0.30 to 0.27 once inertia is included. Both vary widely across persons (standard deviations 0.28 and 0.16), and the credible interval of each excludes zero for about half of the persons.

3.4N = 1 Model 3: ER and NA as two outcomes

For your researchThis model estimates both directions for each person: reappraisal predicting NA, and NA predicting later reappraisal (for example, whether high NA is followed by more reappraisal).

Question. Does earlier NA also predict later ER? With ER as a second outcome, the model becomes a bivariate system:

yt​xt​​=νy​+ϕy​yt−1​+βy​xt​+ζyt​=νx​+ϕx​xt−1​+βx​yt−1​+ζxt​​

In plain EnglishTwo equations for one person. NA is predicted by its own previous value and by the reappraisal reported at the same prompt (which refers to the interval since the previous prompt). Reappraisal is predicted by its own previous value and by NA at the previous prompt.

Mplus input, our ER version
VARIABLE:  ...
           LAGGED = negaff(1) er(1);
           TINTERVAL = hours(2);
MODEL:     negaff ON negaff&1;      ! NA inertia          (phi_y)
           negaff ON er;            ! ER -> NA            (beta_y)
           er ON er&1;              ! ER autoregression   (phi_x)
           er ON negaff&1;          ! earlier NA -> ER    (beta_x)

This is close to a VAR(1) model (Section 7.4 of the "Concepts and models" tab), with one difference. Because NA is regressed on ER at the same prompt, the two residuals cannot also be allowed to correlate: the model would not be identified.

Original output:

Original Mplus output from Hamaker et al. (negative affect and unpleasant events)
MODEL RESULTS

  NA_PRE&1            0.000     0.3638     0.2780     0.1762     0.2090 0.504 0.496
  UE_PRE              0.000     0.2496     0.1740     0.1547     0.0923 0.620 0.380

 UE_PRE     ON
  UE_PRE&1            0.000     0.0375     0.2321     0.2064     0.0548 0.938 0.062
  NA_PRE&1            0.000     0.1007     0.2414     0.2151     0.0680 0.876 0.124

  UE_PRE              0.000     0.0056     0.0372     0.1551     0.0014 1.000 0.000

  NA_PRE              0.500     0.7404     0.2253     0.1927     0.1082 0.442 1.000
  UE_PRE              0.500     0.9537     0.1220     0.2494     0.2206 0.163 1.000

Interpretation. For NA, both inertia (0.36 on average) and the effect of events (0.25) have credible intervals that exclude zero for many persons (49.6% and 38.0%). For events, there is little carryover (0.04 on average, with an interval excluding zero for only 6.2% of persons) and only some spillover from earlier NA (0.10; 12.4% of persons). About three times as many persons showed an effect of events on NA as showed the reverse (Hamaker et al., 2023).

3.5Limitations of separate per-person models

For your researchSeparate per-person models cannot relate the person-specific parameters to each other or to person-level variables. The multilevel models in Part 2 can.

The replicated N = 1 approach shows how much people differ. It cannot answer questions such as "do people with more inertia also react more strongly to events?" or "does depression predict inertia?" because the per-person results are not combined in one model. Each person's estimates are also based on that person's data only, which makes them imprecise (Hamaker et al.'s participants answered at most 60 beeps each). The multilevel models in Part 2 address both limitations.

In addition, in typical ESM datasets, person-specific VAR(1) models predicted new data less accurately than multilevel VAR(1) models (Bulteel et al., 2018, as described by Lafit, 2026a, p. 216).

4Part 2: Multilevel models for all persons

For your researchA multilevel model for all persons estimates the average dynamics, how much people differ in them, and how these differences relate to each other and to depression.

4.1Within-person and between-person parts

For your researchHow the multilevel model splits each person's NA and reappraisal into a person mean and momentary deviations, and which Mplus lines specify this.

Instead of 150 separate analyses, one model is now fitted to all persons. Every observed score is split into two parts:

yit​=yit(w)​+yi(b)​,xit​=xit(w)​+xi(b)​.

In plain EnglishEach person's NA (y) and reappraisal (x) at a prompt equal their usual level (between part, b) plus their deviation at that prompt (within part, w).

  • The between part yi(b)​ is person i's own mean: a latent variable, estimated inside the model (latent centering).
  • The within part yit(w)​ is the deviation from that mean at prompt t. The time-series model is written for these within parts.

The input changes as follows:

Mplus input, our ER version
DATA:      FILE = ema.dat;          ! one long file with all persons
VARIABLE:  NAMES = id day prompt hours er negaff dep_pre dep_post;
           USEVARIABLES = negaff er;
           CLUSTER = id;            ! rows with the same id belong to one person
           MISSING = ALL(-999);
ANALYSIS:  TYPE = TWOLEVEL;         ! split every variable into within and between
           ESTIMATOR = BAYES;
           PROC = 2;
           BITER = (3000);
           BSEED = 6974;
           THIN = 5;
PLOT:      TYPE = PLOT3;            ! trace plots, posterior plots, autocorrelations
  • CLUSTER = id tells Mplus which rows belong to the same person.
  • TYPE = TWOLEVEL splits each variable into its within and between parts. The model then has a %WITHIN% part and a %BETWEEN% part.
  • STANDARDIZE is removed from DEFINE. In one file with everyone, STANDARDIZE would use the total variance, which mixes within and between variation. Instead, Mplus standardizes each person's coefficients with that person's own within-person variance (Section 13.3 of the "Concepts and models" tab).

Adding FACTORS = ALL (500); to the PLOT command makes Mplus run 500 × 100 extra iterations and save every 100th draw of every person's random effects. The person-specific plots and rankings below are based on these saved draws.

4.2Model 0: Intraclass correlations

For your researchThis is usually the first model to run. It shows how much of the variance in NA and in reappraisal reflects stable differences between people, and therefore how much within-person variance is available for studying dynamics.

Question. What share of the variance in NA, and in ER, comes from stable differences between people? This share is the intraclass correlation (ICC):

ICCy​=var(y(b))+var(y(w))var(y(b))​.

In plain EnglishThe share of NA's total variation that comes from stable differences between people.

Model 0 is an "empty" model: no regressions, only variances and covariances at each level. Giving the variances labels lets us compute the ICCs inside the model:

Mplus input, our ER version
MODEL:     %WITHIN%
           negaff WITH er;
           negaff (wv_na);          ! label the within-person variances
           er (wv_er);
           %BETWEEN%
           negaff WITH er;
           negaff (bv_na);          ! label the between-person variances
           er (bv_er);
MODEL CONSTRAINT:
           NEW (icc_na); icc_na = bv_na/(bv_na + wv_na);
           NEW (icc_er); icc_er = bv_er/(bv_er + wv_er);

MODEL CONSTRAINT does not constrain anything here. It computes a new quantity from the labeled parameters at every MCMC iteration, so the ICC gets its own posterior distribution and credible interval.

Original output:

Original Mplus output from Hamaker et al. (negative affect and unpleasant events)
MODEL RESULTS

                                Posterior  One-Tailed         95% C.I.
                    Estimate       S.D.      P-Value   Lower 2.5%  Upper 2.5%  Significance

Within Level

 NA_PRE   WITH
    UE_PRE             0.415       0.019      0.000       0.378       0.452      *

 Variances
    NA_PRE             0.682       0.012      0.000       0.659       0.707      *
    UE_PRE             2.842       0.052      0.000       2.742       2.945      *

Between Level

 NA_PRE   WITH
    UE_PRE             0.171       0.045      0.000       0.090       0.266      *

 Means
    NA_PRE             2.068       0.067      0.000       1.936       2.200      *
    UE_PRE            -1.246       0.052      0.000      -1.346      -1.144      *

    NA_PRE             0.569       0.077      0.000       0.443       0.742      *
    UE_PRE             0.287       0.047      0.000       0.213       0.392      *

New/Additional Parameters
    ICC_NA             0.455       0.033      0.000       0.392       0.523      *
    ICC_UE             0.092       0.014      0.000       0.070       0.121      *

Interpretation. About 46% of the variance in NA (0.455) lies between persons, but only about 9% of the variance in unpleasant events (0.092). Events mostly vary from moment to moment, whereas NA also has a large stable, trait-like component. A credible interval for a variance or an ICC can never include zero, because these quantities cannot be negative. An interval that excludes zero is therefore not evidence that the ICC is above zero. Look at how close the lower bound is to zero instead.

For comparison, ICCs between 0.2 and 0.4 are typical in ESM studies (Bolger & Laurenceau, 2013, as cited in Eisele et al., 2026, p. 91). NA in Hamaker et al.'s sample lies above that range, and events below it.

4.3Model 1: Fixed within-person effects

For your researchThis model estimates the dynamics under the assumption that all persons have the same within-person parameters. It serves as a baseline and is rarely the final model.

Question. On average, how strong are NA inertia, ER → NA, ER autoregression, and NA → later ER, if we assume that everyone has the same values?

At the within level, the Model 3 time series from Part 1 is now written for the within parts:

xit(w)​yit(w)​​=ϕx​xi,t−1(w)​+βx​yi,t−1(w)​+ζxit​=ϕy​yi,t−1(w)​+βy​xit(w)​+ζyit​​

In plain EnglishWithin each person: reappraisal is predicted by its own previous value and by previous NA. NA is predicted by its own previous value and by the reappraisal reported at the same prompt (which refers to the preceding interval).

At the between level there are only the two person means, which may correlate. All four slopes and both residual variances are fixed, that is, the same for everyone.

Mplus input, our ER version
VARIABLE:  ...
           LAGGED = negaff(1) er(1);
           TINTERVAL = hours(2);
MODEL:     %WITHIN%
           negaff ON negaff&1;      ! NA inertia
           negaff ON er;            ! ER -> NA (same prompt, implicit lag)
           er ON er&1;              ! ER autoregression
           er ON negaff&1;          ! earlier NA -> ER
           %BETWEEN%
           negaff WITH er;          ! person means may correlate

The between-person model is:

NAi(b)​=2.06+uNA,i​,var=0.56;UEi(b)​=−1.26+uUE,i​,var=0.27;cov=0.16.

In plain EnglishThe average person's mean NA is 2.06 and their mean events score is −1.26. People differ around these averages, and the two person means go together across people.

Interpretation of the standardized output.

  • Inertia hardly changes with standardization (0.534 in both), because its predictor and outcome are the same variable.
  • The events → NA slope becomes 0.221 and the NA → events slope 0.108: in effect-size terms, events predict NA about twice as strongly as NA predicts later events.
  • The between-level correlation of 0.405 means that people with higher average NA also rate their events as more unpleasant on average.
  • The R-square shows that, within persons, 37% of the variance in NA is predicted by the model, but only about 5% of the variance in events.

Model 1 is very restrictive: everyone is assumed to have the same dynamics and the same sensitivity to events. Part 1 showed that this assumption does not hold, and the following models drop it.

4.4Model 2: Random within-person effects

For your researchThis model is the basic DSEM for an emotion regulation study. For each dynamic parameter, it estimates the average across persons and the variance between persons. It also estimates the correlations between the person-specific parameters, for example whether people with higher NA inertia also have a stronger association between reappraisal and NA.

Question. How much do people differ in their inertia, their ER → NA slope, their ER autoregression, their NA → ER slope, and the size of their unexplained fluctuations, and how are these person-specific parameters related to each other?

Every slope and both residual variances now become random effects, with a separate value for each person. Together with the two person means, each person has eight random effects. At the between level they come from one multivariate normal distribution, and all of them may correlate. The residual variances enter the between level on the log scale, which keeps them positive when transformed back.

Mplus input, our ER version
ANALYSIS:  TYPE = TWOLEVEL RANDOM;  ! RANDOM allows random slopes and variances
           ...
MODEL:     %WITHIN%
           phi_na | negaff ON negaff&1;   ! each person's NA inertia
           b_na   | negaff ON er;         ! each person's ER -> NA slope
           phi_er | er ON er&1;           ! each person's ER autoregression
           b_er   | er ON negaff&1;       ! each person's NA -> later ER slope
           psi_na | negaff;               ! each person's NA residual variance
           psi_er | er;                   ! each person's ER residual variance
           %BETWEEN%
           negaff er phi_na-psi_er WITH er phi_na-psi_er;   ! all may correlate
OUTPUT:    TECH1 TECH8 STDYX FSCOMPARISON STAND(CLUSTER);
PLOT:      TYPE = PLOT3;
           FACTORS = ALL (500);
  • The vertical bar | makes a parameter random. The name on its left (for example phi_na) is the random effect, which then exists as a latent variable at the between level.
  • phi_na-psi_er is shorthand for all random effects from phi_na to psi_er, in the order they were defined.
  • STDYX gives standardized results; STAND(CLUSTER) gives them separately for each person; FSCOMPARISON ranks persons on each random effect (this needs FACTORS = ALL (500)).

Warning about autoregressions above 1. With random inertia, some MCMC draws for some persons have an autoregression above 1, which describes a process whose deviations do not decay. Mplus excludes these draws when computing standardized estimates and prints a warning that lists the persons concerned:

Original Mplus output from Hamaker et al. (negative affect and unpleasant events)
    WARNING: PROBLEMS OCCURRED IN SEVERAL ITERATIONS IN THE COMPUTATION OF THE STANDARDIZED
    ESTIMATES FOR SEVERAL CLUSTERS. THIS IS MOST LIKELY DUE TO AR COEFFICIENTS GREATER
    THAN 1 OR PARAMETERS GIVING NON-STATIONARY MODELS. SUCH POSTERIOR DRAWS ARE REMOVED.
    THE FOLLOWING CLUSTERS HAD SUCH PROBLEMS:
      120 66 39 134 116 144 28 117 3 141

This warning is common and usually does not change the results. To check, inspect these persons' data and individual posterior distributions, or rerun the model without them and compare the results.

Interpretation.

  • All parameters are at the between level. Because every within-level parameter is random, the output lists 8 means (the averages of the random effects), 8 variances (how much people differ), and 8×7/2=28 covariances.
  • The Means describe the average person. Average NA inertia is 0.470, and the average events → NA slope is 0.111.
  • Log variances need back-transforming. The mean log residual variance of NA is −1.160, so the typical residual variance is e−1.160=0.31.
  • The variances describe differences between persons. The variance of inertia is 0.051, a standard deviation of about 0.051​=0.23. Because inertia mostly lies between 0 and 1, this is a large difference between persons.

The standardized results come in two parts. At the within level, each person's coefficients are standardized with that person's own variances and then averaged:

4.5Model 3: Baseline depression as a predictor of the random effects

For your researchThis model applies when a person-level variable, here baseline depression, is the predictor of interest. It shows which daily dynamics differ between more and less depressed people.

Question. Do people who were more depressed before the EMA period have higher mean NA, stronger NA inertia, a different ER → NA slope, or larger NA fluctuations?

The within level is the same as in Model 2. At the between level, all eight random effects are regressed on the person-level predictor Pi​ (baseline depression). For example, for NA inertia:

ϕyi​=γy10​+γy11​Pi​+uy1i​.

In plain EnglishEach person's NA inertia equals the inertia expected for a person with Pi​=0 (γy10​), plus a shift of γy11​ for each unit of baseline depression (Pi​), plus the person's own deviation (uy1i​).

Mplus input, our ER version
VARIABLE:  ...
           USEVARIABLES = negaff er dep_pre;
           BETWEEN = dep_pre;               ! dep_pre only varies between persons
DEFINE:    STANDARDIZE(dep_pre);            ! so 0 = average baseline depression
MODEL:     %WITHIN%
           ...                              ! as in Model 2
           %BETWEEN%
           negaff er phi_na-psi_er ON dep_pre;

Standardizing dep_pre. After standardization, Pi​=0 is the average person, so each intercept γ is the average random effect: the expected value for a person with average baseline depression.

By default, Mplus also lets the residuals of the two person means (negaff and er) correlate at the between level. The other residuals are uncorrelated unless you add WITH statements.

Original output (Hamaker et al.'s random effects are named PHI_NA, BETA_NA, PHI_UE, BETA_UE, PSI_NA, PSI_UE; the predictor is HAM_PRE):

People with higher baseline depression have higher mean NA (0.303) and rate their events as more unpleasant on average (0.114). They also react more strongly to events (BETA_NA, 0.020), have larger unexplained NA fluctuations (PSI_NA, 0.415), and their NA spills over less into events (BETA_UE, −0.086). The credible interval for the effect of baseline depression on NA inertia includes zero (PHI_NA, −0.013, interval from −0.057 to 0.032).

4.6Model 4: A common factor for the random effects

For your researchThis model applies when several person-specific parameters are expected to reflect one underlying trait, so that one factor can summarize them.

Question. Do the eight person-specific parameters share a common dimension Ci​, such as a general vulnerability?

This is a factor model at the between level, with the eight random effects as the indicators:

ϕyi​=γy10​+γy11​Ci​+uy1i​(and similarly for the other seven).

In plain EnglishEach person-specific feature, such as inertia, partly reflects one shared underlying dimension, Ci​.

Mplus input, our ER version
MODEL:     %WITHIN%
           ...                                   ! as in Model 2
           %BETWEEN%
           c BY negaff@1 er phi_na-psi_er*.1;    ! one factor for all eight

negaff@1 fixes the first loading to 1 to give the factor a scale (the usual Mplus default does not work here), and *.1 gives starting values to the other loadings.

Interpretation. Four of the eight indicators have loadings whose 95% credible intervals exclude zero. The strongest are the person's mean NA (standardized loading 0.856), their NA residual variance (0.804), and their events → NA slope (0.757). The common factor can therefore be interpreted as a general "negative affect reactivity" dimension: people with high scores have higher mean NA, react more strongly to events, and have larger unexplained NA fluctuations.

4.7Model 5: Mediation through each random effect

For your researchThis model, with eight mediators, could not be estimated reliably from the data of 129 participants. Its output shows the typical signs of a model that is too complex for the data.

Question. Does baseline depression predict later depression through the person-specific parameters? For example: depression before → stronger NA inertia → depression after.

The model adds the person-level outcome Oi​ (later depression) and regresses it on the baseline score and on all eight random effects. Each indirect effect is the product of two paths, computed in MODEL CONSTRAINT:

Mplus input, our ER version
VARIABLE:  ...
           USEVARIABLES = negaff er dep_pre dep_post;
           BETWEEN = dep_pre dep_post;
MODEL:     %WITHIN%
           ...                                           ! as in Model 2
           %BETWEEN%
           negaff er phi_na-psi_er ON dep_pre (a1-a8);   ! a paths
           dep_post ON dep_pre;                          ! direct path
           dep_post ON negaff er phi_na-psi_er (b1-b8);  ! b paths
MODEL CONSTRAINT:
           NEW (i_mn_na);   i_mn_na   = a1*b1;   ! through mean NA
           NEW (i_mn_er);   i_mn_er   = a2*b2;   ! through mean ER
           NEW (i_phi_na);  i_phi_na  = a3*b3;   ! through NA inertia
           NEW (i_b_na);    i_b_na    = a4*b4;   ! through ER -> NA slope
           NEW (i_phi_er);  i_phi_er  = a5*b5;   ! through ER autoregression
           NEW (i_b_er);    i_b_er    = a6*b6;   ! through NA -> ER slope
           NEW (i_psi_na);  i_psi_na  = a7*b7;   ! through NA residual variance
           NEW (i_psi_er);  i_psi_er  = a8*b8;   ! through ER residual variance

4.8Model 6: Mediation through the common factor

For your researchA simpler test of whether daily dynamics mediate the association between earlier and later depression, with one common factor as the mediator.

Question. Does baseline depression predict later depression through the common factor of Model 4?

Ci​=τ3​Pi​+ϵCi​,Oi​=τ0​+τ1​Pi​+τ2​Ci​+ϵOi​.

In plain EnglishThe shared dimension is predicted by baseline depression (Pi​), and later depression (Oi​) is predicted by baseline depression and by the shared dimension. The indirect route is the product of the two paths.

The direct effect is τ1​, and the indirect effect is τ3​×τ2​.

Mplus input, our ER version
MODEL:     %WITHIN%
           ...                                  ! as in Model 2
           %BETWEEN%
           c BY negaff@1 er phi_na-psi_er*.1;   ! common factor (as in Model 4)
           c ON dep_pre (a);                    ! a path
           dep_post ON c (b);                   ! b path
           dep_post ON dep_pre (d);             ! direct path
MODEL CONSTRAINT:
           NEW (indirect); indirect = a*b;      ! indirect effect through c

(Our input writes the three paths on separate lines. The original input labeled the first path s but then computed a*b. See Section 6.)

4.9Comparison of estimates across models

For your researchThe average within-person estimates change little across the multilevel models.

The averaged, standardized within-person estimates are very stable across Models 1, 2, and 3 (Hamaker et al., 2023, Table 31.3). The largest change is in NA inertia: 0.534 when everyone must share one value (Model 1), and about 0.47 once it may differ between persons. The figure compares these with the per-person averages from Part 1.

5Part 3: Pretest-posttest design with an intervention

For your researchThis part tests whether an intervention, such as an emotion regulation training, changed people's daily dynamics: their mean NA, their NA inertia, and the association between reappraisal and NA.

5.1Design

For your researchThe design has one EMA period before and one after the training, and a randomized control group.

In Hamaker et al.'s study, the EMA period of Parts 1 and 2 was only the first of two. After it, participants were randomly assigned to a mindfulness training or a control group, and then completed a second EMA period. Our version compares an ER training with a control group, with an EMA burst before and after.

The question is whether the training changed the dynamics of people's NA as well as its level. The parameters of interest are the changes in:

  • mean NA, Δyi(b)​=y2i(b)​−y1i(b)​,
  • NA inertia, Δϕi​=ϕ2i​−ϕ1i​,
  • the ER → NA slope, Δβi​=β2i​−β1i​,
  • the size of the unexplained NA fluctuations, Δlog(ψi​)=log(ψ2i​)−log(ψ1i​),
  • mean ER, Δxi(b)​=x2i(b)​−x1i(b)​.

5.2Data layout for two EMA periods

For your researchHow to arrange the data so that each person has separate parameters for the period before and the period after the training.

Each EMA period gets its own columns. Measures from the first period go into na_pre and er_pre, and are missing during the second period. Measures from the second period go into na_post and er_post, and are missing during the first. The rows stay in long format. Each variable is then split into its own within and between parts, so each person gets a separate mean, inertia, slope, and residual variance for each period.

5.3Model for initial differences, time effects, and treatment effects

For your researchThe model separates initial group differences, change in the control group, and the additional change in the training group.

At the within level, each period has its own random parameters:

y1it(w)​y2it(w)​​=ϕ1i​y1i,t−1(w)​+β1i​x1it(w)​+ζ1it​=ϕ2i​y2i,t−1(w)​+β2i​x2it(w)​+ζ2it​​

In plain EnglishBefore (1) and after (2) the training, each person has their own inertia and their own reappraisal-to-NA link.

At the between level, each period-1 parameter and each change is regressed on the group dummy Gi​ (1 = training, 0 = control). For NA inertia:

ϕ1i​=γ10​+γ11​Gi​+u1i​,Δϕi​=γ60​+γ61​Gi​+u6i​.

In plain EnglishInertia before the training may differ between groups (γ11​). The change in inertia has a part shared by everyone (γ60​, the time effect) and an extra part for the training group (γ61​, the treatment effect).

The coefficients correspond to the following questions:

  • γ11​ (and the other period-1 slopes): were the groups different before the training? With random assignment, these differences are zero in expectation, so any difference in the sample is due to chance.
  • γ60​ (and the other change intercepts): did the control group change over time? This is a time effect.
  • γ61​ (and the other change slopes): did the training group change more? This is the treatment effect.

Fixing a coefficient at 1. Mplus cannot regress a difference between two random effects on a predictor, but the change equation can be rewritten as a regression of the period-2 effect on the period-1 effect:

ϕ2i​−ϕ1i​=γ60​+γ61​Gi​+u6i​⟺ϕ2i​=γ60​+γ61​Gi​+1⋅ϕ1i​+u6i​.

In plain EnglishSaying "the change equals something" is the same as saying "the after-value equals the before-value plus that something." Mplus can estimate the second form.

Regressing the period-2 effect on the period-1 effect, with that coefficient fixed at 1, and on the group dummy is therefore equivalent to the change model.

5.4Mplus input

For your researchThe Mplus input for the pretest-posttest model. The DATA and OUTPUT commands must be added.

Mplus input, our ER version
VARIABLE:  NAMES = id day prompt hours er_pre na_pre er_post na_post group;
           USEVARIABLES = na_pre na_post er_pre er_post group;
           CLUSTER = id;
           BETWEEN = group;                 ! 1 = ER training, 0 = control
           LAGGED = na_pre(1) na_post(1);
           TINTERVAL = hours(2);
           MISSING = ALL(-999);
ANALYSIS:  TYPE = TWOLEVEL RANDOM;
           ESTIMATOR = BAYES;
           PROC = 2;
           BITER = (3000);
           BSEED = 8386;
           THIN = 5;
MODEL:     %WITHIN%
           phi_pre  | na_pre ON na_pre&1;      ! inertia, before
           b_pre    | na_pre ON er_pre;        ! ER -> NA, before
           psi_pre  | na_pre;                  ! residual variance, before
           phi_post | na_post ON na_post&1;    ! inertia, after
           b_post   | na_post ON er_post;      ! ER -> NA, after
           psi_post | na_post;                 ! residual variance, after
           er_pre WITH er_post@0;           ! never observed at the same prompt
           %BETWEEN%
           na_pre er_pre phi_pre b_pre psi_pre ON group;      ! initial differences
           na_post ON na_pre@1 group;                         ! change in mean NA
           er_post ON er_pre@1 group;                         ! change in mean ER
           phi_post ON phi_pre@1 group;                       ! change in inertia
           b_post ON b_pre@1 group;                           ! change in ER -> NA
           psi_post ON psi_pre@1 group;                       ! change in log residual variance

The line er_pre WITH er_post@0. At any prompt, one of the two is always missing, so their covariance cannot be estimated. Fixing it at zero prevents Mplus from attempting to estimate it. The NA variables need no such line, because their residual variances are random (|), and random residual variances are by definition uncorrelated with other components.

Interpretation (Hamaker et al.'s study, with mindfulness training and unpleasant events):

  • No clear initial differences. The credible intervals for all group differences in the period-1 effects include zero (for example inertia, 0.079, interval −0.005 to 0.159), so the groups were similar at baseline on these parameters. This similarity describes the present sample only. It does not test whether the randomization was carried out correctly, which depends on how participants were allocated.
  • Three treatment effects. Compared with the control group, the trained group's mean NA fell more (γ51​=−0.286), their mean unpleasantness of events fell more (γ91​=−0.264), and their NA inertia fell more (γ61​=−0.132). In plain terms, compared with the control group, the trained group showed larger decreases in NA, in how unpleasant they rated events, and in how much departures from their usual NA level carried over from one prompt to the next. The last point is a change in a model coefficient. Under the fitted model, it means that NA deviations faded faster after the training, but it is not a direct measurement of how quickly people recovered from particular bad moods.
  • One time effect. The intercept for the change in the log residual variance of NA is −0.267 (γ80​): in the control group, unexplained NA fluctuations became smaller over time, and the change in the trained group did not differ from it (−0.240, interval −0.574 to 0.116).
  • A caveat about the inertia effect. The baseline group difference in inertia (0.079) is the one closest to excluding zero, and inertia is also a parameter with a treatment effect. Because the model analyzes change, a group that starts slightly higher by chance can show a larger decrease partly through regression toward the mean. A common check in randomized trials is to regress the period-2 parameter on group while controlling for the period-1 parameter (an ANCOVA-type model). This check was not part of the original analysis.

6Corrections to the original materials

For your researchSmall errors that we found in the original materials, listed for readers who compare this tab with the original website.

While checking every number against the output, we found a few small errors in the original website and chapter. Most are typographical, and item 7 concerns an interpretation.

  1. Multilevel Model 1, between-level equations (website). The text writes UEi(b)​=2.06 and NAi(b)​=−1.26. The output shows the reverse: the mean of NA is 2.061 and the mean of events is −1.255. Section 4.3 above uses the correct labels. The within-level residual variance of NA is also given as 0.46, while the output shows 0.445.
  2. Multilevel Model 6, input (website). The paths are labeled c ON ham_pre (s); and ham_post ON c ham_pre (b d);, but the indirect effect is computed as indirect = a*b, with an a that was never defined. The intended product is the path from baseline depression to the factor times the path from the factor to later depression. Section 4.8 above labels the paths separately.
  3. Multilevel Model 5, equation (website, and Table 31.2 in the chapter). The last two terms are written τ8​log(ψxi​)+τ9​log(ψxi​). The second should be log(ψyi​).
  4. Multilevel Model 5, input (website). The line ham_post ON ham_pre; appears on the same line as the comment above it, which in Mplus would turn it into part of the comment. The output shows that the direct path was estimated, so this is a formatting problem on the page only.
  5. Pretest-posttest model (website). In the list of changes, the change in residual variance is written Δϕi​ and the change in mean events Δψi​. They should be Δlog(ψi​) and Δxi(b)​. The two within-level equations both use ζxit​, although both are residuals of NA. And x1it(b)​ carries a time subscript, although between parts do not vary over time. Table 31.4 in the chapter shares the last two slips (ζxit​ in Equation 1, and x1it(b)​ and Δxit(b)​ in Equations 6 and 12).
  6. Pretest-posttest model (chapter text). The time effect on the log residual variance of NA is called γ90​. In Table 31.4 and on the website, it is γ80​.
  7. Multilevel Model 5, interpretation (website). The text says there is evidence for an effect of baseline depression on later depression, but in the Model 5 output the credible interval of that path includes zero (−0.035 to 1.541). Only its one-tailed p-value (0.028) is below 0.05.
  8. Table 31.1 (chapter) versus website output. For N = 1 Model 1, the chapter reports an average of 0.307, with credible intervals excluding zero for 52.7% of persons, whereas the website output shows 0.304 and 50.4%. For Model 3, the chapter gives the standard deviation of the inertia estimates as 0.174, whereas the website output shows 0.278. The differences are small and may come from different runs. This tab shows the website output.

7Mplus keywords used in this walkthrough

For your researchThe Mplus keywords used on this tab, with their function.

Keyword What it does
CLUSTER = id; Rows with the same id belong to the same person
BETWEEN = dep_pre; The variable only varies between persons
LAGGED = negaff(1); Creates negaff&1, the value one grid step earlier
TINTERVAL = hours(2); Places observations on a 2-hour grid and inserts missing rows in empty slots
TYPE = TWOLEVEL; Splits variables into within and between parts
TYPE = TWOLEVEL RANDOM; Also allows random slopes and random residual variances
name | y ON x; A random slope called name
name | y; A random residual variance called name (log scale at the between level)
y ON x (a); Labels a parameter a so it can be used in MODEL CONSTRAINT
MODEL CONSTRAINT: NEW (ab); ab = a*b; Computes a new quantity, with its own posterior, at every iteration
c BY y1@1 y2 y3; A factor c, with the first loading fixed at 1
y2 ON y1@1 g; Regression with the coefficient of y1 fixed at 1 (used for change models)
ESTIMATOR = BAYES; Bayesian MCMC estimation
BITER = (5000); / FBITER = 5000; Minimum / fixed number of iterations per chain
THIN = 10; Keep every 10th draw
BSEED = 9371; Reproducible random seed
TYPE = MONTECARLO; (in DATA) Treats a list of files as replications; used here to analyze persons one by one
STANDARDIZE(x); (in DEFINE) Standardizes x (within each file for Monte Carlo data)
OUTPUT: TECH8; Prints the PSR convergence history
OUTPUT: STDYX STAND(CLUSTER) FSCOMPARISON; Standardized results; per-person results; rankings of persons
PLOT: TYPE = PLOT3; FACTORS = ALL (500); Diagnostic plots; saves draws of each person's random effects

Investigating heterogeneity with DSEM

Under construction

This tab is still under construction. It will cover how to use DSEM to investigate different forms of heterogeneity in the population.

Heterogeneity here means that people in the population differ from one another, not only in their average levels of reappraisal or negative affect, but also in their dynamics: for example, in how strongly reappraisal at one prompt predicts negative affect at the next.
